title: VLAMotor: Test-Guided Enhancement of Vision-Language-Action Models via Agent-BasedData Synthesis
summary:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models follow a data-driven paradigm and are constrained by the coverage of training data, making them prone to failure on edge-case configurations after deployment. To mitigate such risks, it is essential to expose high-quality failure modes and convert the resulting failures into supervisory data for model enhancement. Existing studies largely stop at failure detection and lack a mechanism for leveraging discovered failures for model repair.
  We propose VLAMotor, the first analysis framework for VLA enhancement, which integrates distance-aware model testing for failure exposure and agent-based data synthesis for model finetunning. First, VLAMotor estimates input uncertainty based on the distance to training samples, and combines uncertainty ranking with redundancy elimination to build compact test sets that expose diverse failures. Then, VLAMotor abstracts failure trajectories into structured semantic representations, and plans parameterized repair-skill sequences, which are then realized as executable trajectories through inverse kinematics and motion execution. The resulting successful trajectories are automatically labeled and used to fine-tune the original VLA model, yielding an enhanced VLA model. Evaluation on four representative robotic manipulation tasks shows that 92.33% of the in-simulation test cases generated by VLAMotor trigger VLA failures, and VLAMotor improves test coverage over the state-of-the-art tool by 18.93%. By fine-tuning VLA models with synthetic data derived from failed test cases, VLAMotor further enhances the overall success rate of VLA models by 49.25%. When deployed on real hardware, the simulation-enhanced models improve the success rate over the original VLA models by 57.50%, demonstrating an effective and low-cost direction for VLA enhancement.

AI.tldr: VLAMotor is the first analysis framework for VLA model enhancement that exposes failures via distance-aware testing and repairs models via agent-based synthetic data finetuning, achieving 92.33% failure-triggering test cases and 49.25% success rate improvement in simulation, with 57.50% real-world hardware improvement.
AI.motivation: VLA models are constrained by training data coverage and fail on edge cases after deployment; existing studies stop at failure detection and lack mechanisms to leverage failures for model repair.
AI.method: VLAMotor uses distance-aware model testing (uncertainty ranking + redundancy elimination) to expose diverse failures, then abstracts failure trajectories into structured semantic representations, plans parameterized repair-skill sequences, and generates executable successful trajectories via inverse kinematics and motion execution for automatic labeling and finetuning.
AI.result: 92.33% of in-simulation test cases trigger VLA failures; 18.93% improvement in test coverage over SOTA; 49.25% improvement in overall success rate via synthetic data finetuning; 57.50% success rate improvement on real hardware deployment.
AI.conclusion: VLAMotor provides an effective and low-cost direction for VLA enhancement by closing the loop from failure exposure to model repair via synthetic data generation.

title: From Human Videos to Robot Manipulation: A Survey on Scalable Vision-Language-Action Learning with Human-Centric Data
comment: Accepted to IJCAI 2026 Survey Track. Project page: https://aaronfengzy.github.io/HumanCentricToVLA-Survey/
summary: Recent progress in generalizable embodied control has been driven by large-scale pretraining of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. However, most existing approaches rely on large collections of robot demonstrations, which are costly to obtain and tightly coupled to specific embodiments. Human videos, by contrast, are abundant and capture rich interactions, providing diverse semantic and physical cues for real-world manipulation. Yet, embodiment differences and the frequent absence of task-aligned annotations make their direct use in VLA models challenging. This survey provides a unified view of how human videos are transformed into effective knowledge for VLA models. We categorize existing approaches into four classes based on the action-related information they derive: (i) latent action representations that encode inter-frame changes; (ii) predictive world models that forecast future frames; (iii) explicit 2D supervision that extracts image-plane cues; and (iv) explicit 3D reconstruction that recovers geometry or motion. Beyond this taxonomy, we highlight three key open challenges in this area: structuring unstructured videos into training-ready episodes, grounding video-derived supervision into robot-executable actions under embodiment and viewpoint heterogeneity, and designing evaluation protocols that better predict real-world deployment performance and transfer efficiency, thereby informing future research directions. A curated list of papers and resources is available at https://github.com/AaronFengZY/HumanCentricToVLA-Survey.

AI.tldr: This survey categorizes approaches for leveraging abundant human videos to train Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for embodied control into four classes: latent action representations, predictive world models, explicit 2D supervision, and explicit 3D reconstruction. It also identifies three open challenges: structuring unstructured videos, grounding video-derived supervision to robot actions, and designing better evaluation protocols.
AI.motivation: Robot demonstrations are costly and embodiment-specific, while human videos are abundant and rich but challenging to directly use due to embodiment differences and lack of task annotations. This survey aims to unify and categorize methods that transform human videos into effective knowledge for VLA models.
AI.method: The paper categorizes existing approaches into four classes based on action-related information derived from human videos: (i) latent action representations encoding inter-frame changes; (ii) predictive world models forecasting future frames; (iii) explicit 2D supervision for image-plane cues; and (iv) explicit 3D reconstruction for geometry or motion recovery. It also highlights three open challenges.
AI.result: A unified taxonomy of four classes of methods for transferring human video knowledge to VLA models, plus identification of three key open challenges: structuring unstructured videos into training-ready episodes, grounding video supervision to executable robot actions despite embodiment/viewpoint differences, and designing evaluation protocols that predict real-world deployment performance.
AI.conclusion: The survey provides a structured overview of how human videos can be leveraged for VLA model training and outlines future research directions for overcoming remaining challenges in embodiment transfer, data structuring, and evaluation.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Optimal Experiment Design in Parameter Identification of Mechatronic Systems
summary: Informative excitation signals are critical for accurate system identification of mechatronic systems, yet classical system identification (SI) approaches require expert knowledge and hand-crafted signal design to respect hardware safety constraints, limiting their generalizability. We propose a reinforcement learning (RL) agent that learns optimal excitation signals for a Quanser Aero 2 testbed while autonomously enforcing safety constraints through reward shaping. Evaluated across 10 independent training seeds, our comprehensive agent achieves competitive estimation accuracy across all three identified parameters, outperforming classical baselines while incurring only 0.75% safety violations.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a reinforcement learning (RL) agent to automatically generate optimal excitation signals for system identification of mechatronic systems, achieving competitive accuracy on a Quanser Aero 2 testbed with only 0.75% safety violations, outperforming classical methods without requiring expert knowledge.
AI.motivation: Classical system identification approaches require expert knowledge and hand-crafted excitation signal design to respect hardware safety constraints, which limits generalizability. The authors aim to automate this process while maintaining safety.
AI.method: A reinforcement learning agent is trained to learn optimal excitation signals for the Quanser Aero 2 testbed, with safety constraints enforced through reward shaping. The agent is evaluated across 10 independent training seeds.
AI.result: The RL agent achieves competitive estimation accuracy across all three identified parameters, outperforming classical baselines with only 0.75% safety violations.
AI.conclusion: RL-based excitation signal generation can match or exceed classical methods in system identification accuracy while autonomously enforcing hardware safety constraints, reducing the need for expert intervention.

title: Linear Motility Maps in Nonlinear Viscous Fluids
summary: Systems moving in low Reynolds number fluid regimes are known to be governed by a ``motility map'' which linearly relates their shape change rates to they body frame velocity moving through the fluid. A consequence of this is ``Purcell's Scallop Theorem'' -- a locomotion system that undergoes shape changes that follow the same path forward and backward in time (reciprocal body deformations) cannot achieve net displacement, regardless of pacing of those changes.We show that linear-in-velocity motility maps extend to any power law viscosity (a.k.a. Ostwald--de Waele fluid), and therefore to many biological fluids in intermediate shear ranges. We also show that the linear-in-velocity property can be violated in Carreau-Yasuda fluids to produce net motion using an ``inchworm'' model consisting of two unequal masses with unequal drag coefficients performing reciprocal motions. Interestingly, the direction of motion can be switched by changing speeds. Our results show that the linear motility map of geometric mechaincs can be used to analyze and design locomotion in power-law fluids, and that some nonlinear drag relationships such as Carreau-Yasuda can be exploited to generate net locomotion in seeming violation of the ``scallop theorem''.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that Purcell's Scallop Theorem extends to power-law viscosity fluids (linear motility map holds), but can be violated in Carreau-Yasuda fluids, enabling net reciprocal locomotion where direction switches with speed.
AI.motivation: To understand how the linear motility map and Purcell's Scallop Theorem generalize to non-Newtonian biological fluids, and to identify fluid regimes where reciprocal motions can still achieve net displacement.
AI.method: The authors analyze the motility map for power-law (Ostwald-de Waele) fluids and Carreau-Yasuda fluids, using an inchworm model with two unequal masses and unequal drag coefficients performing reciprocal motions.
AI.result: Linear-in-velocity motility maps hold for power-law fluids, but are violated in Carreau-Yasuda fluids, allowing net motion via reciprocal shape changes. The direction of motion is speed-dependent and switchable.
AI.conclusion: Geometric mechanics frameworks for low-Reynolds locomotion apply to power-law fluids, while Carreau-Yasuda fluids offer new opportunities for designing microswimmers that break the scallop theorem through nonlinear drag.

title: Position Paper: Post-Solve Robustness in Decision Engines: Feasible Regions and Smoothness Under Perturbations
summary: Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) decision engines routinely output nominally optimal plans for high-stakes industrial systems. Yet deployment rarely matches solve-time assumptions: small perturbations in costs, demands, or resource availability can invalidate feasibility or trigger discontinuous shifts to qualitatively different solutions. We argue that this post-solve robustness gap is a missing layer in today's optimization pipelines and a missing evaluation dimension for learning-enabled decision systems. Rather than replacing robust optimization or stochastic programming, the proposed layer audits a solved incumbent and returns solver-backed evidence about how far that solution can be trusted. We formalize two central objects: (i) an $ε$-near-optimal feasible neighborhood in parameter space, capturing when an incumbent remains feasible and near-optimal under perturbations, and (ii) solution smoothness in decision space, capturing whether nearby alternatives with small combinatorial edits remain competitive. We then synthesize the most relevant partial answers from sensitivity and stability analysis, robust optimization, neighborhood search, adversarial testing, and learning-based enhancements, and articulate an agenda for a unified post-solve robustness layer. Concretely, we call for certified inner approximations around the incumbent, probabilistic robustness estimation with calibrated uncertainty, adversarial robustness margins, and learning-based prediction and explanation aligned with solver-backed verification. We conclude with a compact reporting template and evaluation protocol that would make robustness a first-class output of decision engines.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a "post-solve robustness gap" in MILP-based decision engines—where nominal optimal solutions may fail under parameter perturbations—and proposes a formal layer to audit solutions, providing solver-backed evidence on how far they can be trusted. It introduces ε-near-optimal feasible neighborhoods and solution smoothness, synthesizes relevant prior work, and outlines an agenda including certified inner approximations, probabilistic robustness estimation, adversarial margins, and learning-based verification, concluding with a reporting template and evaluation protocol.
AI.motivation: MILP decision engines produce nominally optimal plans for high-stakes industrial systems, but small perturbations in costs, demands, or resource availability can invalidate feasibility or cause discontinuous solution shifts. This "post-solve robustness gap" is a missing layer in optimization pipelines and a missing evaluation dimension for learning-enabled decision systems.
AI.method: The paper formalizes two central objects: (i) an ε-near-optimal feasible neighborhood in parameter space, and (ii) solution smoothness in decision space. It synthesizes partial answers from sensitivity/stability analysis, robust optimization, neighborhood search, adversarial testing, and learning-based enhancements into a unified agenda involving certified inner approximations, probabilistic robustness estimation, adversarial robustness margins, and learning-based prediction/explanation with solver-backed verification.
AI.result: The paper does not present experimental results; it is a position/agenda paper that synthesizes existing work and proposes a formalized post-solve robustness layer. It concludes with a compact reporting template and evaluation protocol to make robustness a first-class output of decision engines.
AI.conclusion: The authors call for making robustness a first-class output of decision engines via certified inner approximations, probabilistic robustness estimation, adversarial margins, and learning-based verification, supported by a standardized reporting template and evaluation protocol.

title: Invascal: Inverse-Vacuity Self-Calibration for Uncertainty-Aware LiDAR Range-View Semantic Segmentation
comment: Accepted for publication at the 2026 IEEE 29th International Conference on Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITSC)
summary: LiDAR semantic segmentation is a core perception capability for autonomous vehicles and mobile robots. However, safe operation also depends on knowing when predictions are unreliable. Existing approaches typically rely on softmax confidence, which is often miscalibrated and overconfident, while stronger uncertainty estimates from Monte Carlo dropout or ensembles are often computationally expensive for real-time use. To this end, we introduce a novel, architecture-agnostic uncertainty-aware Adapter Head. It decomposes the prediction into a Preference Head for class ranking and a Strength Head that refines uncertainty assessment, thereby enabling a principled construction of evidential Dirichlet representations. Building on this design, we propose our inverse-vacuity self-calibration objective (Invascal), which directly supervises the strength signal to produce reliable and well-calibrated uncertainty estimates while preventing runaway evidence growth. We evaluate our framework across multiple LiDAR datasets and backbone architectures. We compare against deterministic training, Monte Carlo dropout and ensembles, and prior evidential methods. Our approach consistently improves uncertainty calibration over traditional deterministic methods with minimal computational overhead. At the same time, it preserves competitive segmentation accuracy, where prior evidential methods often suffer performance degradation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an architecture-agnostic uncertainty-aware Adapter Head with a Preference Head for class ranking and a Strength Head for uncertainty refinement, plus an inverse-vacuity self-calibration objective (Invascal) that supervises strength signals to produce well-calibrated uncertainty estimates for LiDAR semantic segmentation with minimal computational overhead.
AI.motivation: Existing uncertainty estimation methods for LiDAR semantic segmentation rely on softmax confidence (miscalibrated/overconfident) or computationally expensive techniques like Monte Carlo dropout and ensembles, hindering real-time deployment in safety-critical autonomous driving systems.
AI.method: The framework consists of: (1) an uncertainty-aware Adapter Head with a Preference Head for class ranking and a Strength Head for refining uncertainty, enabling evidential Dirichlet representations; and (2) an inverse-vacuity self-calibration objective (Invascal) that directly supervises the strength signal for reliable, well-calibrated uncertainty while preventing runaway evidence growth.
AI.result: The approach consistently improves uncertainty calibration over deterministic methods with minimal computational overhead, preserves competitive segmentation accuracy, and outperforms prior evidential methods that often suffer performance degradation, across multiple LiDAR datasets and backbone architectures.
AI.conclusion: The proposed uncertainty-aware Adapter Head with Invascal provides a lightweight, architecture-agnostic solution for reliable uncertainty estimation in LiDAR semantic segmentation, achieving strong calibration and accuracy without the computational burden of sampling-based or ensemble methods.

title: Emergent Collaborative Deliberation in Multi-Model AI Systems: A BFT-Derived Protocol for Epistemic Synthesis
summary: We present the Consilium Protocol, a Byzantine Fault Tolerance-derived architecture for structured multi-model AI deliberation that treats inter-model disagreement as epistemic signal rather than error. The protocol assigns engineered cognitive personas to language models -- separating what a model is from how it reasons -- and introduces an In-Sample/Out-of-Sample validation framework adapted from quantitative finance to distinguish training-data consensus from empirically grounded conclusions. Across 1,478 deliberation sessions spanning 32 topics in 10 domain categories, we demonstrate that (1) the cognitive persona, not the underlying model, determines epistemic behavior: free edge-inference models costing 0.0002 USD per batch produced comparable analytical output to frontier models costing 10.69 USD; (2) RLHF alignment training creates measurable, domain-specific epistemic blind spots -- contested policy topics exhibit 12.3 percentage points less adversarial challenge than settled science topics, and AI safety topics show asymmetric bias ($Δ$=11.6%) where models challenge claims that AI is dangerous far more vigorously than claims that AI risk is overstated; (3) the protocol exhibits no directional bias of its own (immigration $Δ$=2.3%, renewables $Δ$=1.2%); and (4) out-of-sample evidence retrieval validated 239 claims with 100% evidence retrieval and surfaced 167 blind-spot discoveries invisible to training-data deliberation. Run-to-run reproducibility across randomized model$\times$persona assignments averages $\pm$2.2% standard deviation. Total cost for the complete battery including all overhead: 217 USD. We release the protocol specification under MIT license to enable independent verification.

AI.tldr: The Consilium Protocol is a BFT-derived architecture for multi-model AI deliberation that treats disagreement as epistemic signal. Using engineered cognitive personas and an In-Sample/Out-of-Sample validation framework, it shows that persona (not model) determines epistemic behavior, RLHF creates domain-specific blind spots, the protocol has no directional bias, and out-of-sample retrieval surfaces blind spots invisible to training data—all for $217 total cost.
AI.motivation: To design a structured deliberation protocol that leverages inter-model disagreement as useful epistemic signal rather than treating it as error, while detecting and mitigating biases introduced by alignment training (RLHF) and training-data consensus.
AI.method: The Consilium Protocol uses Byzantine Fault Tolerance-derived architecture with engineered cognitive personas assigned to LLMs (separating model identity from reasoning approach) and an In-Sample/Out-of-Sample validation framework adapted from quantitative finance. Testing involved 1,478 deliberation sessions across 32 topics in 10 domains with randomized model×persona assignments.
AI.result: (1) Cognitive persona, not underlying model, determines epistemic behavior (free edge-inference at $0.0002/batch matches frontier models at $10.69). (2) RLHF creates domain-specific blind spots: 12.3 pp less adversarial challenge on contested policy vs. settled science; asymmetric AI safety bias (Δ=11.6%). (3) Protocol shows no directional bias (immigration Δ=2.3%, renewables Δ=1.2%). (4) Out-of-sample retrieval validated 239 claims with 100% success and surfaced 167 blind-spot discoveries. Run-to-run reproducibility at ±2.2% SD. Total cost: $217.
AI.conclusion: The protocol is cost-effective, reproducible, and bias-resistant—capable of producing frontier-quality deliberation from cheap models by decoupling persona from model. The authors release the specification under MIT license for independent verification, suggesting a new paradigm for structured AI reasoning that treats disagreement as signal.

title: Balancing Accuracy and Efficiency: Adaptive Dynamics Orchestration for Model Predictive Control
summary: Model Predictive Control (MPC) for autonomous navigation faces a fundamental trade-off between model accuracy and real-time efficiency. High-fidelity dynamics models can accurately predict complex vehicle-terrain interactions during trajectory rollouts, but incur significant computational cost, increasing inference latency and reducing control frequency. Conversely, lightweight models enable fast updates and dense sampling, yet may produce erroneous predictions under safety-critical conditions, potentially leading to catastrophic failures such as vehicle rollover. To address this trade-off, we propose Adaptive Dynamics Orchestration (ADO), a framework that dynamically selects the most appropriate dynamics model for the current navigation context. ADO maintains a library of models spanning diverse accuracy-efficiency profiles and continuously refines terrain-conditioned performance estimates using residual errors from online counterfactual rollouts, where executed control actions are replayed across the model library to assess predictive discrepancy. These estimates guide model selection in real time, balancing computational efficiency and predictive accuracy. Real-world experiments on an off-road ground robot demonstrate that ADO significantly reduces modeling error compared to a fixed low-latency baseline, while approaching the accuracy of the highest-fidelity model without incurring its computational cost, resulting in more reliable and effective navigation in challenging terrain.

AI.tldr: ADO dynamically selects from a library of dynamics models with different accuracy-efficiency trade-offs for MPC-based off-road navigation, using online counterfactual rollouts to estimate terrain-conditioned performance and reduce modeling error without the computational cost of the highest-fidelity model.
AI.motivation: MPC for autonomous navigation faces a fundamental trade-off between model accuracy (high-fidelity models are computationally expensive, increasing latency) and real-time efficiency (lightweight models are fast but can produce erroneous predictions under safety-critical conditions, leading to failures like rollover).
AI.method: Adaptive Dynamics Orchestration (ADO) maintains a library of dynamics models with varying accuracy-efficiency profiles. It refines terrain-conditioned performance estimates using residual errors from online counterfactual rollouts (replaying executed actions across the model library to assess predictive discrepancy), and uses these estimates to select the appropriate model in real time.
AI.result: Real-world experiments on an off-road ground robot show ADO significantly reduces modeling error compared to a fixed low-latency baseline, while approaching the accuracy of the highest-fidelity model without incurring its full computational cost.
AI.conclusion: ADO enables more reliable and effective navigation in challenging terrain by dynamically balancing computational efficiency and predictive accuracy.

title: Deliberative Curation: A Protocol for Multi-Agent Knowledge Bases
comment: 29 pages, 1 figure, 6 tables. Open-source implementation available at https://github.com/StevenJohnson998/AIngram
summary:
As AI agents transition from isolated tools to collaborative participants in shared knowledge ecosystems, governing collective knowledge curation becomes a critical challenge. Human platform governance mechanisms do not transfer directly: agent statelessness undermines deterrence-based sanctions, model homogeneity violates independence assumptions underlying crowd wisdom, and sycophancy collapses deliberative consensus.
  We propose a deliberative curation protocol combining three governance layers: (1) a knowledge artifact lifecycle formalized as a labeled transition system; (2) reputation-weighted deliberative voting integrating Beta Reputation with EigenTrust amplification; and (3) graduated sanctions adapted for stateless agents, including broken agent handling distinguishing malfunction from adversarial behavior.
  We evaluate the protocol through agent-based simulation with 100 agents across seven behavioral archetypes under two adversity scenarios (30 seeds, paired t-tests). The protocol trades modest precision under benign conditions for substantially better resilience under adversity: 0.826 vs 0.791 for majority vote under moderate adversity (p<0.001), widening to 0.807 vs 0.740 under stress (p<0.001). The protocol degrades roughly three times more slowly than majority vote. Ablation analysis identifies commit-reveal vote concealment as the most impactful single component (8.2-8.6pp precision improvement, p<0.001), outperforming reputation weighting and deliberation combined. Graduated sanctions were not exercised in simulation and remain empirically unvalidated.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a deliberative curation protocol for governing collective knowledge in AI agent ecosystems, using reputation-weighted voting and a knowledge artifact lifecycle. Simulations show it trades modest benign-case precision for substantially better adversarial resilience (0.826 vs 0.791 under moderate adversity, p<0.001), degrading ~3x slower than majority voting, with commit-reveal voting as the most impactful component.
AI.motivation: AI agents are evolving from isolated tools into collaborative participants in shared knowledge ecosystems, but existing human platform governance mechanisms fail due to agent statelessness (undermining deterrence), model homogeneity (violating crowd wisdom independence assumptions), and sycophancy (collapsing deliberative consensus).
AI.method: Three-layer deliberative curation protocol: (1) knowledge artifact lifecycle as a labeled transition system; (2) reputation-weighted deliberative voting combining Beta Reputation with EigenTrust amplification; (3) graduated sanctions adapted for stateless agents including broken agent handling. Evaluated via agent-based simulation with 100 agents across 7 behavioral archetypes under 2 adversity scenarios with 30 seeds and paired t-tests.
AI.result: Under moderate adversity: 0.826 vs 0.791 for majority vote (p<0.001); under stress: 0.807 vs 0.740 (p<0.001). Protocol degrades ~3x slower than majority vote. Commit-reveal vote concealment provides 8.2-8.6pp precision improvement (p<0.001), outperforming reputation weighting and deliberation combined. Graduated sanctions were not exercised in simulation and remain unvalidated.
AI.conclusion: The proposed deliberative protocol offers substantially better resilience under adversarial conditions compared to majority voting, though at a modest cost in benign precision. Commit-reveal mechanisms are the most critical component. Graduated sanctions for stateless agents require further empirical validation.

title: Whole-Body Inverse Kinematics with Graph Diffusion
summary: Inverse kinematics (IK) is a fundamental problem in robotics, requiring the generation of joint configurations that satisfy target end-effector poses. Existing approaches often struggle to generalize across diverse robot morphologies and to effectively model the multi-modal nature of IK, particularly in articulated systems with multiple kinematic branches. In this work, we propose GraphDiff-IK, a structure-aware graph diffusion framework for inverse kinematics. Specifically, we represent the robot as a kinematic graph constructed from the robot URDF, where nodes correspond to actuated joints and edges encode kinematic dependencies. Building upon this representation, we formulate IK as a conditional graph diffusion process that directly generates joint configurations on the robot graph. To better capture structural dependencies in articulated systems, we further introduce a structure-aware graph reasoning framework with hierarchical stage-wise message passing and torso-aware conditioning for multi-branch robots. In addition, we incorporate noisy forward kinematics feedback and task-space supervision to improve geometric consistency during denoising. The proposed framework provides a unified formulation that naturally supports single-arm robots, dual-arm systems, and articulated robots with torso or waist structures. Extensive experiments on diverse robotic platforms demonstrate that the proposed method achieves accurate and stable IK performance while preserving the ability to generate multiple feasible solutions for redundant robotic systems.

AI.tldr: GraphDiff-IK is a structure-aware graph diffusion framework for inverse kinematics that represents robots as kinematic graphs and generates joint configurations via conditional graph diffusion with hierarchical message passing, achieving accurate multi-solution IK across diverse robot morphologies.
AI.motivation: Existing IK methods struggle to generalize across diverse robot morphologies and fail to effectively model the multi-modal nature of IK, especially in articulated systems with multiple kinematic branches.
AI.method: Represent robots as kinematic graphs from URDF; formulate IK as conditional graph diffusion; introduce hierarchical stage-wise message passing and torso-aware conditioning for multi-branch robots; incorporate noisy forward kinematics feedback and task-space supervision for geometric consistency.
AI.result: Accurate and stable IK performance across diverse robotic platforms (single-arm, dual-arm, articulated with torso/waist), with ability to generate multiple feasible solutions for redundant systems.
AI.conclusion: GraphDiff-IK provides a unified IK formulation that generalizes across robot morphologies and captures the multi-modal solution space of redundant systems effectively.

title: Agents on a Tree: Pathwise Coordination for Multi-Objective Molecular Optimization
summary: Multi-objective molecular optimization requires searching vast chemical spaces under conflicting objectives, where early design decisions strongly constrain downstream outcomes. Existing methods typically rely on a single policy or fixed scalarization, which limits their ability to represent diverse trade-offs and to explore multiple promising design trajectories. We propose ATOM, a multi-agent framework that formulates molecular optimization as a tree-structured search. Each node corresponds to an atomic operation and hosts an agent specialized for a particular objective or decision context. Agents coordinate along different paths of the tree rather than enforcing a global consensus, enabling the method to maintain and compare alternative molecular evolution trajectories. A global memory of past optimization behaviors further supports balanced exploration and exploitation across objectives. This tree-structured interaction enables reasoning over long-horizon dependencies inherent in molecular design. Experiments on challenging multi-objective benchmarks involving activity, synthesizability, and ADMET-related properties show that ATOM consistently achieves improved Pareto coverage and hypervolume over strong baselines. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of pathwise multi-agent coordination for molecular optimization. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ATOM-41CE.

AI.tldr: ATOM is a multi-agent framework for multi-objective molecular optimization that formulates the problem as a tree-structured search, where each node hosts an agent specialized for a particular objective or decision context, enabling pathwise coordination to explore diverse trade-offs and achieve improved Pareto coverage and hypervolume over baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing methods rely on a single policy or fixed scalarization, limiting their ability to represent diverse trade-offs and explore multiple promising design trajectories in multi-objective molecular optimization.
AI.method: ATOM formulates molecular optimization as a tree-structured search where each node corresponds to an atomic operation and hosts an objective-specialized agent. Agents coordinate along different paths rather than enforcing global consensus, with a global memory of past optimization behaviors to balance exploration and exploitation.
AI.result: On benchmarks involving activity, synthesizability, and ADMET properties, ATOM consistently achieves improved Pareto coverage and hypervolume over strong baselines.
AI.conclusion: Pathwise multi-agent coordination is effective for molecular optimization, demonstrating the value of tree-structured interaction for long-horizon dependency reasoning.

title: Can Predicted Dynamics Exist in the Physical World?
summary: Predictive Physical AI systems output state rollouts, action chunks, and latent plans, yet a low root-mean-square error (RMSE) does not imply that a particular proposal is physically executable. We formulate physical admissibility as a prediction-control interface: before execution, a decoded proposal is treated as candidate dynamics and evaluated using kinematic, dynamic, and direct-to-composed horizon conditions. Passing is not a certificate of task success; rejection identifies violation of the specified physical envelope and gives a component-level reason. On Hugging Face LeRobot PushT, controlled falsification shows that one-step prediction-RMSE and standardized dynamics residuals reach area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) 0.982 and 0.972, kinematic-only conditions reach AUC 0.592, and the full gate reaches AUC 0.957 with condition-level attribution. In replay-based intervention experiments, residual-based filters and the full physical-admissibility gate prevent 87-$89% of invalid proposals while preserving mean progress near 0.998.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes "physical admissibility" as a prediction-control interface that evaluates whether AI-generated physical predictions (state rollouts, action chunks, latent plans) are physically executable, using kinematic, dynamic, and composite horizon conditions. The method achieves high AUC scores in detecting invalid proposals and can prevent 87-89% of them while maintaining near-perfect progress.
AI.motivation: Low RMSE in predictive physical AI does not guarantee physical executability of proposals, necessitating a formal framework to verify physical admissibility before execution.
AI.method: The paper formulates physical admissibility as a prediction-control interface with three gate conditions: kinematic, dynamic, and direct-to-composed horizon conditions. Proposals are decoded as candidate dynamics and evaluated. Rejection identifies specific violated physical envelope components.
AI.result: On Hugging Face LeRobot PushT, one-step prediction-RMSE and standardized dynamics residuals achieve AUC 0.982 and 0.972, kinematic-only conditions reach AUC 0.592, and the full gate reaches AUC 0.957 with condition-level attribution. Residual-based filters and the full gate prevent 87-89% of invalid proposals while preserving mean progress near 0.998.
AI.conclusion: The physical admissibility framework effectively identifies physically invalid proposals with high accuracy and provides component-level attribution, serving as a reliable interface between prediction and control in physical AI systems.

title: Optimal Transport-based Permutation-Invariant Bayesian Optimization of Offshore Wind Farm Layouts
summary: Bayesian Optimization (BO) is widely and successfully adopted for solving optimization problems having an expensive-to-evaluate, black-box, and non-convex objective function. However, the vanilla BO algorithm is not able to exploit possible symmetries characterizing the target problem. An intuitive case is given by optimal location problems, whose decision variables refer to a finite set of points within a continuous space, with the order of points not affecting the value of the objective function. We refer to this setting as optimization over layouts to distinguish from optimization over point-clouds where, instead, the order of points counts. As an instance of optimization over layouts we consider a real-life industrial-relevant application, that is the optimization of the layout of an offshore wind farm: given identical wind turbines, switching any pair of them has not any effect on the annual energy production. Based on Optimal Transport theory, we propose a Permutation-Invariant BO approach, namely PIBO, proved to provide better wind farm layouts when compared to the vanilla BO approach while cutting computation time roughly in half.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes PIBO, a Permutation-Invariant Bayesian Optimization method based on Optimal Transport theory, which handles optimization problems where the order of decision variables doesn't affect the objective function (e.g., wind farm layout optimization). PIBO outperforms vanilla BO in both solution quality and computational efficiency (roughly half the time).
AI.motivation: Vanilla Bayesian Optimization cannot exploit symmetries in optimization problems where the order of decision variables (e.g., points in a layout) does not affect the objective value, such as in optimal location problems and wind farm layout design.
AI.method: The authors propose PIBO (Permutation-Invariant Bayesian Optimization), which leverages Optimal Transport theory to incorporate permutation invariance into the BO framework, ensuring that the algorithm treats layouts as unordered sets rather than ordered point-clouds.
AI.result: PIBO provides better wind farm layouts compared to vanilla BO while cutting computation time roughly in half.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating permutation invariance via Optimal Transport theory significantly improves both the effectiveness and efficiency of Bayesian Optimization for layout optimization problems where the ordering of decision variables is irrelevant.

title: Silent Failures in Physical AI: A Literature Review of Runtime Action Authorization for Autonomous Systems
summary:
Physical AI systems increasingly map multimodal observations, language instructions, and learned world representations into physically consequential actions. Robotics foundation models, vision-language-action models, and world-model-based autonomous systems can condition decisions that move vehicles, robots, drones, and industrial machines. This transition exposes a safety problem that is not fully captured by conventional AI content moderation or by classical robot safety alone: a black-box model may issue a physically consequential action while appearing confident, plausible, and semantically aligned. The resulting failure can be silent, arising from sensor drift, occlusion, state-estimation error, distribution shift, hallucinated affordances, or invalid physical assumptions before downstream hardware controllers detect a violation.
  Across embodied foundation models, world models, robotics simulation, embodied safety benchmarks, safe control, runtime assurance, uncertainty estimation, verification, and guardrail evaluation, model capability and safety mechanisms have advanced along largely separate technical tracks. A recurring gap synthesized here is that no single stream surveyed in this review supplies a complete runtime authorization boundary between black-box Physical AI models and physical execution. The resulting analysis develops a bounded problem formulation, a definition of silent physical-action failure, a taxonomy of runtime guardrail functions, and evaluation requirements for comparing guardrails as Physical AI assurance mechanisms.

AI.tldr: Physical AI systems can produce "silent physical-action failures" where models issue plausible but physically consequential actions that are unsafe, and current safety mechanisms across embodied AI, world models, and robotics fail to provide a complete runtime authorization boundary between black-box models and execution.
AI.motivation: Conventional AI content moderation and classical robot safety do not fully capture the safety problem where Physical AI models (robotics foundation models, VLA models, world models) may issue physically consequential actions that appear confident and semantically aligned but are actually unsafe due to sensor drift, occlusion, state-estimation error, distribution shift, hallucinated affordances, or invalid physical assumptions.
AI.method: The paper synthesizes across embodied foundation models, world models, robotics simulation, embodied safety benchmarks, safe control, runtime assurance, uncertainty estimation, verification, and guardrail evaluation, identifying that no single stream supplies a complete runtime authorization boundary between black-box Physical AI models and physical execution.
AI.result: Development of a bounded problem formulation, a definition of silent physical-action failure, a taxonomy of runtime guardrail functions, and evaluation requirements for comparing guardrails as Physical AI assurance mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: There is a critical gap in runtime authorization boundaries for Physical AI systems; the proposed taxonomy and evaluation framework for guardrails aims to address silent failures that escape both conventional content moderation and classical robot safety mechanisms.

title: MindGames Arena Generalization Track: In2AI Solution with Delayed Per-Step Reward Attribution
comment: 18 pages, 2 figures, 9 tables. Technical report. First place in both Open and Efficient tracks of MindGames Arena Generalization Track at NeurIPS 2025
summary: Training language model agents for multi-agent strategic interaction presents a core difficulty: the quality of any action may depend on future events that never materialize, on moves that violate game rules, or on decisions made by other players. Standard reinforcement learning assumes that rewards can be assigned at each step, but this assumption fails in settings where outcomes are entangled across time and agents. We introduce delayed per-step reward attribution with eligibility gating, an episode lifecycle and postprocessing pipeline that computes rewards only at episode end, propagates them back to originating steps according to task-specific semantics, and excludes steps that lack valid dependent information from training. Together with asynchronous rollout generation via vLLM's continuous batching, curriculum-based opponent sampling, and multi-level stratified batch construction, this approach enables stable, sample-efficient RL training in multi-agent environments. We evaluate on the MindGames Arena benchmark at NeurIPS 2025, where a single 8-billion-parameter open-source model trained with our method matched or surpassed substantially larger proprietary systems, including GPT-5, in head-to-head play and took first place in both the Open (unrestricted) and Efficient (<=8B parameters) tracks.

AI.tldr: A delayed per-step reward attribution with eligibility gating method enables stable multi-agent RL training by computing rewards only at episode end, propagating them back to originating steps, and excluding invalid steps. Combined with asynchronous rollout generation, curriculum opponent sampling, and multi-level batch construction, an 8B open-source model trained this way beats much larger proprietary systems (including GPT-5) in the MindGames Arena benchmark at NeurIPS 2025, winning both Open and Efficient tracks.
AI.motivation: Standard RL assumes per-step reward assignment, which fails in multi-agent strategic settings where outcomes are entangled across time and agents—actions may depend on future events that never occur, invalid moves, or other players' decisions.
AI.method: (1) Delayed per-step reward attribution with eligibility gating: computes rewards only at episode end, propagates them back to originating steps with task-specific semantics, and excludes steps lacking valid dependent information. (2) Asynchronous rollout generation via vLLM's continuous batching. (3) Curriculum-based opponent sampling. (4) Multi-level stratified batch construction.
AI.result: An 8B open-source model trained with this method matched or surpassed substantially larger proprietary systems including GPT-5 in head-to-head play, winning first place in both the Open and Efficient tracks of the MindGames Arena benchmark at NeurIPS 2025.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach enables stable, sample-efficient RL training in multi-agent environments, allowing smaller open-source models to compete with and outperform much larger proprietary systems.

title: RocketSmith: An Agentic System for High-Powered Rocket Design and Manufacturing
summary: This work presents RocketSmith, an agentic system capable of the design, manufacturing, and optimization processes in high powered rocket development. The system enables the intelligent automation of software tools as to not only validate factors such as flight stability but also generate the parametric design components for the rocket assembly. A collection of subagents and skills enable optimization workflows of flight parameters via iteration in both zero-shot and human-in-the-loop workflows. With this system, four distinct high power rockets with various motor and assembly configurations were developed utilizing the unique design capabilities of additive manufacturing. These assembly components were fabricated using various FDM printers, manually evaluated for flight readiness, and flight tested at a launch event. From these tests, all rockets achieved a stable launched and two of the four rockets were successfully recovered in reflyable condition. Within the collected flight data, an 84% accuracy was achieved when comparing measured apogee to that calculated in flight simulations.

AI.tldr: RocketSmith is an agentic system for automated high-powered rocket design, manufacturing, and optimization, enabling parametric design, flight stability validation, and iterative optimization via subagents. It produced four additively manufactured rockets, all achieving stable flight, with two recovered in re-flyable condition and 84% accuracy between simulated and measured apogee.
AI.motivation: To automate and streamline the complex, multi-stage workflow of high-powered rocket development—spanning design, simulation, manufacturing, and testing—by integrating intelligent software agents that reduce manual iteration and human error.
AI.method: RocketSmith employs a collection of subagents and skills to automate software tools for flight stability validation and parametric CAD component generation. It supports both zero-shot and human-in-the-loop optimization workflows. The system was used to develop four distinct rockets with varied motor and assembly configurations, fabricated via FDM additive manufacturing.
AI.result: All four rockets achieved stable launches; two were successfully recovered in re-flyable condition. Flight data showed 84% accuracy between measured apogee and simulation predictions.
AI.conclusion: RocketSmith demonstrates that an agentic AI system can effectively handle the end-to-end rocket development pipeline—from parametric design to flight testing—with promising flight performance and simulation accuracy, highlighting viability for automated aerospace manufacturing workflows.

title: Universal Quantum Transformer
summary: Classical continuous-space neural networks fundamentally struggle to lock into exact mathematical symmetries, such as modular arithmetic and non-commutative algebra. To approximate these discrete logical rules, they often rely on massive parameter scaling, resulting in stochastic instability even after delayed generalization phenomena known as grokking. Here, we introduce the Universal Quantum Transformer (UQT), a fundamentally novel, quantum-native computing architecture that uses the physical properties of multi-qubit systems as a universal inductive bias for exact mathematical and algebraic reasoning. Rather than translating classical neural mechanisms, our framework relies entirely on parameterized geometric phase embedding and $SU(2)$ wave-interference. We demonstrate that the quantum attention circuit, operating on a highly compact 5-qubit substrate, perfectly learns two highly distinct formal classes: cyclic modular arithmetic ($\mathbb{Z}_{11}$) and non-Abelian algebra (the $S_4$ permutation group). While classical attention-based networks exhibit stochastic instability at convergence, the UQT achieves mathematically exact, deterministic generalization. We refer to this phenomenon as crystallization: a step beyond the well-known phenomenon of grokking. Crucially, this framework yields massive computational and memory advantages by theoretically bypassing the quadratic bottleneck of classical self-attention, and by logarithmically compressing the required representation dimension to eliminate the massive over-parameterization inherent to classical networks. Finally, we deploy this architecture on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware, proving its viability on current IBM Quantum computers. These results establish parameterized quantum topology as a universally superior physical substrate for exact artificial intelligence.

AI.tldr: The Universal Quantum Transformer (UQT) uses multi-qubit systems and geometric phase embedding with SU(2) wave-interference to achieve mathematically exact reasoning on tasks like modular arithmetic (Z11) and non-Abelian algebra (S4), outperforming classical attention-based networks that suffer from stochastic instability. The architecture demonstrates "crystallization" (beyond grokking), bypasses quadratic self-attention bottlenecks, and operates viably on NISQ hardware.
AI.motivation: Classical neural networks struggle to learn exact discrete mathematical symmetries (e.g., modular arithmetic, non-commutative algebra), relying on massive parameter scaling and exhibiting stochastic instability even after grokking. The paper aims to develop a fundamentally different computing paradigm that can lock into exact logical rules without over-parameterization.
AI.method: The UQT is a quantum-native architecture using parameterized geometric phase embedding and SU(2) wave-interference. It employs a quantum attention circuit operating on a compact 5-qubit substrate, leveraging the physical properties of multi-qubit systems as an inductive bias for exact mathematical reasoning.
AI.result: The UQT perfectly learns cyclic modular arithmetic (Z11) and non-Abelian S4 permutation group on 5 qubits. It achieves mathematically exact, deterministic generalization ("crystallization") where classical attention networks show stochastic instability. The architecture bypasses quadratic self-attention bottlenecks, logarithmically compresses representation dimensions, and works on current IBM Quantum NISQ hardware.
AI.conclusion: Parameterized quantum topology constitutes a universally superior physical substrate for exact artificial intelligence, enabling deterministic logical reasoning that classical networks cannot achieve without over-parameterization and instability.

title: PEACE: A Planner-Executor Agent with Constraint Enforcement for UAVs
comment: Accepted to ICRA 2026 Workshop on Semantics for Reliable Robot Autonomy: From Environment Understanding and Reasoning to Safe Interaction
summary: Foundation models are increasingly used to drive autonomous systems, yet existing approaches either keep the model in a tight control loop, raising latency and hallucination risk, or compile natural language into opaque end-to-end policies that are hard to explain, constraint and require domain-specific datasets and fine-tuning. We propose a planner-executor agent for PX4-based drones that decouples high-level mission planning from low-level control. A large language model performs single-pass task planning, while execution is handled through a structured ROS 2 tool-calling interface bridged to MAVLink. The system constructs a world model by combining modular 2D detectors (e.g., YOLO or vision-language models) with a pinhole depth projection module for 3D object localization. A constraint enforcement layer enforces altitude limits and horizontal geofencing, and bounded replanning enables recovery from execution-time action failures. We position our approach within three common design patterns for foundation-model-based robotics systems and demonstrate its feasibility in PX4 software-in-the-loop simulations in Gazebo. Results highlight improved explainability, constraint enforcement, and reduced LLM calls compared to tightly coupled LLM control. The code, dataset, videos, and other material can be found at the following link: https://github.com/erdemuysalx/PEACE

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a planner-executor agent for PX4-based drones that decouples high-level mission planning using a large language model from low-level control via a structured ROS 2/MAVLink interface, with a world model combining 2D detectors and depth projection, constraint enforcement, and bounded replanning, demonstrating improved explainability, constraint enforcement, and reduced LLM calls over tightly coupled LLM control in Gazebo simulations.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches either keep foundation models in a tight control loop (causing latency and hallucination risks) or compile natural language into opaque end-to-end policies that are hard to explain, constrain, and require domain-specific datasets and fine-tuning.
AI.method: A planner-executor agent for PX4-based drones that: (1) uses an LLM for single-pass task planning; (2) executes via a structured ROS 2 tool-calling interface bridged to MAVLink; (3) constructs a world model combining modular 2D detectors (YOLO or VLMs) with pinhole depth projection for 3D localization; (4) enforces constraints (altitude limits, horizontal geofencing); and (5) supports bounded replanning for recovery from action failures.
AI.result: Improved explainability, constraint enforcement, and reduced LLM calls compared to tightly coupled LLM control, demonstrated in PX4 software-in-the-loop simulations in Gazebo.
AI.conclusion: The decoupled planner-executor architecture offers a feasible, explainable, and constraint-aware alternative to tightly coupled LLM control for autonomous drone systems, reducing latency and hallucination risks while maintaining structured low-level control via ROS 2/MAVLink.

title: Grokers: Bottom-Up Inductive Comprehension and Write-Time Intelligence over Typed Knowledge Graphs
comment: 6 pages; second in a series with the Magarshak Machine / SPACER paper and the Context paper
summary: We present Grokers, an architecture for building persistent, structured comprehension of typed knowledge graphs through bottom-up inductive traversal of dependency subgraphs. Unlike retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which pays full comprehension cost at every query, Grokers pushes intelligence to write time: autonomous Groker agents analyze nodes in a typed stream graph, extract structured attributes via governed language model (LM) calls, and inductively compose that understanding upward through dependency relations, writing enriched typed attributes that serve all future queries at zero additional LM cost. We prove three formal properties: (1) the Byte-Identity Theorem, establishing that context blocks assembled from a transactionally-maintained denormalization index are byte-identical across LM turns between semantic changes, enabling KV-cache hit rates approaching 100%; (2) the Accumulation Monotonicity Theorem, establishing that the fraction of interactions resolved without LM calls is non-decreasing in the number of completed interactions under a governed wisdom library growth protocol; and (3) the Dual-Traversal Ordering Theorem, establishing that top-down generation and bottom-up comprehension are the unique correct traversal orderings for their respective tasks over a dependency DAG, and that their composition closes into a complete generation-comprehension cycle. We further present a deterministic alternative to embedding-based semantic search, with a synonym caching protocol whose LM fallback rate converges to zero for finite-vocabulary domains. A reference implementation is provided in the open-source Qbix / Safebox / Safebots stack.

AI.tldr: Grokers is an architecture for persistent knowledge graph comprehension that uses bottom-up inductive traversal of dependency subgraphs to pre-compute structured understanding at write time, enabling zero-cost LM inference at query time through byte-identical context blocks, monotonic accumulation of wisdom, and a complete generation-comprehension cycle.
AI.motivation: To overcome the inefficiency of RAG systems that pay full comprehension cost at every query, by shifting computational expense to write time so that future queries incur zero additional LM cost.
AI.method: Grokers uses autonomous agents (Groker agents) that traverse typed stream graphs bottom-up, extract structured attributes via governed LM calls, and inductively compose understanding upward through dependency relations. It maintains a transactionally-consistent denormalization index ensuring byte-identical context blocks across turns, a wisdom library that grows monotonically, and a dual-traversal ordering (bottom-up comprehension, top-down generation) that forms a complete cycle. A deterministic synonym caching protocol replaces embedding-based semantic search.
AI.result: Three formal theorems are proven: (1) Byte-Identity Theorem — context blocks are byte-identical across LM turns between semantic changes, enabling KV-cache hit rates approaching 100%; (2) Accumulation Monotonicity Theorem — the fraction of interactions resolved without LM calls is non-decreasing over time; (3) Dual-Traversal Ordering Theorem — bottom-up comprehension and top-down generation are the unique correct traversals over a dependency DAG. The synonym caching protocol's LM fallback rate converges to zero for finite-vocabulary domains.
AI.conclusion: Grokers offers a principled alternative to RAG by pre-computing structured knowledge at write time, with formal guarantees on consistency, monotonic improvement, and traversal correctness. The open-source implementation is available in the Qbix/Safebox/Safebots stack.

title: World Models for Robotic Manipulation: A Survey
summary: Robotic manipulation depends on the ability to anticipate how actions reshape objects, contacts, and scene geometry before execution. Learned world models provide this capability by predicting task-relevant future evolution under robot intervention, yet the term now spans latent dynamics models, action-conditioned video generators, three- and four-dimensional scene predictors, physics-informed simulators, and predictive modules inside vision-language-action systems. This breadth has fragmented the literature and obscured the design choices that matter for manipulation. We survey world models for robotic manipulation through three questions: what future representation is predicted, how prediction is connected to action, and when prediction is used in the robot-learning pipeline. We operationally define a world model as an action-conditioned predictive system and distinguish it from perception modules, inverse models, policies, rewards, and value functions. We then organize existing work into five representation families, develop a functional taxonomy that separates integrated prediction-action models from explicit predictive planners, and characterize infrastructure roles including synthetic experience generation, candidate filtering, search-based evaluation, learned environments, and outcome verification. We further map these roles across pretraining, post-training, and inference adaptation, review 34 manipulation datasets, and synthesize evaluation protocols for predictive fidelity, task performance, and simulator reliability. This survey shows that world models are evolving from task-specific dynamics predictors into predictive infrastructure for robot learning, while exposing open challenges in contact modeling, hallucination control, action alignment, and benchmarking under closed-loop use.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive survey on world models for robotic manipulation, organizing them by predicted representation, action connection, and usage timing, while proposing a functional taxonomy across five representation families and seven infrastructure roles.
AI.motivation: The term "world model" has become fragmented across latent dynamics models, video generators, 3D/4D predictors, physics simulators, and VLA predictive modules, obscuring design choices critical for manipulation. The survey aims to clarify this landscape.
AI.method: The authors systematically survey world models through three lens questions (what representation is predicted, how prediction connects to action, when prediction is used), propose an operational definition, organize work into five representation families, develop a functional taxonomy separating integrated prediction-action models from explicit predictive planners, and characterize seven infrastructure roles across pretraining/post-training/inference.
AI.result: World models are evolving from task-specific dynamics predictors into predictive infrastructure for robot learning. The survey reviews 34 manipulation datasets and synthesizes evaluation protocols for predictive fidelity, task performance, and simulator reliability.
AI.conclusion: Open challenges remain in contact modeling, hallucination control, action alignment, and benchmarking under closed-loop use in robotic manipulation.

title: Product-Aware Deep Autoencoders for Robust Process Monitoring in Multi-Product Cyber-Physical Systems
summary: As Industry 4.0 accelerates the integration of Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) in manufacturing, robust anomaly detection has become critical for ensuring process safety and security. Current data-driven approaches typically employ "product-agnostic" or global models trained on the aggregate of all normal operating data. However, modern industrial facilities frequently operate under diverse product grades. While computationally simple, these global models inherently expand their decision boundaries to accommodate the variance of multiple modes, creating a "blind spot" where subtle anomalies or targeted cyber-physical attacks may be masked by the wide acceptance region of the model. In this work, we first demonstrate that the vulnerability described above is present in global-agnostic models operating across multiple product grades. We then present a Product-Aware Autoencoder as a principled mitigation that restricts the learning domain to grade-specific distributions. While this approach reduces the identified blind-spot risk, we do not claim it as the optimal mitigation among all possible alternatives. We rigorously validate this approach against a Global Agnostic baseline using the Extended Tennessee Eastman Process (TEP) benchmark. Our empirical results indicate that the Product-Aware framework performs comparably to the global baseline on standard detection metrics, while offering improved robustness to product-grade-specific operating modes. Most critically, stress tests simulating our hypothetical attack scenarios reveal that while the global model fails to detect operational deviations in 77.8% of the scenarios, the product-aware system achieves 100% detection accuracy. These findings suggest that, in flexible manufacturing environments, generalized anomaly detectors can pose non-trivial security risks, motivating a shift toward mode-aware diagnostic architectures.

AI.tldr: Global anomaly detection models in manufacturing have "blind spots" due to multi-grade variance, masking subtle attacks. A Product-Aware Autoencoder that learns grade-specific distributions mitigates this, achieving 100% detection in stress tests vs. 77.8% failure for global models.
AI.motivation: Current "product-agnostic" global models for anomaly detection in CPS expand decision boundaries across multiple product grades, creating blind spots where subtle anomalies or cyber-physical attacks can be masked by the wide acceptance region.
AI.method: The authors demonstrate the vulnerability of global-agnostic models, then propose a Product-Aware Autoencoder that restricts learning to grade-specific distributions. Validation uses the Extended Tennessee Eastman Process (TEP) benchmark against a Global Agnostic baseline.
AI.result: The Product-Aware framework performs comparably on standard detection metrics but offers improved robustness. In stress tests simulating hypothetical attacks, the global model failed to detect deviations in 77.8% of scenarios, while the product-aware system achieved 100% detection accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Generalized anomaly detectors in flexible manufacturing pose non-trivial security risks, motivating a shift toward mode-aware diagnostic architectures.

title: Ontology-Guided Reasoning for Affordance-Based Explanations of Robot Navigation
summary: This paper proposes ontology-guided reasoning for affordance-based explanations of robot navigation. In human environments, it is not sufficient for a robot to detect that its route is blocked. It must also reason about what nearby objects afford, which state changes are possible, and which of these changes would allow it to continue safely. We address this problem by representing nearby entities, their affordances, affordance states, and qualitative spatial relations in a local affordance ontology and by evaluating hypothetical object--affordance state changes as candidate explanation factors. This yields explanations that are not only semantically grounded but also actionable. We instantiate the approach in a lightweight benchmark centered on a robot librarian scenario and evaluate it on procedurally generated navigation cases. The results show that ontology-guided reasoning identifies relevant explanation factors more accurately than a semantic-only baseline and remains robust as semantic clutter increases. Overall, the paper argues that affordance ontologies can serve not merely as semantic descriptions of the environment, but as reasoning foundations for explainability and reliable robot autonomy.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using an affordance ontology to guide robot reasoning for generating semantically grounded and actionable explanations when navigation is blocked, outperforming semantic-only baselines in identifying relevant explanation factors.
AI.motivation: Robots operating in human environments need not only to detect blocked routes but also to reason about what nearby objects afford, possible state changes, and which changes allow safe continuation, requiring semantically grounded and actionable explanations beyond simple obstacle detection.
AI.method: The approach represents entities, affordances, affordance states, and qualitative spatial relations in a local affordance ontology, then evaluates hypothetical object-affordance state changes as candidate explanation factors. It is instantiated in a robot librarian benchmark with procedurally generated navigation cases.
AI.result: Ontology-guided reasoning identifies relevant explanation factors more accurately than a semantic-only baseline and remains robust as semantic clutter increases.
AI.conclusion: Affordance ontologies can serve not merely as semantic environment descriptions but as reasoning foundations for explainability and reliable robot autonomy.

title: On the evolution of the concept of probability as a mirror of the evolution of reason
summary: Over the centuries, probability theory has grown from the calculus of games of chance into a central framework for reasoning under uncertainty. This article interprets that evolution not merely as a mathematical history, but as a transformation of rationality itself. From Pascal and Fermat's combinatorial symmetry to the inductive logic of Bayes and Laplace, from Poisson's statistics of events to Kolmogorov's axiomatic formalization, probability progressively incorporated uncertainty, time, and coherence into scientific judgment. This trajectory reaches a mature epistemological form in modern Bayesian inference, especially in Tarantola's view of probability as a logic of information, where prior knowledge and data are combined coherently. Yet this framework also exposes a limit: probability quantifies uncertainty about well-defined propositions, but does not by itself formalize the vagueness of the concepts used to describe them. The article therefore examines how rationality extends beyond probability. Fuzzy logic is presented as a rigorous language for graded meaning and qualitative judgment, while deep learning is analyzed as a distinct, powerful mode of prediction based on geometric interpolation and optimization rather than explicit inference. By situating probability, fuzzy logic, and deep learning in a common historical and epistemological perspective, the article clarifies their roles and limits. It argues that contemporary scientific rationality cannot be reduced to data-driven performance alone, but requires the explicit articulation of uncertainty, vagueness, and inference.

AI.tldr: This article traces the evolution of probability theory from games of chance to a logic of information, examining how Bayesian inference, fuzzy logic, and deep learning each address different aspects of rational reasoning under uncertainty, vagueness, and prediction.
AI.motivation: To interpret the historical development of probability theory as a transformation of rationality itself, and to show that contemporary scientific reasoning requires explicit handling of uncertainty, vagueness, and inference beyond data-driven performance alone.
AI.method: Historical and epistemological analysis tracing probability from Pascal/Fermat through Bayes/Laplace, Poisson, Kolmogorov, and Tarantola's Bayesian framework, then comparing with fuzzy logic and deep learning as complementary modes of reasoning.
AI.result: Identifies that probability quantifies uncertainty about well-defined propositions but not conceptual vagueness; fuzzy logic formalizes graded meaning; deep learning provides geometric interpolation/optimization-based prediction rather than explicit inference.
AI.conclusion: Scientific rationality requires the explicit articulation of uncertainty (probability), vagueness (fuzzy logic), and inference (Bayesian reasoning) — it cannot be reduced to purely data-driven performance.

title: V2I Work Zone Geometry Reconstruction with Pose-Conditioned UWB Range Denoising
summary: Reliable work zone mapping is important for connected and autonomous vehicles (CAVs) to navigate safely and smoothly through work zone areas. Cone-mounted ultra-wideband (UWB) roadside units (RSU) offer a cost-effective way for work zone layout inference, as roadside anchors and vehicle tags provide direct vehicle-to-infrastructure (V2I) range constraints for work zone geometry reconstruction. However, UWB range estimation is degraded by bursty outliers, non-line-of-sight (NLOS) errors, arbitrary anchor-ordering issues, and vehicle pose uncertainties in practical field deployments. To address these challenges, this study proposes a pose-conditioned, permutation-equivariant predictive denoiser for multi-anchor UWB ranging. The model employs shared anchor-wise temporal prediction to capture range dynamics, symmetric set aggregation to handle unordered and missing anchors, and pose-conditioned residual decoding to incorporate vehicle motion as a geometric prior. A two-stage training strategy first learns prediction from observed ranges, and then fine-tunes the denoiser with NLOS-weighted supervision. The method is evaluated on rare real-world V2I UWB field data collected with a CAV, as well as on controlled large-scale simulation benchmarks for ablative insights. Results show that the proposed method substantially improves range accuracy, cone localization, and work zone geometry reconstruction in challenging NLOS-dominated regimes, remains robust to anchor re-indexing and moderate anchor dropout, and reduces measurement-weighted field MSE by 66.9% relative to the raw input.

AI.tldr: Proposes a pose-conditioned, permutation-equivariant predictive denoiser for multi-anchor UWB ranging to improve work zone mapping for CAVs, reducing measurement-weighted field MSE by 66.9% relative to raw input.
AI.motivation: Reliable work zone mapping is critical for CAV safety. UWB range estimation suffers from bursty outliers, NLOS errors, anchor-ordering issues, and vehicle pose uncertainties in real deployments.
AI.method: A pose-conditioned, permutation-equivariant predictive denoiser with shared anchor-wise temporal prediction, symmetric set aggregation, and pose-conditioned residual decoding. Two-stage training: first learn prediction from observed ranges, then fine-tune with NLOS-weighted supervision.
AI.result: Substantially improves range accuracy, cone localization, and work zone geometry reconstruction. Reduces measurement-weighted field MSE by 66.9% relative to raw input. Robust to anchor re-indexing and moderate dropout.
AI.conclusion: The proposed denoising method effectively addresses key UWB challenges in real-world V2I deployments, enabling more reliable work zone mapping for CAVs.

title: Evaluating Interactive Reasoning in Large Language Models: A Hierarchical Benchmark with Executable Games
summary: We introduce a multi-turn interactive framework for reasoning evaluation that treats reasoning as active evidence acquisition and belief updating. Wherein, LLMs receive only the task rules, must issue targeted queries to a hidden environment, integrate partial observations over time, and decide when to submit a final answer. Beyond standard success rate and interaction efficiency, we evaluate contextual robustness under controlled contextual perturbations, and metacognitive adaptation through counterfactual revision and necessity judgment. We instantiate the framework as a benchmark of 474 executable games, each evaluated under five fixed configuration search spaces corresponding to five difficulty levels, and evaluate a broad set of frontier LLMs. Results show that the benchmark is highly discriminative, exposing large differences not only in success rate but also in interaction efficiency. Moreover, we empirically show that contextual perturbations cause moderate but consistent declines, whereas counterfactual revision and necessity judgment lead to much larger drops.

AI.tldr: A multi-turn interactive framework for reasoning evaluation where LLMs actively query hidden environments, integrate evidence, and make decisions; tested on 474 games across 5 difficulty levels, revealing significant performance gaps among frontier models, with contextual perturbations causing moderate declines and counterfactual reasoning causing larger drops.
AI.motivation: Existing reasoning benchmarks typically evaluate LLMs on static, single-turn tasks that do not capture interactive evidence acquisition, belief updating, contextual robustness, or metacognitive adaptation (e.g., counterfactual revision and necessity judgment).
AI.method: A multi-turn interactive framework where LLMs receive only task rules, must issue targeted queries to a hidden environment, integrate partial observations, and decide when to submit a final answer. The framework measures success rate, interaction efficiency, contextual robustness under perturbations, and metacognitive adaptation via counterfactual revision and necessity judgment. Instantiated as a benchmark of 474 executable games across five difficulty levels with fixed configuration search spaces.
AI.result: The benchmark is highly discriminative, exposing large differences in success rate and interaction efficiency across frontier LLMs. Contextual perturbations cause moderate but consistent declines, while counterfactual revision and necessity judgment lead to much larger performance drops.
AI.conclusion: Interactive, multi-turn evaluation reveals critical deficiencies in LLM reasoning beyond static benchmarks, particularly in metacognitive abilities like counterfactual reasoning, which remain challenging even for advanced models.

title: Completion at the Boundary (CaB): Deployable Switching with Completion-Aware Control under Limited Calibration
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) agents can execute natural-language instructions, yet deployed systems still lack an operational interface: deciding when the instruction is complete. This gap is acute in short composites ("do A, then B"), where mistimed handoffs cascade into downstream failures. Completion is inherently closed-loop because switching is an intervention that changes the instruction context and thus future actions and observations. We study completion under a deployable low-calibration regime motivated by open-ended instruction spaces, enforcing no test-time relearning and a single globally calibrated switching rule selected once on development set and reused unchanged on test set. Under this constraint, collapsing asymmetric boundary evidence into a single scalar can be brittle under polarity shifts across tasks.
