It is fully untethered, uses motor encoder feedback for state estimation, and shows reliable pose estimation, material discrimination, and task-specific sensing in validation.
AI.motivation: To address the need for lightweight, low-profile, and modular soft wearable robotic systems that assist hand function while integrating sensing for safe and adaptive control.
AI.method: The system uses 3D-printed flexible materials for a modular exoskeleton, tendon-driven DC motor actuation, a conductive spring (StretchSense) for both passive extension and proprioceptive sensing, and a magnet-magnetometer pair (MagSense) embedded in a soft fingertip for tactile sensing. Control is via an embedded microcontroller with motor encoder feedback for state estimation.
AI.result: Experimental validation shows reliable pose estimation, the ability to distinguish materials with different stiffness, and distinct sensor signatures across various grasping tasks.
AI.conclusion: SoFiE serves as a proof of concept for modular, soft, and assistive wearable robotics, demonstrating integrated actuation and multimodal sensing in a fully untethered platform.

title: The Deterministic Horizon: When Extended Reasoning Fails and Tool Delegation Becomes Necessary
comment: Accepted at ICML 2026. 4 figures. 51 pages including appendices
summary: Extended chain-of-thought reasoning can degrade performance on deterministic state-tracking tasks, not due to preference biases, but limits rooted in the information-theoretic capacity of decoder-only attention. We establish: (1) an Attention Bottleneck Theorem with a complementary achievability construction, bounding state-tracking capacity as $O(H \cdot \log(L/H) \cdot \sqrt{d_h})$; (2) a context-dependent error model yielding super-exponential accuracy decay; (3) the State-Space Jaccard metric distinguishing capability from preference failures; (4) a Deterministic Horizon $d^* \in [19, 31]$ beyond which tool delegation becomes necessary. Across 12 models and 8 task domains (including SWE-Bench, WebArena, and SQL-Multi), tool-integrated reasoning consistently outperforms neural chain-of-thought; on the primary model suite it reaches 86-94% accuracy versus 24-42% for neural chain-of-thought. Fine-tuning on optimal-length traces yields $<$5% improvement, confirming an architectural ceiling, and high cross-model correlation ($r = 0.81$-$0.91$) indicates these failures are architectural rather than training-specific. Our results provide principled guidance for when pure neural reasoning should yield to hybrid approaches in agentic systems.

AI.tldr: Decoder-only attention models suffer from fundamental information-theoretic limits on state-tracking tasks, causing chain-of-thought reasoning to degrade beyond a deterministic horizon (~19-31 steps), where tool delegation becomes necessary. Tool-integrated reasoning achieves 86-94% accuracy vs. 24-42% for neural chain-of-thought across 12 models and 8 domains, and fine-tuning yields <5% improvement, confirming an architectural ceiling.
AI.motivation: To understand why extended chain-of-thought reasoning degrades on deterministic state-tracking tasks, and to determine whether this stems from preference biases or fundamental architectural limits in decoder-only attention models.
AI.method: The paper derives (1) an Attention Bottleneck Theorem with achievability construction bounding state-tracking capacity as O(H·log(L/H)·√d_h); (2) a context-dependent error model predicting super-exponential accuracy decay; (3) the State-Space Jaccard metric to distinguish capability from preference failures; and (4) empirical evaluation across 12 models and 8 task domains (SWE-Bench, WebArena, SQL-Multi, etc.) comparing neural chain-of-thought vs. tool-integrated reasoning, plus fine-tuning on optimal-length traces.
AI.result: Tool-integrated reasoning consistently outperforms neural chain-of-thought: 86-94% vs. 24-42% accuracy. A Deterministic Horizon d* ∈ [19, 31] is identified beyond which tool delegation becomes necessary. Fine-tuning yields <5% improvement. High cross-model correlation (r = 0.81-0.91) confirms architectural (not training-specific) failures.
AI.conclusion: Pure neural reasoning has a fundamental architectural ceiling for state-tracking tasks, and hybrid approaches (neural + tool delegation) are necessary beyond a deterministic horizon of ~19-31 steps. This provides principled guidance for designing agentic systems.

title: Literary Emotions in Motion: A Soft Robotics Installation for Tactile Storytelling
summary: Soft robotics is increasingly explored in artistic contexts, where tactile interaction provides audiences with embodied engagement beyond visual or auditory signals. This work presents an interactive installation that maps semantic emotion analysis of narrative text into variable stiffness of soft pneumatic modules. A natural language model identifies two dominant emotions from a predefined set of six, driving the inflation of seven hexagonally arranged soft actuators. The central actuator represents the primary emotion, while the surrounding ones express the secondary. We develop and mechanically characterize silicone actuators, called soft modules, featuring a thin membrane layer, demonstrating how this morphological control expands the achievable stiffness range while preserving simplicity and low-cost fabrication. A user study with ten participants further evaluates how multisensory coupling of stiffness and LEDs intensity influences emotional perception. The results suggest that stiffness modulation accompanied by color change can support emotionally meaningful and engaging tactile interaction in soft robotic installations.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an interactive soft robotic installation that maps narrative text emotions (detected via NLP) into variable stiffness of hexagonal soft pneumatic actuators, with a user study showing that combining stiffness modulation with color change enhances emotionally meaningful tactile interaction.
AI.motivation: To explore how soft robotics can enable embodied tactile engagement in artistic contexts by translating semantic emotional content from narrative text into physically perceivable stiffness changes.
AI.method: A natural language model identifies two dominant emotions from six predefined categories, driving seven hexagonally arranged soft pneumatic actuators (central = primary emotion, surrounding = secondary). Silicone actuators with a thin membrane layer are developed and mechanically characterized to achieve variable stiffness. A user study (N=10) evaluates multisensory coupling of stiffness and LED intensity on emotional perception.
AI.result: The morphological design (thin membrane layer) expands the achievable stiffness range while maintaining simplicity and low cost. The user study indicates that stiffness modulation combined with color change supports emotionally meaningful and engaging tactile interaction.
AI.conclusion: Variable stiffness soft robotics combined with multisensory feedback (color + stiffness) can effectively convey emotional meaning in interactive art installations, offering a promising direction for embodied tactile engagement.

title: VESTA: Visual Exploration with Statistical Tool Agents
summary: Fitting quantitative models to data is a central step in scientific workflows, yet it remains one of the least automated. Recent agent-based systems leverage language and vision-language models (VLMs) to iteratively propose and refine statistical models, but these systems struggle on more challenging modeling tasks. To address these limitations, we introduce VESTA: Visual Exploration with Statistical Tool Agents, a framework that equips VLMs with a dynamically growing exploration toolkit to guide model refinement through data transformations, hypothesis-driven visualizations, and robust statistical tests. Unlike prior systems that rely on iterative critique alone, VESTA actively explores data before and during refinement by selecting or creating diagnostic tools, which accumulate in the model's context and can be reused later. We evaluate VESTA against established baselines in three toolkit configurations: no tools, static expert-written tools, and dynamic model-written tools. To support this evaluation, we introduce DAWN (Dataset for Automated Workflows and Numerical Modeling), a benchmark targeting distribution fitting and time series modeling with varying difficulty tiers, and culminating in real-world astronomy tasks including modeling initial mass functions and gravitational-wave chirp signals. We find that VESTA's dynamic tool creation outperforms prior agentic pipelines, with the largest gains on complex and domain-specific tasks. We further show that dynamically generated tools are substantially more sophisticated than those produced by existing visual tool-creation systems, covering more diagnostic categories per function and strongly preferring visual outputs that the VLM critic can reason over directly.

AI.tldr: VESTA is a framework that equips VLMs with a dynamically growing exploration toolkit (data transformations, visualizations, statistical tests) to improve automated model fitting, outperforming prior agentic pipelines on complex and domain-specific tasks like astronomy.
AI.motivation: Fitting quantitative models to data remains one of the least automated steps in scientific workflows, and existing agent-based systems using VLMs struggle on challenging modeling tasks.
AI.method: VESTA (Visual Exploration with Statistical Tool Agents) equips VLMs with a dynamically growing exploration toolkit: it actively explores data before and during refinement by selecting or creating diagnostic tools (data transformations, hypothesis-driven visualizations, robust statistical tests) that accumulate in context for reuse. Evaluated in three configurations (no tools, static expert-written tools, dynamic model-written tools) against DAWN benchmark (distribution fitting, time series, real astronomy tasks like IMFs and gravitational-wave chirps).
AI.result: VESTA's dynamic tool creation outperforms prior agentic pipelines, with largest gains on complex/domain-specific tasks. Dynamically generated tools are more sophisticated than existing visual tool-creation systems, covering more diagnostic categories per function and favoring visual outputs for direct VLM reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic tool creation and exploration-driven refinement substantially improve automated statistical modeling, particularly for challenging scientific tasks.

title: ROG-Grasp: Root-Oriented Geometry for Robotic Grasping and Placement
summary: Orientation-aware manipulation is essential in post-harvest agricultural processing, where produce must be grasped and placed in consistent configurations. This paper presents ROG-Grasp, a geometry-based robotic grasping and placement framework that estimates the produce orientation from root surface geometry using RGB-D perception. A YOLO-based root detector and point cloud plane fitting are used to infer the root normal, enabling stable grasp pose generation and orientation-constrained Cartesian motion planning. Experiments on tomatoes and onions demonstrate high success rates and stable execution time in both isolated and cluttered scenarios. Compared with vision-language-action (VLA) policies, the proposed method achieves more reliable and accurate grasp completion with faster execution. These results highlight the effectiveness of geometry-driven perception for practical orientation-controlled manipulation tasks. A video of our paper is available online https://youtu.be/Ir2UtGODdMo.

AI.tldr: ROG-Grasp is a geometry-based robotic grasping framework that uses RGB-D perception to estimate produce orientation from root surface geometry, enabling orientation-aware manipulation for post-harvest agricultural tasks like grasping and placing tomatoes and onions. It outperforms VLA policies in accuracy, reliability, and speed.
AI.motivation: Orientation-aware manipulation is essential in post-harvest agricultural processing, where produce must be grasped and placed in consistent configurations.
AI.method: A YOLO-based root detector and point cloud plane fitting are used to infer the root normal, enabling stable grasp pose generation and orientation-constrained Cartesian motion planning.
AI.result: Experiments on tomatoes and onions demonstrate high success rates and stable execution time in both isolated and cluttered scenarios. Compared with VLA policies, the proposed method achieves more reliable and accurate grasp completion with faster execution.
AI.conclusion: These results highlight the effectiveness of geometry-driven perception for practical orientation-controlled manipulation tasks.

title: Weak Critics Make Strong Learners: On-Policy Critique Distillation for Scalable Oversight
summary: As large language models become stronger, weak supervisors may fail to provide reliable labels, preferences, or final judgments for complex outputs, limiting both weak-to-strong generalization and scalable oversight. We study a more tractable form of weak supervision: using a weak model as a critic rather than as a labeler or judge. Instead of solving the task or selecting the correct answer, the weak critic only needs to provide a non-misleading revision direction that helps the strong model better use its own knowledge. We call this setting *weak-critic strong oversight*. We first show that weak critiques can improve frozen strong models at inference time, and that critique quality is key to this improvement. We then propose progressive on-policy critique distillation (**OPCD**), which filters high-quality critiques and distills critic-guided behavior into the strong model through adaptive self-teacher signals. Experiments on reasoning and alignment benchmarks show that our method improves strong models over training epochs, suggesting an effective path for scalable oversight with weak supervision.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using weak models as critics (providing revision directions) rather than as labelers/judges to improve strong model performance, and introduces Progressive On-Policy Critique Distillation (OPCD) which filters high-quality critiques and distills critic-guided behavior into strong models through adaptive self-teacher signals, showing improvements on reasoning and alignment benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Strong language models often surpass weak supervisors, making it difficult for weak models to provide reliable labels, preferences, or judgments for complex outputs. This limits weak-to-strong generalization and scalable oversight, motivating a more tractable form of weak supervision where the weak model serves as a critic rather than a labeler.
AI.method: The paper introduces weak-critic strong oversight where weak models provide non-misleading revision directions instead of solving tasks. It proposes Progressive On-Policy Critique Distillation (OPCD), which filters high-quality critiques and distills critic-guided behavior into strong models using adaptive self-teacher signals.
AI.result: Weak critiques can improve frozen strong models at inference time, with critique quality being key. The OPCD method improves strong models over training epochs on reasoning and alignment benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Using weak models as critics provides an effective path for scalable oversight with weak supervision, suggesting that critique-based weak supervision is a promising direction for improving strong model performance.

title: Adaptive PD Gains for Energy-Conscious Control in Physical Human-Robot Interaction
summary: Compliant force or torque control are approaches often investigated to achieve safe physical human-robot interaction (pHRI). However, these approaches have limitations. Force control requires a robot to be equipped with external force sensors to track the amplitude and direction of applied forces. Torque control requires torque sensing or estimation in each joint. As this is not available on every robot, energy-based approaches offer a promising alternative. Such approaches aim to achieve safe pHRI by limiting the mechanical energy of the robot. Current schemes leveraging an energy-based approach tend to have a complex implementation, and some may require further stability verification. We hence propose an adaptive proportional-derivative (PD) controller that can limit a robot's energy under any given limit to achieve safe pHRI. The proposed controller can limit both the kinetic and potential energy of a robot, and the behaviour of the controller gains can be shaped using various parameters, defining precisely the cutoff limit and sharpness. We construct a stability proof for the controller and define a condition to ensure the controller's stability. The proposed controller's behaviour and compliance are tested on the TALOS robot from PAL Robotics both in simulation and on hardware, verifying the expected compliant and energy-limiting behaviour of the controller.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an adaptive PD controller that limits a robot's kinetic and potential energy to achieve safe physical human-robot interaction, with tunable cutoff parameters, stability guarantees, and validation on the TALOS robot in simulation and hardware.
AI.motivation: Existing force/torque control approaches for safe pHRI require external sensors or joint torque estimation unavailable on many robots, while current energy-based methods have complex implementations and lack stability verification.
AI.method: An adaptive proportional-derivative (PD) controller is designed with tunable parameters that limit both kinetic and potential energy under a given bound, with a formal stability condition derived for the controller.
AI.result: The controller was validated on the TALOS robot from PAL Robotics, demonstrating compliant and energy-limiting behavior in both simulation and real hardware experiments.
AI.conclusion: The adaptive PD controller provides a simpler, stable, and sensor-free alternative for safe pHRI by directly limiting mechanical energy with configurable compliance behavior.

title: SDR: Set-Distance Rewards for Radiology Report Generation
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has rapidly advanced reasoning in vision--language models. However, for chest X-ray report generation, the standard rewards (i.e. exact-match accuracy and step-level processes) are incompatible because the reports consist of unordered and orthogonal findings, rather than a causal reasoning chain. We address this gap with a set-based view: each report is split into sentences and embedded by a frozen sentence transformer, yielding unordered embedding sets. We propose the use of set-to-set distances between generated and reference embeddings as continuous, permutation-invariant rewards. Across two datasets and three vision--language models (Qwen3-VL-2B/4B, Gemma3-4B), post-training with set-to-set distance based rewards via GRPO consistently outperforms supervised fine-tuning and exact-match GRPO on all headline metrics (BERTScore, RadGraph F1 and CheXbert F1 by average \%6.80, \%7.82 and \%4.45 relative improvements respectively). The same set distances also enable test-time best-of-$N$ selection: scoring candidates by their distance to training-report embeddings outperforms random selection on our trained models as well as three closed-source LLMs (Mistral-Small, Gemini-2.5 Flash-Lite, GPT-4o-mini) with on average \%16.4 relative improvement on BERTScore. Used as a streaming signal, they support a more efficient form of test-time scaling: pruning low-scoring candidates mid-generation reduces generated tokens by over 50\% while preserving the Findings quality of full best-of-$N$ selection. Together these results establish set-distance rewards as a unified signal for both post-training and test-time scaling in chest X-ray report generation. Our code is publicly \href{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Set-Distance-Rewards-CXR-BFDA}{available}.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes set-to-set distance rewards (using sentence embeddings) as a permutation-invariant reward for reinforcement learning in chest X-ray report generation. This approach outperforms supervised fine-tuning and exact-match GRPO across multiple models and metrics, and also enables test-time best-of-N selection with improved efficiency via mid-generation pruning.
AI.motivation: Standard RL rewards (exact-match accuracy, step-level processes) are incompatible with chest X-ray report generation because reports consist of unordered and orthogonal findings rather than a causal reasoning chain.
AI.method: Reports are split into sentences and embedded via a frozen sentence transformer to form unordered embedding sets. Set-to-set distances between generated and reference embeddings serve as continuous, permutation-invariant rewards for GRPO-based post-training. The same distances are also used for test-time best-of-N selection and streaming mid-generation pruning.
AI.result: Across two datasets and three VLMs (Qwen3-VL-2B/4B, Gemma3-4B), set-distance GRPO outperforms SFT and exact-match GRPO on BERTScore (+6.80%), RadGraph F1 (+7.82%), and CheXbert F1 (+4.45%). Test-time best-of-N selection improves BERTScore by 16.4% on average. Mid-generation pruning reduces tokens by over 50% while preserving quality.
AI.conclusion: Set-distance rewards provide a unified signal for both post-training and test-time scaling in chest X-ray report generation, enabling efficient and effective performance gains.

title: A passive universal grasping mechanism based on an everting shell
summary: A passive monolithic compliant grasping mechanism that works based on the eversion of an elastically deformable bistable shell is conceptualized. It comprises grasping arms made of beam segments that work in conjunction with the everting shell. The grasper is capable of picking up a stiff object of any shape up to a maximum size and weight. The bistable shell everts upon contact with the object to enable the grasping arms envelop the object forming an enclosure. The mechanism then stays in that configuration until it is actuated again to turn the shell back to its original configuration and thereby opening the enclosure to release the object. The stiffness of the arms decides the payload of the mechanism. The size of the arms decides the largest object that can be grasped and held. The arms have distributed compliance so that they can conform to the shape of the object without applying undue force on it.

AI.tldr: A passive monolithic compliant grasper that uses eversion of a bistable shell to envelop and hold objects of any shape up to a maximum size/weight, staying latched until re-actuated.
AI.motivation: To develop a simple, passive grasping mechanism that can conform to arbitrary object shapes without active control or excessive force application.
AI.method: Monolithic compliant design combining a bistable shell (which everts upon contact) with grasping arms made of beam segments; arms have distributed compliance for shape conformability; shell bistability provides latching without continuous power.
AI.result: Payload is determined by arm stiffness; maximum object size is determined by arm length; the mechanism can grasp stiff objects of any shape within those bounds.
AI.conclusion: The mechanism offers a passive, latching, shape-adaptive grasping solution that requires actuation only to release, not to maintain grip.

title: Doing What They Say, Not What They Reason: Locating the Faithfulness Gap in LLM Agents
comment: submitted to COLM social simulation with LLM workshop
summary: Do LLM agents act on the reasoning they state? This question of process fidelity is central to using LLMs in social simulation, yet it is hard to measure where no reference for correct behavior exists. We study it in acontrolled setting, a Texas Poker simulator with a verifiable reference action for every decision by decomposing the faithfulness gap into two steps: reasoning-conclusion and conclusion-action. The two steps behave oppositely.

AI.tldr: LLM agents show a faithfulness gap between stated reasoning and actual actions in Texas Poker, with reasoning-conclusion and conclusion-action steps behaving in opposite directions.
AI.motivation: The question of process fidelity (whether LLM agents act on the reasoning they state) is central to using LLMs in social simulation, yet it is hard to measure where no reference for correct behavior exists.
AI.method: Study the faithfulness gap in a controlled Texas Poker simulator with verifiable reference actions, decomposing the gap into two steps: reasoning-conclusion and conclusion-action.
AI.result: The two steps (reasoning-conclusion and conclusion-action) behave oppositely.
AI.conclusion: There is a faithfulness gap between LLM agents' stated reasoning and their actual actions, revealed by decomposing it into two oppositely-behaving steps.

title: PaCo-VLA: Passivity-Shielded Compliance Prior for Contact-Rich Vision-Language-Action Manipulation
comment: Under review, code will be available soon
summary: Contact-rich manipulation demands both high-level semantic reasoning and the safe regulation of high-frequency contact dynamics. While Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models provide unprecedented semantic generalization, their low-rate outputs lack the reliability required for direct plant authority in force-sensitive tasks. To bridge this semantic-to-control gap, we introduce PaCo-VLA, a passivity-shielded compliance prior that recasts the VLA interface. Rather than trusting VLAs with direct motor commands, PaCo-VLA treats network outputs as task-level compliance proposals: semantic bindings, task stages, and admittance schedules. A high-frequency, proposal-independent passivity shield governs these proposals through energy-tank accounting and boundary checks, preventing invalid, stale, or unverified model predictions from bypassing low-level contact physics. This decoupled architecture also enables causal evaluation, isolating semantic contributions from geometric shortcuts. Extensive simulated and real-world connector-insertion experiments demonstrate that PaCo-VLA achieves superior precision over unshielded VLA baselines, sustaining zero passivity violations even under adversarial compliance shifts. This framework establishes a provably sampled-passive runtime contract at the admittance port and provides a runtime interface for deploying foundation models in contact-rich domains.

AI.tldr: PaCo-VLA introduces a passivity-shielded compliance prior that treats VLA outputs as task-level compliance proposals rather than direct motor commands, using energy-tank accounting and boundary checks to prevent invalid predictions from bypassing contact physics, achieving zero passivity violations in connector-insertion tasks.
AI.motivation: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer strong semantic generalization but their low-rate outputs lack reliability for direct control in force-sensitive tasks, creating a semantic-to-control gap that needs bridging.
AI.method: PaCo-VLA decouples semantic reasoning from low-level control by treating VLA outputs as compliance proposals (semantic bindings, task stages, admittance schedules), governed by a high-frequency passivity shield using energy-tank accounting and boundary checks to reject invalid or stale predictions.
AI.result: Superior precision over unshielded VLA baselines in simulated and real-world connector-insertion tasks, sustaining zero passivity violations even under adversarial compliance shifts.
AI.conclusion: The framework establishes a provably sampled-passive runtime contract at the admittance port, providing a safe runtime interface for deploying foundation models in contact-rich manipulation domains.

title: TAPS: Target-Aware Prefix Tree Selection for Diffusion-Drafted Speculative Decoding
summary: Using a diffusion model for parallel drafting is a promising approach for speculative decoding. By predicting tokens at multiple future positions in a single forward pass, diffusion drafters substantially reduce drafting latency. However, this shifts the bottleneck to verification: verifying a single sequence limits acceptance length, while verifying large draft trees incurs excessive target-model latency. We identify a key mismatch in existing draft-tree methods: existing diffusion-tree methods rank nodes by the marginal probability, ignoring that verification is prefix-conditioned. As a result, they may verify unreachable descendants of rejected prefixes, increasing latency with limited acceptance gains. To address this, we propose TAPS, a target-aware prefix selection method that turns diffusion marginals into path-conditioned acceptance estimates. TAPS then selects a compact prefix-closed subtree under a fixed verification budget, improving the acceptance-cost tradeoff rather than simply expanding the draft tree. Experiments across diverse datasets and model families demonstrate that TAPS achieves up to 7.9x lossless end-to-end speedup over vanilla autoregressive decoding, outperforming state-of-the-art DFlash and DDTree by 1.36x and 1.74x respectively. Our work is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TAPS-EMNLP2026-53DD

AI.tldr: TAPS introduces target-aware prefix selection for diffusion-based speculative decoding, replacing marginal-probability-based draft tree construction with path-conditioned acceptance estimates to improve the acceptance-cost tradeoff under a fixed verification budget, achieving up to 7.9x speedup over vanilla autoregressive decoding.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion draft-tree methods rank nodes by marginal probability, ignoring that verification is prefix-conditioned, leading to verification of unreachable descendants of rejected prefixes, which increases latency with limited acceptance gains.
AI.method: TAPS converts diffusion marginals into path-conditioned acceptance estimates and selects a compact prefix-closed subtree under a fixed verification budget, optimizing the acceptance-cost tradeoff rather than simply expanding the draft tree.
AI.result: Up to 7.9x lossless end-to-end speedup over vanilla autoregressive decoding; outperforms DFlash by 1.36x and DDTree by 1.74x across diverse datasets and model families.
AI.conclusion: Target-aware prefix selection effectively addresses the mismatch in diffusion-tree methods, significantly improving speculative decoding efficiency.

title: DriveAnchor: Progressive Anchor-based Flow Learning for Autonomous Driving Planning
summary: We present DriveAnchor, a three-stage framework for autonomous driving planning that achieves behavioral diversity, controllability, and safety in a composable pipeline. Demonstration Flow Pretraining replaces the unstructured Gaussian prior with a vocabulary of 2,398 trajectory shapes constructed by farthest-point sampling, structurally grounding behavioral diversity in vocabulary coverage. Guided Flow Post-training jointly post-trains an Energy Field module with flow matching (FM), conditioning the Energy Field on static road geometry alone, to relocate anchors toward user-specified corridor polygons before flow generation, adding controllability without differentiable guidance; after Stage 2, new corridor presets require only Energy Field updates, not FM retraining. Reward-Refined Flow Fine-tuning applies zeroth-order reinforcement learning to align each anchor's output with collision-avoidance objectives: because the flow-matching model is a deterministic feedforward network in single-step mode, each anchor uniquely determines the output trajectory, reducing reward optimization to a direction search in anchor space without log-likelihood computation or ODE-to-SDE conversion. Evaluated on approximately 2 million held-out driving scenarios, DriveAnchor reduces near-range collision rates by 89% and improves mean reward by 32% without degradation in imitation accuracy, with 2.06 ms inference on NVIDIA Drive Orin. DriveAnchor has been validated through real-world vehicle testing, confirming its practicality for production deployment.

AI.tldr: DriveAnchor is a three-stage autonomous driving planning framework that uses Demonstration Flow Pretraining with 2,398 trajectory anchors, Guided Flow Post-training with Energy Fields for user-controllable corridor-based planning, and Reward-Refined Flow Fine-tuning via zeroth-order RL for collision avoidance. It achieves 89% fewer near-range collisions and 32% higher reward on 2M held-out scenarios, with 2.06 ms inference on NVIDIA Drive Orin, validated in real-world vehicles.
AI.motivation: To achieve behavioral diversity, controllability, and safety in autonomous driving planning within a composable pipeline, addressing limitations of unstructured Gaussian priors and lack of user-specified control in existing flow-based planning methods.
AI.method: Three-stage pipeline: (1) Demonstration Flow Pretraining replaces Gaussian prior with a vocabulary of 2,398 trajectory shapes via farthest-point sampling; (2) Guided Flow Post-training jointly trains an Energy Field module with flow matching, conditioned on static road geometry, to relocate anchors to user-specified corridor polygons; (3) Reward-Refined Flow Fine-tuning applies zeroth-order reinforcement learning in anchor space (deterministic feedforward in single-step mode) for collision-avoidance alignment.
AI.result: On ~2M held-out driving scenarios: 89% reduction in near-range collision rates, 32% improvement in mean reward, no degradation in imitation accuracy, 2.06 ms inference on NVIDIA Drive Orin. Validated through real-world vehicle testing.
AI.conclusion: DriveAnchor provides a practical, production-deployable autonomous driving planning framework that combines behavioral diversity, controllability, and safety without compromising imitation accuracy or inference speed.

title: EnergyMamba: An Uncertainty-Aware Graph-Enhanced Selective State Space Model for Energy Consumption Prediction
summary: Energy consumption prediction is essential for efficient grid management, demand-side optimization, and sustainable energy planning. Although advanced machine learning methods have been employed for better prediction performance, existing works have two key limitations: (1) they usually formulate this task as a purely time-series prediction problem without explicitly modeling the spatial dependencies among different regions, and (2) they fail to provide reliable predictions with uncertainty estimates under abnormal situations such as extreme weather events. To advance existing research, we propose EnergyMamba, an uncertainty-aware spatiotemporal learning framework for accurate and reliable energy consumption prediction, which comprises two key components: (i) a novel Graph-Enhanced Selective State Space Model (GE-Mamba) that injects spatial context learned from the grid topology into the temporal dynamics, enabling coupled spatiotemporal modeling, and (ii) an Adaptive Sequential Conformalized Quantile Regression (AS-CQR) module, which includes locally adaptive normalization and an online feedback mechanism to dynamically calibrate prediction intervals under potential distribution shifts. We evaluate EnergyMamba on four large-scale real-world datasets from Florida, New York, and California. Results show EnergyMamba achieves around 5% improvement in prediction accuracy and 6% improvement in uncertainty quantification over 15 state-of-the-art baselines.

AI.tldr: EnergyMamba is an uncertainty-aware spatiotemporal framework for energy consumption prediction that uses a Graph-Enhanced Selective State Space Model (GE-Mamba) for coupled spatial-temporal modeling and an Adaptive Sequential Conformalized Quantile Regression (AS-CQR) module for dynamic uncertainty calibration, achieving ~5% better accuracy and ~6% better uncertainty quantification than 15 baselines on real-world datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing energy consumption prediction methods treat it as purely time-series problems, failing to model spatial dependencies between regions and lacking reliable uncertainty estimates under abnormal conditions like extreme weather.
AI.method: EnergyMamba consists of two components: (1) GE-Mamba, a Graph-Enhanced Selective State Space Model that injects spatial context from grid topology into temporal dynamics, and (2) AS-CQR, an Adaptive Sequential Conformalized Quantile Regression module with locally adaptive normalization and online feedback for dynamic prediction interval calibration under distribution shifts.
AI.result: On four large-scale real-world datasets from Florida, New York, and California, EnergyMamba achieves ~5% improvement in prediction accuracy and ~6% improvement in uncertainty quantification over 15 state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: EnergyMamba demonstrates that explicitly modeling spatial dependencies via graph-enhanced state space models and adaptively calibrating uncertainty under distribution shifts significantly improves both the accuracy and reliability of energy consumption predictions.

title: PACE: Phase-Aware Chunk Execution for Robot Policies with Action Chunking
summary: Recent vision-language-action and diffusion-based robot policies often use action chunking, where each policy query predicts a sequence of future actions and the robot executes an open-loop prefix before re-querying. While this interface improves local motion continuity, deployment still requires choosing the execution horizon: how much of each predicted chunk should be executed before acquiring a new observation. However, our experiments show that success is strongly task-dependent and non-monotonic with respect to the execution horizon, making a single constant horizon an unreliable deployment rule. We propose PACE (Phase-Aware Chunk Execution), a training-free test-time execution method that selects the execution horizon online from the predicted chunk itself. PACE exploits the phase-dependent kinematic structure of manipulation trajectories by identifying low-speed transition points in the predicted speed profile and using them as candidate replanning boundaries. Because PACE uses only the predicted action chunk, it is plug-and-play and requires no retraining or access to policy internals. We validate PACE through large-scale evaluations in both simulation and real-robot settings. On 50 RoboTwin2.0 tasks, PACE raises the average success rate from 57.8% to 64.2%. In real-robot experiments on bimanual ALOHA and single-arm Franka platforms, PACE improves the average task score from 60.7 to 77.7 and the average success rate from 50.7% to 70.4%. Ablations and rollout-level analyses show that PACE adapts execution horizons across manipulation phases, shortening near transitions while preserving longer execution during coherent motion.

AI.tldr: PACE is a training-free, plug-and-play method that selects execution horizons online by identifying low-speed transition points in predicted action chunks, improving robot policy success rates across simulation and real-world tasks.
AI.motivation: Action chunking in robot policies requires choosing an execution horizon (how many actions to execute before re-querying), but success rates are strongly task-dependent and non-monotonic with respect to this horizon, making a single constant horizon unreliable.
AI.method: PACE (Phase-Aware Chunk Execution) selects the execution horizon online from the predicted action chunk by detecting low-speed transition points in the predicted speed profile, using them as candidate replanning boundaries. It requires no retraining or access to policy internals.
AI.result: On 50 RoboTwin2.0 tasks: success rate from 57.8% to 64.2%. On real robots: bimanual ALOHA and Franka platforms improved average task score from 60.7 to 77.7 and success rate from 50.7% to 70.4%.
AI.conclusion: PACE effectively adapts execution horizons across manipulation phases, shortening near transitions while preserving longer execution during coherent motion, leading to substantial improvements across diverse tasks and robot platforms.

title: Threshold-Based Exclusive Batching for LLM Inference
summary: Mixed batching (MB)--interleaving prefill and decode in a single batch--has become the standard scheduling strategy for large language model (LLM) inference due to its efficiency in maximizing compute and memory utilization. However, through controlled experiments, we find that prefill-decode interference inflates MB's per-step marginal cost above that of pure decode. On the high-bandwidth H200 (4.8 TB/s), this occurs only when decode tokens exceed 80% of the batch; however, on the bandwidth-constrained RTX PRO 6000 (1.792 TB/s), this threshold plummets to just 20%. Consequently, the optimal choice between MB and exclusive batching (EB) fundamentally depends on GPU memory bandwidth, model size, and workload composition. We derive a closed-form condition for this EB-MB performance crossover, along with asymptotically optimal phase-switching thresholds and memory-safe batch sizing for EB. Optimized EB achieves up to 41.9% higher throughput on bandwidth-constrained GPUs, while MB retains its advantage on high-bandwidth hardware with larger models. Our hybrid scheduler EB+ applies this condition online to dynamically switch between EB and MB without manual intervention. Under non-stationary traffic with distribution or concurrency shifts, EB+ attains the highest or near-highest throughput in every setting, outperforming MB by up to 36.4%.

AI.tldr: Mixed batching (MB) suffers from prefill-decode interference, increasing marginal cost above pure decode. The crossover point between MB and exclusive batching (EB) depends on GPU bandwidth, model size, and workload. The hybrid scheduler EB+ dynamically switches between EB and MB, achieving up to 36.4% higher throughput than MB under non-stationary traffic.
AI.motivation: Despite MB being the standard for LLM inference scheduling, its prefill-decode interference can inflate per-step costs. The optimal scheduling choice (MB vs. EB) is not well-understood across different hardware and workload conditions, motivating the need for a principled analysis and adaptive scheduler.
AI.method: Controlled experiments on H200 (high-bandwidth) and RTX PRO 6000 (bandwidth-constrained) GPUs to measure prefill-decode interference thresholds. Derivation of a closed-form condition for EB-MB performance crossover, asymptotically optimal phase-switching thresholds, and memory-safe batch sizing for EB. Implementation of a hybrid scheduler, EB+, that dynamically switches between EB and MB online.
AI.result: On H200, decode tokens >80% of batch cause interference; on RTX PRO 6000, threshold is only 20%. Optimized EB achieves up to 41.9% higher throughput on bandwidth-constrained GPUs. EB+ outperforms MB by up to 36.4% under non-stationary traffic.
AI.conclusion: The optimal batching strategy depends on GPU memory bandwidth, model size, and workload composition. A hybrid approach (EB+) that dynamically switches between EB and MB achieves the highest or near-highest throughput across diverse settings without manual tuning.

title: Dynamic Resilient Spatio-Semantic Memory with Hybrid Localization for Mobile Manipulation
comment: Code, CAD model, and real-robot demonstrations are available at https://bjhyzj.github.io/dream-web
summary: Reliable mobile manipulation in dynamic indoor environments requires a scene representation that remains geometrically consistent, semantically queryable, and computationally bounded as the environment changes. Existing systems often rely on pre-built maps, static-scene assumptions, or highly accurate camera poses, which can lead to stale or misaligned scene information when target objects are relocated or pose estimates are corrected. This paper presents DREAM, a real-robot mobile manipulation framework that integrates perception, memory, localization, navigation, and manipulation in previously unseen indoor environments without a pre-built map. DREAM constructs an online spatio-semantic voxel memory from RGB-D observations registered by a LiDAR-inertial-visual SLAM backend. It further introduces pose-graph-aware Redundancy-Aware Memory Pruning (RMP) to update historical observations after pose corrections while keeping long-horizon observation history bounded. For target localization and reacquisition, DREAM combines language-conditioned 3D retrieval, open-vocabulary image detection, and multimodal large language model based semantic verification. Real-robot experiments in four dynamic indoor laboratory scenes show that DREAM improves long-horizon task success rates from 40%-60% with DynaMem to 55%-70%, while maintaining a memory footprint of 0.37-0.63 GB and an online memory-update time of 0.43-0.53 s across scenes.

AI.tldr: DREAM is a real-robot mobile manipulation framework that builds an online spatio-semantic voxel memory from RGB-D and LiDAR-inertial-visual SLAM, uses Pose-Graph-Aware Redundancy-Aware Memory Pruning (RMP) to maintain bounded memory under pose corrections, and combines language-conditioned 3D retrieval, open-vocabulary detection, and MLLM-based verification for target reacquisition. Experiments show improved task success (55-70% vs 40-60%) with low memory (0.37-0.63 GB) and update latency (0.43-0.53 s).
AI.motivation: Existing mobile manipulation systems rely on pre-built maps, static-scene assumptions, or accurate camera poses, causing stale or misaligned scene information when objects are relocated or pose estimates are corrected. The goal is to achieve reliable long-horizon manipulation in dynamic indoor environments without a pre-built map.
AI.method: DREAM (1) constructs an online spatio-semantic voxel memory from RGB-D observations registered by a LiDAR-inertial-visual SLAM backend; (2) introduces Pose-Graph-Aware Redundancy-Aware Memory Pruning (RMP) to update historical observations after pose corrections while bounding memory growth; (3) combines language-conditioned 3D retrieval, open-vocabulary image detection, and multimodal LLM-based semantic verification for target localization and reacquisition.
AI.result: In four dynamic indoor laboratory scenes, DREAM improves long-horizon task success rates from 40-60% (DynaMem baseline) to 55-70%, while maintaining a memory footprint of 0.37-0.63 GB and an online memory-update time of 0.43-0.53 s.
AI.conclusion: DREAM enables robust, efficient mobile manipulation in dynamic, unknown indoor environments by fusing online spatio-semantic memory with pose-graph-aware pruning and multi-modal semantic verification, achieving higher task success with bounded computational cost.

title: Global-Local Attention Decomposition for Terrain Encoding in Humanoid Perceptive Locomotion
summary: Although reinforcement learning has significantly advanced humanoid locomotion, perceptive policies still struggle on sparse-foothold terrain and constrained environments. Success in these scenarios requires both broad terrain awareness and precise foothold selection, two perceptual roles that conventional encoders often entangle. To address this challenge, we propose Global-Local Attention Decomposition (GLAD) for terrain encoding in humanoid locomotion. Realized by a coarse-to-fine encoder over a robot-centric elevation map, GLAD explicitly separates these objectives: a global attention branch utilizes attention pooling to summarize the surrounding terrain context, while a state-conditioned local attention branch sparsifies and encodes precise foothold-relevant geometry. This explicit attention decomposition prevents the dilution of fine-grained spatial cues while reducing training overhead. Experiments demonstrate that GLAD enables reliable locomotion over challenging gaps, stepping stones, and stairs. Furthermore, the learned policy exhibits emergent terrain-responsive behaviors, autonomously following narrow paths and avoiding obstacles under simple velocity commands without explicit navigation planners. In real-world deployment on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot using onboard LiDAR, the proposed method achieves robust zero-shot sim-to-real transfer across diverse sparse-foothold and obstacle-rich domains.

AI.tldr: GLAD proposes Global-Local Attention Decomposition for terrain encoding in humanoid locomotion, separating broad terrain awareness from precise foothold selection via coarse-to-fine attention, enabling robust sim-to-real transfer on sparse-foothold terrain.
AI.motivation: Perceptive policies for humanoid locomotion struggle on sparse-foothold terrain and constrained environments because conventional encoders entangle two distinct perceptual roles: broad terrain awareness and precise foothold selection.
AI.method: GLAD uses a coarse-to-fine encoder over a robot-centric elevation map with two explicit branches: a global attention branch (attention pooling for surrounding terrain context) and a state-conditioned local attention branch (sparsifies and encodes foothold-relevant geometry).
AI.result: Achieves reliable locomotion over gaps, stepping stones, and stairs; exhibits emergent terrain-responsive behaviors (path following, obstacle avoidance) without explicit planners; robust zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on Unitree G1 humanoid robot using onboard LiDAR.
AI.conclusion: Explicit attention decomposition prevents dilution of fine-grained spatial cues while reducing training overhead, enabling effective perceptive locomotion in sparse-foothold and obstacle-rich environments.

title: KACE: Knowledge-Adaptive Context Engineering for Mathematical Reasoning
summary: Context engineering can improve large language models without updating their weights, but mathematical reasoning exposes a key limitation: feedback accumulated in one growing prompt causes context bloat and limits the amount of learned guidance that can be used. Existing methods often conflate storage, what is learned across runs, with usage, what is included for a particular problem, and therefore inherit this prompt-size ceiling. We introduce Knowledge-Adaptive Context Engineering (KACE), which separates storage from usage through difficulty- and domain-based organization. Offline, a self-reflective learning loop distills training traces into an epistemic tree: a knowledge base of typed cards stratified by problem difficulty and epistemic domain. Each card is assigned to the difficulty-domain node corresponding to the failure from which it originated. At evaluation time, tiered self-consistency with per-tier agreement gates dynamically classifies each problem as easy, medium, or hard. Easy problems exit without retrieved cards, while harder problems retrieve only the matching branch of the tree. This tiered scheme matches or exceeds Best-of-N while using comparable compute, and it classifies problem difficulty with 78 percent pairwise concordance. The main empirical contribution is the construction and use of a difficulty- and domain-stratified knowledge base enabled by tiered self-consistency. On AIME 2025, KACE achieves 62.2 percent accuracy, a 10.4-point absolute gain over fixed Best-of-5 self-consistency at a comparable solver-call budget and a 5.6-point gain over the strongest learned-context baseline, Tiered + GEPA. We also observe consistent gains on MATH-HARD and the verifiable subset of OlymMATH.

AI.tldr: KACE introduces difficulty- and domain-stratified knowledge organization with tiered self-consistency to separate storage from usage, achieving 62.2% on AIME 2025 (+10.4 vs. Best-of-5 SC) without context bloat.
AI.motivation: Existing context engineering methods for LLMs conflate storage (what is learned across runs) with usage (what is included per problem), causing context bloat that limits mathematical reasoning performance as feedback accumulates in one growing prompt.
AI.method: KACE separates storage from usage via (1) offline self-reflective learning that distills training traces into an epistemic tree of typed cards stratified by problem difficulty and epistemic domain; (2) online tiered self-consistency with per-tier agreement gates that dynamically classify problem difficulty, retrieving only the matching tree branch for harder problems while easy problems exit without retrieval.
AI.result: 62.2% on AIME 2025 (+10.4 vs. fixed Best-of-5 SC, +5.6 vs. Tiered+GEPA), 78% pairwise difficulty concordance, consistent gains on MATH-HARD and OlymMATH.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling knowledge storage from per-instance retrieval via difficulty-domain stratification effectively prevents context bloat and improves mathematical reasoning; tiered self-consistency enables practical difficulty classification without separate models.

title: SKIP: Sparse Keyframe Interpolation Paradigm for Efficient Embodied World Models
summary: Embodied world models have emerged as a promising paradigm in robotics by predicting how robot actions affect the surrounding scene. However, the rollout inference remains computationally expensive in pixel space, as long-horizon manipulation videos typically have to be generated frame by frame. This cost cannot be easily reduced by indiscriminately dropping frames, since downstream policies rely on complete preservation of sparse task-relevant events such as approach, contact, grasp, and release. To address this challenge, we propose Sparse Keyframe Interpolation Paradigm (SKIP), an event-preserving sparse-to-dense framework that avoids dense frame-by-frame generation. SKIP first identifies task-relevant keyframes by leveraging robot-aware multimodal features. It then synthesizes only these keyframes with a sparse video diffusion model. A learned gap predictor and an action-conditioned interpolator subsequently reconstruct the missing intervals according to the robot actions. On LIBERO, SKIP generates dense rollouts $4.16\times$ faster than a dense baseline while improving visual fidelity and reducing aggregate FVD by $89.0\%$. Importantly, SKIP-generated videos are effective policy-training data. Even when they fully replace real demonstrations, $π_{0.5}$ success drops only $1.3$ pp in LIBERO simulation and $6.7$ pp on the real robot, whereas fully dense frame-by-frame generation collapses by $48$ to $58$ pp.

AI.tldr: SKIP is an event-preserving sparse-to-dense video generation framework that speeds up embodied world model rollout by 4.16× through selective keyframe generation and action-conditioned interpolation, while maintaining sufficient quality for policy training.
AI.motivation: Rollout inference in embodied world models is computationally expensive because long-horizon manipulation videos must be generated frame by frame in pixel space, and indiscriminately dropping frames harms downstream policies that rely on sparse task-relevant events (e.g., approach, contact, grasp, release).
AI.method: SKIP first uses robot-aware multimodal features to identify task-relevant keyframes, then synthesizes only those keyframes with a sparse video diffusion model. A learned gap predictor and action-conditioned interpolator reconstruct missing intervals conditioned on robot actions.
AI.result: On LIBERO, SKIP generates dense rollouts 4.16× faster, reduces aggregate FVD by 89.0%, and when replacing real demonstrations entirely, π_0.5 success drops only 1.3 pp in simulation and 6.7 pp on real robot, versus 48–58 pp collapse for dense frame-by-frame generation.
AI.conclusion: Sparse keyframe generation with action-conditioned interpolation is a viable and efficient alternative to dense video generation for embodied world models, preserving task-relevant events while drastically reducing computational cost.

title: Probe Before You Edit: Probing-Guided Molecular Optimization for LLM Agents in Structure-Based Drug Design
summary: Structure-based drug design increasingly employs LLM agents to iteratively refine ligands against a target pocket, yet a viable ligand must satisfy two often-conflicting objectives -- binding affinity and druggability -- which single optimization steps rarely improve together. To quantify this difficulty, we introduce two diagnostic metrics: the first measures how often a single edit improves both objectives, and the second measures how often a gain on one objective comes with a loss on the other. Applying these diagnostics to current LLM-agent pipelines exposes a consistent failure mode: the agent performs molecular editing without knowing how the pocket-ligand complex responds to local modifications, thus rarely achieving joint improvement. Inspired by medicinal chemists, who probe the pocket-ligand complex with controlled analog edits before choosing an optimization direction, we propose \textbf{PROBE}, an optimization framework built around edit-response probing. PROBE first decomposes the ligand into editable sites and builds a pocket-specific \textbf{site map} that flags where joint gains are plausible, where the two objectives are likely in tension, and where liability substructures should be changed; it then performs controlled probe edits whose responses are distilled into an \textbf{EditManual}. Guided by the site map and EditManual, PROBE runs an iterative multi-agent loop in which an affinity agent, a druggability agent, and a co-optimization agent jointly produce edits. On the CrossDocked2020 benchmark, PROBE achieves state-of-the-art performance and substantially mitigates the failure modes exposed by our diagnostics metrics.

AI.tldr: PROBE is an optimization framework that uses edit-response probing to jointly improve binding affinity and druggability in structure-based drug design, achieving state-of-the-art performance on CrossDocked2020 by mitigating the failure mode where single edits rarely improve both objectives.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-agent pipelines for structure-based drug design struggle because molecular editing is performed without understanding how the pocket-ligand complex responds to local modifications, leading to a consistent failure where single edits rarely improve both binding affinity and druggability simultaneously.
AI.method: PROBE first decomposes ligands into editable sites and builds a pocket-specific site map that flags where joint gains are plausible, objectives conflict, or liability substructures exist. Controlled probe edits are then performed and distilled into an EditManual. A multi-agent loop (affinity agent, druggability agent, co-optimization agent) jointly produces edits guided by the site map and EditManual.
AI.result: On the CrossDocked2020 benchmark, PROBE achieves state-of-the-art performance and substantially mitigates the failure modes exposed by the two diagnostic metrics introduced in the paper.
AI.conclusion: Inspired by medicinal chemists who probe pocket-ligand complexes with controlled analog edits before choosing optimization directions, PROBE demonstrates that understanding local edit responses is key to jointly optimizing conflicting objectives in drug design.

title: Shape Your Body: Value Gradients for Multi-Embodiment Robot Design
summary: We propose to turn generalist multi-embodiment value functions into reusable models for robot design. Instead of running a new reinforcement learning co-design loop for each robot, we first train an embodiment-aware policy and value function across many robot designs. After training, the frozen value function is used as a differentiable surrogate to optimize candidate embodiments through value gradients. We evaluate our approach across different robot design settings, from perturbed single robots to held-out robots across morphology classes, with single models trained on up to 50 robots and design spaces of over 1100 continuous embodiment parameters. Beyond optimizing complete embodiments, we show that value gradients can identify performance-limiting design and control parameters, enabling both the optimization and the analysis of new robot designs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using a frozen, embodiment-aware value function (trained across many robot designs) as a differentiable surrogate to optimize robot embodiments via value gradients, eliminating the need for separate RL co-design loops per robot.
AI.motivation: Traditional robot co-design requires running a new reinforcement learning loop for each robot design, which is computationally expensive and inefficient. The authors aim to create a reusable model that can optimize multiple robot embodiments without retraining.
AI.method: First, train a single embodiment-aware policy and value function across many robot designs. Then, freeze the value function and use it as a differentiable surrogate to optimize candidate embodiments through value gradients (gradient-based optimization of design parameters).
AI.result: Evaluated across various settings (perturbed single robots, held-out robots across morphology classes) with single models trained on up to 50 robots and design spaces of over 1100 continuous embodiment parameters. Value gradients also identify performance-limiting design and control parameters.
AI.conclusion: The approach enables both optimization and analysis of new robot designs without running new RL co-design loops, making multi-embodiment value functions reusable for robot design.

title: PropLLM: Propagation-Aware Scene Reconstruction for Network Fault Diagnosis
summary: Network faults propagate layer by layer along topology and protocol dependencies, yet operations systems typically observe only symptomatic alerts at the tail end of propagation chains, where distinct root-cause faults may produce highly similar end-point symptoms. Existing approaches, whether rule-based, machine learning (ML)-based, or large language model (LLM)-based, fundamentally map the alert set to a diagnosis in a single pass and are structurally incapable of resolving this end-point ambiguity. This paper proposes PropLLM, which is the first to integrate the hop-by-hop scene reconstruction paradigm with the generative reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Starting from end-point alerts, PropLLM traces back hop-by-hop along the propagation path, retrieving verifiable factual evidence from a dual-layer knowledge graph (KG) at each hop, while the proposed Temporal Causal Propagation Attention (TCPA) mechanism encodes known topological causal priors directly into the attention computation to guide the model along the correct causal direction, ultimately localizing the root cause and determining the fault type through a fully evidenced causal chain. On a real-world Wi-Fi multimodal fault dataset, PropLLM improves fault type diagnosis accuracy by 3.9\% and root cause localization accuracy by 4.7\% over the strongest baseline, while reducing the hallucination rate by 50.8\%. Supplementary experiments on the TeleLogs 5G dataset further demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method across different network scenarios.

AI.tldr: PropLLM integrates hop-by-hop scene reconstruction with LLMs and a dual-layer KG with TCPA mechanism to trace fault propagation paths backwards, improving diagnosis accuracy by 3.9-4.7% and reducing hallucinations by 50.8% on real-world network datasets.
AI.motivation: Network faults propagate along topology and protocol dependencies, but existing systems only observe symptomatic alerts at propagation endpoints where distinct root causes produce similar symptoms. Current rule-based, ML-based, and LLM-based methods map alerts to diagnoses in a single pass, which is structurally incapable of resolving this end-point ambiguity.
AI.method: PropLLM traces faults hop-by-hop backward along the propagation path using LLM generative reasoning. At each hop, it retrieves verifiable evidence from a dual-layer knowledge graph (KG). The novel Temporal Causal Propagation Attention (TCPA) mechanism encodes topological causal priors into attention computation to guide the model along the correct causal direction, ultimately producing a fully evidenced causal chain for root cause localization and fault type determination.
AI.result: On a real-world Wi-Fi multimodal fault dataset: +3.9% fault type diagnosis accuracy, +4.7% root cause localization accuracy, -50.8% hallucination rate vs. strongest baseline. Supplementary experiments on TeleLogs 5G dataset confirm effectiveness across different network scenarios.
AI.conclusion: PropLLM demonstrates that integrating hop-by-hop propagation tracing with LLMs, structured KG evidence retrieval, and causal attention mechanisms significantly outperforms single-pass diagnosis methods, reducing ambiguity and hallucinations in network fault diagnosis.

title: BEVIO: Efficient Bird's-Eye-View based Sparse-Update Visual-Inertial Odometry for Lunar Day-Night Navigation
comment: Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation, Vienna
summary: Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO) provides smooth, high-rate state estimates and has been widely used for robotic navigation in both terrestrial and planetary applications. However, its performance is typically dependent on the frequency of visual updates, which is a challenge for planetary rovers operating under extreme resource constraints and low frame rates. This work investigates enabling reliable VIO with very sparse visual updates for lunar rover applications, addressing both day and night-time operations where feature associations become especially difficult under self-illumination conditions. We propose a Bird's Eye View (BEV)-based image matching scheme that remains robust to larger inter-frame motions and more reliable feature matching despite significant visual appearance changes. We extensively evaluate our proposed approach, BEVIO, through high-fidelity photorealistic lunar and real-time robotic experiments conducted using a half-scale lunar rover, in a long-term day-night deployment at Plaster City, CA, USA. The results demonstrate that our method enables reliable day and nighttime self-illuminated traverses at visual update rates as low as 0.25 Hz, underscoring its suitability for navigation on power- and compute-limited lunar rovers.

AI.tldr: BEVIO is a Bird's Eye View-based image matching scheme that enables reliable Visual-Inertial Odometry with very sparse visual updates (as low as 0.25 Hz) for lunar rovers operating under extreme resource constraints, validated through photorealistic simulations and real-world day-night rover experiments.
AI.motivation: VIO performance depends on visual update frequency, which is problematic for planetary rovers facing extreme resource constraints and low frame rates. Feature associations become especially difficult under self-illumination conditions during both day and night operations.
AI.method: Proposes a Bird's Eye View (BEV)-based image matching scheme that remains robust to larger inter-frame motions and provides more reliable feature matching despite significant visual appearance changes.
AI.result: BEVIO enables reliable day and nighttime self-illuminated traverses at visual update rates as low as 0.25 Hz, validated through high-fidelity photorealistic lunar simulations and real-time experiments with a half-scale lunar rover in a long-term day-night deployment.
AI.conclusion: The method is well-suited for navigation on power- and compute-limited lunar rovers, demonstrating robust VIO performance under extreme visual sparsity and challenging illumination conditions.

title: TRACE: Trajectory Risk-Aware Compression for Long-Horizon Agent Safety
summary: Long-horizon LLM agents produce safety evidence across long trajectories, where sparse, delayed, and compositional risk signals often escape local moderation. Existing turn-level or short-context detectors struggle to reliably retain and aggregate such evidence over extended horizons. We reframe long-horizon agent safety detection as trajectory-level evidence compression and propose Trajectory Risk-Aware Compression for Long-Horizon Agent Safety (TRACE). TRACE uses a Compressor-Reader design: the Compressor encodes the full trajectory into a compact latent evidence state under trajectory-level supervision, and the Reader judges the raw trajectory with this latent evidence state as a safety reference. This design helps aggregate dispersed risk cues and reduce premature evidence loss. Across ASSEBench, Pre-Ex-Bench, and R-Judge, TRACE achieves the best accuracy on all evaluated backbones, improving over strong baselines by up to 12.6 percentage points. On LongSafety, TRACE shows smaller performance degradation as context length grows. Attention visualizations and case studies suggest that the compressed reference helps the Reader focus on risk-critical segments and recover cross-step evidence. Code is available at https://github.com/Peregrine123/TRACE_official.

AI.tldr: TRACE is a Compressor-Reader framework that compresses long agent trajectories into a latent safety evidence state, enabling more effective detection of sparse, delayed, and compositional risks over extended horizons, achieving up to +12.6% accuracy over baselines.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon LLM agents produce safety-relevant evidence across long trajectories, but existing turn-level or short-context detectors fail to retain and aggregate sparse, delayed, and compositional risk signals over extended horizons.
AI.method: A Compressor-Reader architecture where the Compressor encodes the full trajectory into a compact latent evidence state under trajectory-level supervision, and the Reader judges the raw trajectory using this latent state as a safety reference.
AI.result: Best accuracy across ASSEBench, Pre-Ex-Bench, and R-Judge on all evaluated backbones, improving over strong baselines by up to 12.6 percentage points; smaller performance degradation on LongSafety as context length grows; attention visualizations show Reader focuses on risk-critical segments.
AI.conclusion: Trajectory-level evidence compression effectively aggregates dispersed risk cues and reduces premature evidence loss, improving long-horizon agent safety detection.

title: Infeasible optimization problems and the hierarchical augmented Lagrangian method in imitation learning
summary: Imitation learning (IL) is an effective approach to train complex robotics policies. Recent works have introduced hard constraints into imitation-learning optimization problems to ensure safety, stability, and robustness of the learned policy. However, we argue that these constraints are sometimes infeasible, which can lead to unstable or difficult training dynamics. We study a simple remedy for such situations based on recent theoretical results on the augmented Lagrangian method in infeasible settings. We show that our approach drives the learned policy toward the solution of a closest-feasible constrained IL problem with desirable properties. The method is illustrated on a toy driving example with a total-acceleration constraint and pedestrian-safety constraints, a setting in which infeasibility can naturally arise while still allowing a safe learned policy.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses infeasibility issues in constrained imitation learning by applying augmented Lagrangian methods to drive the policy toward the closest feasible solution, demonstrated on a driving task with acceleration and safety constraints.
AI.motivation: Hard constraints in imitation learning optimization can be infeasible, leading to unstable or difficult training dynamics. The authors seek a remedy for such infeasible constrained IL problems.
AI.method: The authors apply recent theoretical results on the augmented Lagrangian method in infeasible settings to constrained imitation learning, driving the learned policy toward the solution of the closest-feasible constrained IL problem.
AI.result: The approach drives the learned policy toward the solution of a closest-feasible constrained IL problem with desirable properties, demonstrated on a toy driving example with total-acceleration and pedestrian-safety constraints.
AI.conclusion: The augmented Lagrangian method effectively handles infeasible constraints in imitation learning, yielding stable training and safe policies even when original constraints cannot be strictly satisfied.

title: Efficient Test-time Inference for Generative Planning Models
summary: Generative models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for AI planning, yet their performance remains constrained by the training data distribution. One approach is to improve generated solutions during inference by scaling test-time compute. A more efficient alternative is to optimize the inference process itself. In this paper, we show that a modified version of a classical Open-Closed List (OCL) search provides just such an efficient inference procedure. Our algorithm synergizes two learned components: a generative model that performs fast rollouts from intermediate states and a heuristic model that prioritizes among candidate reasoning paths. Key contributions include novel exploration control mechanisms and integration of learned models within the OCL framework. Across multiple combinatorial planning domains, our approach outperforms both neurosymbolic search baselines and classical solvers in computational efficiency and solution quality.

AI.tldr: A modified Open-Closed List (OCL) search integrates generative and heuristic models to improve inference efficiency and solution quality in AI planning, outperforming neurosymbolic and classical solvers across combinatorial domains.
AI.motivation: Generative models for AI planning are constrained by training data distribution; current approaches either scale test-time compute or optimize inference. This paper aims to provide an efficient inference procedure that overcomes these limitations.
AI.method: A modified Open-Closed List (OCL) search synergizing two learned components: a generative model for fast rollouts from intermediate states and a heuristic model for prioritizing reasoning paths, with novel exploration control mechanisms.
AI.result: The approach outperforms both neurosymbolic search baselines and classical solvers in computational efficiency and solution quality across multiple combinatorial planning domains.
AI.conclusion: Modified OCL search with integrated learned models provides an efficient inference procedure that improves generative model-based planning beyond what training data alone enables.

title: Beyond Pure Sampling: Hybrid Optimization Mechanisms for Non-Convex Model Predictive Control
summary:
This paper investigates the optimization mechanisms of non-convex Model Predictive Control (MPC) using the Maximum Entropy Differential Dynamic Programming (ME-DDP) framework. Navigating non-convex cost landscapes induced by nonlinear dynamics, multiple obstacles, etc. remains a fundamental challenge in robotics, where gradient-based methods frequently converge to suboptimal local minima. We demonstrate a dual-step optimization mechanism designed to overcome these traps. (1) an initial phase of using DDP to exploit the gradient of the cost landscape, followed by (2) disruption of the optimization via sampling from policies characterized by the inverse Hessian of the action-value function. We provide a rigorous analysis of this sampling mechanism of three ME-DDP variants: Unimodal Gaussian ME-DDP, Multimodal Gaussian ME-DDP, and Stein Variational DDP. Furthermore, with navigation tasks of four robotic systems under cluttered environments, we conduct extensive benchmarking of three variants of the ME-DDP, against deterministic DDP, and one of the most successful sampling-based schemes, Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control with three policy parameterizations and update laws that correspond to those of ME-DDPs.
  The results show that in low-dimensional systems where the cost landscapes are relatively simple and local information is sufficiently representative, our framework consistently outperforms MPPIs. In high-dimensional systems, MPPI can occasionally discover aggressive maneuvers that enable it to steer the systems faster than DDP-based methods, whereas our method maintains a higher, more stable success rate.
  Finally, we validate the practical efficacy of the framework through hardware experiments with a quadrotor navigating a dense, non-convex obstacle field, confirming the robustness of the proposed framework for real-world deployment.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes Maximum Entropy Differential Dynamic Programming (ME-DDP) for non-convex MPC in robotics, showing its dual-step optimization (DDP gradient exploitation + Hessian-based sampling) outperforms deterministic DDP and MPPI in both simulation and hardware experiments with quadrotors.
AI.motivation: Non-convex cost landscapes induced by nonlinear dynamics and multiple obstacles cause gradient-based optimization methods to converge to suboptimal local minima, which remains a fundamental challenge in robotics.
AI.method: Dual-step optimization: (1) DDP exploits gradient of cost landscape, (2) sampling from policies characterized by inverse Hessian of action-value function disrupts local optima. Three ME-DDP variants analyzed: Unimodal Gaussian, Multimodal Gaussian, and Stein Variational DDP.
AI.result: In low-dimensional systems with simple cost landscapes, ME-DDP consistently outperforms MPPI. In high-dimensional systems, MPPI occasionally finds faster aggressive maneuvers, but ME-DDP maintains a higher, more stable success rate. Hardware experiments with a quadrotor navigating dense obstacle fields confirmed real-world robustness.
AI.conclusion: The ME-DDP framework provides robust optimization for non-convex MPC in robotics, with superior local optima escape ability via the proposed dual-step mechanism, validated both in simulation and real-world quadrotor deployment.

title: Hidden Thoughts Are Not Secret: Reasoning Trace Exposure in LLMs
summary: Reasoning traces have become a valuable form of learning signals for improving and transferring the capabilities of large language models. In particular, detailed traces can help distill reasoning behavior from stronger teacher models into weaker student models. The value of capability transfer has motivated many deployed systems with reasoning models to hide raw internal traces and expose at most summaries and answers to users. As a result, we ask whether such interface-level trace hiding prevents users from obtaining useful reasoning supervision through prompting. We study this question with Reasoning Exposure Prompting (REP), a lightweight in-context elicitation method that uses shadow-model-generated demonstrations wrapped in auxiliary code-like formats to raise user-visible reasoning traces from a victim model. Across the common reasoning dataset, different victim models, and different student model distillation, REP substantially increases similarity between exposed and REP-conditioned internal traces while preserving useful reasoning signals.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether interface-level hiding of raw reasoning traces in LLMs prevents users from extracting useful reasoning signals. They propose Reasoning Exposure Prompting (REP), a lightweight in-context method using shadow-model demonstrations in code-like formats to elicit reasoning traces from victim models, showing increased similarity to internal traces and preserved reasoning utility for distillation.
AI.motivation: As reasoning models in deployed systems hide raw internal traces (exposing only summaries/answers), the authors investigate whether such hiding effectively prevents users from obtaining useful reasoning supervision through prompting alone.
AI.method: The authors propose Reasoning Exposure Prompting (REP), a lightweight in-context elicitation method that uses shadow-model-generated demonstrations wrapped in auxiliary code-like formats to raise user-visible reasoning traces from a victim model.
