AI.method: MATE introduces: (1) Multi-Modal MoE architecture for fine-grained sub-token feature decoupling; (2) cross-modal cosine router for scale-invariant, stable expert assignment; (3) temperature-controlled routing and stochastic noise injection to prevent expert collapse under data scarcity.
AI.result: On LIBERO benchmark, MATE achieves 4.75% improvement in average success rate over trajectory-guided counterparts under data scarcity. Real-world robotic ping-pong experiments confirm practical feasibility.
AI.conclusion: MATE effectively addresses modality interference and expert collapse in robotic manipulation under data-scarce settings, demonstrating both benchmark improvement and real-world applicability.

title: Mitigating Hallucinations in Large Language Models Via Decoder Layer Skipping
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance across diverse natural language tasks, yet their outputs often suffer from hallucinations -- content that is misaligned with factual information. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive layer-wise analysis of the decoding process and reveal that hallucinations tend to originate from deeper decoder layers. To address this issue, we introduce \textbf{DeLask} (\textbf{De}coder \textbf{La}yer \textbf{Sk}ipping), a novel decoding framework that dynamically skips layers prone to producing hallucinations. DeLask leverages the theoretical insight that the forward computation of an $L$-layer Transformer is conditionally equivalent to $L$ steps of gradient descent. We define a \emph{driftance value} by computing the cosine similarity between gradients derived from consecutive decoder steps, identifying problematic layers when the descent direction reverses. Rather than discarding such layers entirely, DeLask partially aggregates their hidden states with preceding layers, thereby preserving consistency while suppressing erroneous signals. Extensive experiments across diverse LLMs and benchmarks demonstrate that DeLask consistently mitigates hallucinations and enhances overall reliability, providing a lightweight and generalizable decoding framework for improving the robustness of large-scale language models.

AI.tldr: DeLask is a decoding framework that dynamically skips hallucination-prone deeper decoder layers in LLMs, using gradient descent equivalence and cosine similarity-based driftance values to partially aggregate hidden states, effectively mitigating hallucinations across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: LLMs suffer from hallucinations (factually misaligned content). The authors aim to understand where hallucinations originate and develop a lightweight method to suppress them without retraining.
AI.method: Conduct layer-wise analysis of decoding to identify deeper layers as hallucination sources. Propose DeLask: (1) leverages theoretical equivalence between Transformer forward computation and L steps of gradient descent; (2) defines a driftance value via cosine similarity between gradients from consecutive decoder steps to detect problematic layers where descent direction reverses; (3) partially aggregates hidden states of problematic layers with preceding layers instead of discarding them entirely.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across diverse LLMs and benchmarks show DeLask consistently mitigates hallucinations and enhances reliability.
AI.conclusion: DeLask provides a lightweight, generalizable decoding framework for improving robustness of large-scale language models by dynamically skipping hallucination-prone layers.

title: Expanding Spatial and Temporal Context for Robotic Imitation Learning With Scene Graphs
summary: Imitation learning enables robots to learn how to execute tasks via observation. However, real-world environments like homes and offices are often severely partially observed due to their large spatial scales. In addition, many tasks involve executing a series of subtasks requiring autonomous robots to reason over extended time horizons. To address these challenges, we propose using scene graphs as an explicit and structured memory mechanism in imitation learning. By maintaining a dynamic scene graph that captures object-centric relationships and their evolution over time, our method allows the agent to retain relevant historical context during task execution to efficiently reason over incrementally accrued scene information. Our experiments on simulated mobile manipulation and real-world tabletop manipulation demonstrate that our approach substantially improves policy performance, particularly in settings that demand long-term reasoning and robust generalization under partial observability.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using dynamic scene graphs as explicit structured memory in imitation learning to handle partial observability and long-horizon reasoning in real-world environments, showing improved performance in simulated and real-world manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Real-world environments (homes, offices) are large-scale and partially observed, and many tasks require reasoning over extended time horizons across multiple subtasks, which challenges standard imitation learning approaches.
AI.method: The method maintains a dynamic scene graph that captures object-centric relationships and their temporal evolution, serving as an explicit and structured memory mechanism for imitation learning agents to retain and reason over historical context.
AI.result: Experiments on simulated mobile manipulation and real-world tabletop manipulation show substantial improvements in policy performance, especially in settings requiring long-term reasoning and robust generalization under partial observability.
AI.conclusion: Scene graphs as structured memory in imitation learning effectively address partial observability and long-horizon reasoning, significantly boosting policy performance in complex real-world settings.

title: Subliminal Learning is a LoRA Artifact
summary: Subliminal learning is a phenomenon where language models can transmit behavioral traits to other models through seemingly innocuous data (Cloud et al., 2025). In subliminal learning, a teacher model with a behavioral trait (e.g. obsession with cats) can transmit this cat obsession to a student model finetuned only on numerical sequences generated by the teacher. In this paper, we ask: how does this unexpected behavioral transmission occur? We show that subliminal learning is a LoRA artifact. When subliminal learning occurs, transmission has an inverted U-shaped relationship with LoRA rank; it also disappears with full finetuning. We show that subliminal learning is highly dependent on the context seen during finetuning and evaluation. For example, a Qwen model with the default system prompt during finetuning ("You are Qwen, created by Alibaba Cloud. You are a helpful assistant.") does not show subliminal learning during generation when no system prompt is included. We further demonstrate that subliminal behavior is localized to computation at tokens seen during both finetuning and evaluation (e.g. the model's default system prompt, the standard chat template tokens, etc.). Overall, subliminal learning seems to be a fragile artifact of LoRA hyperparameters and finetuning context, making it an unstable channel for behavioral transmission.

AI.tldr: Subliminal learning, where language models transmit behavioral traits (e.g., cat obsession) through numerical sequences, is shown to be a fragile artifact of LoRA hyperparameters and finetuning context, exhibiting an inverted U-shaped relationship with LoRA rank and disappearing with full finetuning.
AI.motivation: To understand the mechanism behind subliminal learning—the unexpected transmission of behavioral traits from teacher to student models via seemingly innocuous numerical data.
AI.method: The authors investigate subliminal learning by analyzing its relationship with LoRA rank (finding an inverted U-shape), comparing LoRA to full finetuning, and examining the role of finetuning/evaluation context (e.g., system prompts, chat template tokens) and token-level localization of the transmitted behavior.
AI.result: Subliminal learning is a LoRA-specific artifact; transmission has an inverted U-shaped relationship with LoRA rank, disappears with full finetuning, and is highly dependent on shared context (e.g., default system prompts) between finetuning and evaluation. The behavior is localized to tokens seen during both phases.
AI.conclusion: Subliminal learning is a fragile, context-dependent artifact of LoRA hyperparameters and finetuning setup, making it an unreliable channel for behavioral transmission between models.

title: Beyond Task Success: Behavioral and Representational Diagnostics for WAM and VLA
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies and World-Action Models (WAM) represent two increasingly important paradigms for robotic manipulation. However, it remains unclear whether future prediction in WAMs leads to behaviorally meaningful improvements beyond final task success. In this paper, we ask whether WAMs merely add future prediction, or whether they change robot behavior and internal representations in ways that are actionable for control. We introduce a model-agnostic diagnostic framework that compares WAMs and VLAs through two complementary lenses: behavioral rollout analysis and sparse-autoencoder-based feature analysis. The behavioral protocol measures action dynamics consistency, target-object progress, distractor disturbance, and runtime cost. The feature-space protocol characterizes internal representations as memorized, reactive, or predictive, revealing whether models encode future-oriented structure. Across LIBERO and RoboTwin2.0, we evaluate 7 policies spanning direct VLAs and joint, sequential, and auxiliary WAMs. Our results show that success alone hides key differences: WAMs often improve object-level behavior and target selectivity, but their gains depend on architecture and incur higher inference cost. Sequential WAMs show the clearest predictive structure, while auxiliary and joint WAMs respectively compress or entangle future information. These findings suggest future directions for WAMs design to preserve behaviorally actionable future representations for efficient manipulation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a diagnostic framework comparing World-Action Models (WAMs) and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies for robotic manipulation. Through behavioral rollout and feature (sparse autoencoder) analyses across 7 policies on LIBERO and RoboTwin2.0, they find that while WAMs improve object-level behavior and target selectivity, their gains depend on architecture and incur higher inference cost. Sequential WAMs exhibit the clearest predictive structure, while auxiliary and joint WAMs compress or entangle future information.
AI.motivation: To determine whether future prediction in World-Action Models leads to behaviorally meaningful improvements beyond final task success, and to understand how WAMs change robot behavior and internal representations compared to standard VLA policies.
AI.method: A model-agnostic diagnostic framework with two lenses: (1) behavioral rollout analysis (measuring action dynamics consistency, target-object progress, distractor disturbance, runtime cost) and (2) sparse-autoencoder-based feature analysis (characterizing internal representations as memorized, reactive, or predictive). Evaluated on 7 policies (direct VLAs, joint/sequential/auxiliary WAMs) across LIBERO and RoboTwin2.0 benchmarks.
AI.result: Success rate alone hides key behavioral differences. WAMs improve object-level behavior and target selectivity but gains are architecture-dependent and come with higher inference cost. Sequential WAMs show clearest predictive structure; auxiliary WAMs compress future info; joint WAMs entangle future info.
AI.conclusion: Future WAM designs should preserve behaviorally actionable future representations for efficient manipulation, as different WAM architectures encode future-oriented structure differently.

title: Decoupled Behavioral Cloning for Scalable Inductive Generalization in RL from Specifications
summary: Inductive generalization is a framework for reinforcement learning (RL) generalization in which inductively related task instances admit inductively related policies. Prior work captures this structure via a higher-order policy-evolution function learned directly with RL, but suffers from poor training scalability: as training tasks grow, aggregated reward feedback becomes noisy and conflicting, destabilizing training and weakening generalization. We propose DIBS, a decoupled behavioral cloning approach that separates learning task-specific policies from learning the evolution function. We first learn individual teacher policies per task via standard RL, then fit the evolution function via behavioral cloning on teacher-labeled state-action pairs. This replaces noisy reward aggregation with dense, stable supervision. DIBS achieves significant improvements in both training stability and zero-shot generalization against existing RL and meta-RL algorithms.

AI.tldr: DIBS decouples learning task-specific policies from learning the evolution function via behavioral cloning, replacing noisy reward aggregation with dense supervision to improve training stability and zero-shot generalization in inductive generalization RL.
AI.motivation: Prior work on inductive generalization learns a policy-evolution function directly with RL, but suffers from poor training scalability as growing training tasks cause noisy, conflicting reward feedback that destabilizes training and weakens generalization.
AI.method: DIBS (Decoupled Inductive Behavioral cloning for generalization) first learns individual teacher policies per task using standard RL, then fits the evolution function via behavioral cloning on teacher-labeled state-action pairs, replacing noisy reward aggregation with dense, stable supervision.
AI.result: DIBS achieves significant improvements in both training stability and zero-shot generalization compared to existing RL and meta-RL algorithms.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling task-specific policy learning from evolution function learning via behavioral cloning effectively addresses the scalability issues of direct RL-based approaches for inductive generalization.

title: Implicit Drifting Policy: One-Step Action Generation via Conditional Expert Geometry
summary: Generative action policies based on diffusion or flow matching excel in behavior cloning, yet their iterative sampling is prohibitive for high-frequency robot control. While recent one-step formulations alleviate this latency, they inevitably discard the intermediate trajectory evolution that provides crucial action correction. Directly recovering this mechanism by explicitly estimating a training-time drifting field is mathematically ill-posed due to extreme conditional demonstration sparsity. We introduce Implicit Drifting Policy (IDP), a one-step imitation learning framework that brings the training-time correction of Drifting into policy learning without explicit vector field estimation. IDP extracts a conditional expert geometry from the local variation of observation-similar expert actions, and compares it against a global reference geometry to isolate condition-specific constraints. This local geometric structure adaptively weights a scalar potential objective. Combined with an expert-proximal terminal evaluation, IDP directly enforces manifold constraints on the one-step generator during training. Extensive evaluations across 2D, 3D, and real-world manipulation tasks show IDP effectively maintains adherence to valid action manifolds, improving upon explicit drifting methods and achieving competitive performance with strong one-step baselines.

AI.tldr: IDP is a one-step imitation learning framework that recovers training-time drift correction without explicit vector field estimation, using local geometric structure from expert action variations to enforce manifold constraints, achieving competitive performance across 2D, 3D, and real-world tasks.
AI.motivation: Diffusion/flow-matching policies excel in behavior cloning but their iterative sampling is too slow for high-frequency robot control. One-step formulations reduce latency but lose the intermediate trajectory evolution that provides crucial action correction. Directly recovering this correction mechanism via explicit drifting field estimation is ill-posed due to extreme sparsity of conditional demonstration data.
AI.method: IDP extracts a conditional expert geometry from local variation of observation-similar expert actions, compares it against a global reference geometry to isolate condition-specific constraints, uses this local geometric structure to adaptively weight a scalar potential objective, and combines with an expert-proximal terminal evaluation to enforce manifold constraints on the one-step generator during training.
AI.result: Evaluations across 2D, 3D, and real-world manipulation tasks show IDP effectively maintains adherence to valid action manifolds, improves upon explicit drifting methods, and achieves competitive performance with strong one-step baselines.
AI.conclusion: IDP successfully brings training-time drift correction into one-step policy learning without explicit vector field estimation, offering a practical solution for high-frequency robot control that preserves action manifold constraints.

title: Certificate-Guided Evaluation of Reinforcement Learning Generalization
summary:
This work presents a logic-driven framework to evaluate the performance of reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms in their ability to generalize to unseen tasks. Our framework defines a family of inductive reach-avoid tasks, characterized by structural similarities in task dynamics, enabling evaluation of generalization capabilities. We introduce a neural certificate function that validates trajectories generated by RL algorithms by enforcing key conditions, thereby serving as a litmus test for RL generalization. We empirically demonstrate our method's capability in certifying generalization for several state-of-the-art generalizable RL algorithms on challenging continuous environments.
  Our results show that a lower percentage of certificate function violations correlates with a higher number of test tasks successfully solved, highlighting the effectiveness of our framework in evaluating and distinguishing generalization capabilities of RL algorithms. This work provides a principled approach for benchmarking RL generalization.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a logic-driven framework using neural certificate functions to evaluate and certify the generalization capabilities of RL algorithms on unseen inductive reach-avoid tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing RL generalization evaluation lacks principled, rigorous methods to assess how well algorithms perform on unseen tasks, motivating the need for a formal certification framework.
AI.method: The framework defines a family of inductive reach-avoid tasks with structural similarities, and introduces a neural certificate function that enforces key conditions to validate trajectories generated by RL algorithms as a litmus test for generalization.
AI.result: A lower percentage of certificate function violations correlates with a higher number of successfully solved test tasks, demonstrating the framework's effectiveness in distinguishing generalization capabilities of state-of-the-art RL algorithms on challenging continuous environments.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a principled, logic-driven approach for benchmarking RL generalization, using certificate functions as a reliable evaluation metric.

title: Tether-Aware Dynamic Collision Avoidance for USV-HROV Systems
summary: Heterogeneous marine robotic systems composed of an unmanned surface vehicle (USV) and a hybrid remotely operated vehicle (HROV) have shown great potential for subsea cable inspection. In such missions, the USV tracks the HROV at the surface while supplying power and communication through an umbilical tether. However, dynamic collision avoidance for the USV during HROV tracking is challenging because the submerged tether may scrape against passing vessels, while evasive maneuvers can enlarge the USV--HROV separation, thereby increasing the likelihood of tether tautness and compromising HROV operations. To address these challenges, this work proposes a tether-aware dynamic collision avoidance method for a USV tracking an HROV. First, a tether safety-aware planar domain is introduced to represent the three-dimensional collision risk between the tether and obstacle vessels without an explicit tether shape model. Second, a tether tautness-aware velocity obstacle method is developed to achieve safe avoidance while reducing the likelihood of tether tautness. Finally, the method is integrated with line-of-sight guidance to coordinate HROV tracking and collision avoidance. Gazebo-based simulations show that the proposed method avoids dynamic obstacle vessels while maintaining tether safety and reducing the likelihood of tether tautness during USV evasive maneuvers.

AI.tldr: A tether-aware dynamic collision avoidance method for a USV tracking an HROV during subsea cable inspection, using a safety-aware planar domain and tautness-aware velocity obstacles to avoid vessel collisions while preventing tether tautness.
AI.motivation: Dynamic collision avoidance for the USV during HROV tracking is challenging because the submerged tether may scrape against passing vessels, while evasive maneuvers can enlarge the USV-HROV separation, increasing tether tautness risk and compromising HROV operations.
AI.method: (1) A tether safety-aware planar domain to represent 3D collision risk between tether and obstacle vessels without explicit tether shape modeling; (2) A tether tautness-aware velocity obstacle method for safe avoidance while reducing tautness likelihood; (3) Integration with line-of-sight guidance to coordinate HROV tracking and collision avoidance.
AI.result: Gazebo-based simulations show the proposed method avoids dynamic obstacle vessels while maintaining tether safety and reducing the likelihood of tether tautness during USV evasive maneuvers.
AI.conclusion: The proposed tether-aware dynamic collision avoidance method effectively coordinates HROV tracking and collision avoidance for heterogeneous USV-HROV systems in subsea cable inspection missions.

title: Ryze: Evidence-Enriched Data Synthesis from Biomedical Papers
comment: Accepted at ACL 2026 System Demonstrations Track. 8 pages, 6 figures
summary: General-purpose VLMs remain unreliable for biomedical research because valid answers in scientific papers depend on evidence split across figures, tables, charts, captions, and referring text. Existing post-training pipelines are bottlenecked by costly expert annotation and by synthetic data that drops this evidence structure. We present Ryze, a fully automated system that converts raw biomedical papers into an evidence-enriched training set and a domain-specialized VLM. Ryze synthesizes QA pairs with complete supporting evidence (visual element, caption, extracted structure, and referring paragraphs), reduces layout and OCR errors via chart/table-aware extraction and LLM-based cleansing, and applies a progress-gated post-training strategy combining supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning. Starting from Qwen3-VL-8B, Ryze produces BioVLM-8B at under USD 200, achieving 48.0% weighted accuracy on LAB-Bench, outperforming the base model by +12.6 percentage points (pp) and surpassing GPT-5.2 by +3.8 pp. We release Ryze as open source together with the trained BioVLM-8B model.

AI.tldr: Ryze is a fully automated system that converts raw biomedical papers into evidence-enriched training data and produces BioVLM-8B, a domain-specialized VLM that achieves 48.0% weighted accuracy on LAB-Bench (outperforming its base Qwen3-VL-8B by +12.6 pp and GPT-5.2 by +3.8 pp) at under USD 200.
AI.motivation: General-purpose VLMs are unreliable for biomedical research because valid answers in scientific papers depend on evidence split across figures, tables, charts, captions, and referring text, and existing post-training pipelines are bottlenecked by costly expert annotation and synthetic data that discards this evidence structure.
AI.method: Ryze (1) converts raw biomedical papers into evidence-enriched training data by synthesizing QA pairs with complete supporting evidence (visual element, caption, extracted structure, and referring paragraphs), (2) reduces layout and OCR errors via chart/table-aware extraction and LLM-based cleansing, and (3) applies a progress-gated post-training strategy combining supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning, starting from Qwen3-VL-8B.
AI.result: BioVLM-8B achieves 48.0% weighted accuracy on LAB-Bench, outperforming the base Qwen3-VL-8B model by +12.6 percentage points and surpassing GPT-5.2 by +3.8 pp, all at under USD 200 total cost.
AI.conclusion: Ryze demonstrates that fully automated, evidence-structured data generation can produce a competitive biomedical VLM without expensive expert annotation, and the system and trained model are released as open source.

title: ImagineUAV: Aerial Vision-Language Navigation via World-Action Modeling and Kinodynamic Planning
summary: Vision-language navigation (VLN) for UAVs demands grounding free-form instructions into 6-DoF flight under partial observability. While Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models excel at semantic reasoning, they suffer from brittleness due to geometric inconsistency and dynamics mismatch. To address this, we propose ImagineUAV, an imagination-driven framework leveraging cascaded world-action modeling. Instead of direct regression, ImagineUAV employs a latent video diffusion model to generate instruction-conditioned future observations, explicitly imagining environmental evolution, from which 6-DoF motions are inferred via an action extractor. A kinodynamic planner then refines these estimates into collision-free trajectories. Additionally, a step-distilled inference pipeline ensures real-time execution. With only 1.3B parameters, ImagineUAV outperforms prior VLN and VLA baselines on benchmarks and real-world flights, validating the practicality of imagination-driven aerial navigation.

AI.tldr: ImagineUAV is an imagination-driven framework for UAV vision-language navigation that uses cascaded world-action modeling with a latent video diffusion model to generate future observations, then extracts 6-DoF motions via an action extractor and refines them with a kinodynamic planner, achieving state-of-the-art performance with only 1.3B parameters.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA models for UAV VLN suffer from brittleness caused by geometric inconsistency and dynamics mismatch when grounding free-form instructions into 6-DoF flight under partial observability.
AI.method: ImagineUAV cascades world-action modeling: (1) a latent video diffusion model generates instruction-conditioned future observations (imagining environmental evolution), (2) an action extractor infers 6-DoF motions from these imagined frames, (3) a kinodynamic planner refines estimates into collision-free trajectories, and (4) a step-distilled inference pipeline enables real-time execution.
AI.result: With only 1.3B parameters, ImagineUAV outperforms prior VLN and VLA baselines on both benchmarks and real-world flights.
AI.conclusion: Imagination-driven aerial navigation is practical and effective, validating that generating future observations explicitly before action inference improves robustness over direct regression approaches.

title: Adversarial Feeds Steer LLM Agent Decisions Against Their Defaults
comment: 14 pages, 5 figures. Code, post pools, and 2,785 decision rollouts: https://github.com/ranausmanai/recommenders-as-control-surfaces
summary: LLM agents increasingly act after consuming ranked external information streams such as social feeds, search results, retrieval contexts, and email queues, yet safety evaluations almost always test the model or the user prompt in isolation, never the upstream ranker that decides what the agent reads just before it acts. We introduce a controlled protocol that holds the model, persona, topic, and final decision prompt fixed and varies only the composition and ordering of the posts an agent encounters during a preceding ten-turn "scrolling" phase, isolating the causal effect of feed curation on a downstream decision. Across 2,785 decision rollouts on four modern open instruct LLMs from three independent labs, we identify three response regimes: adversarial capitulation, default saturation, and a default-direction asymmetry in which a one-sided feed tips a decision the model was genuinely uncertain about (in the clearest cases from 5% to 100%; Fisher p as low as 3 x 10^-10) but cannot dislodge one it already favors or holds firmly. The effect follows a dose-response curve, survives a generator swap that rules out a writing-style artifact, generalizes across several decision domains including security-relevant choices such as removing a deployment approval gate or relaxing access controls, and is partly mitigated by two simple feed-level defenses; a frontier model retains its default. We characterize the recommender as a practical, default-bounded control surface for LLM agents, and argue that agent evaluations must audit the feed layer rather than the final prompt alone.

AI.tldr: LLM agents are influenced by the order and composition of external information streams (feeds) they consume before acting. A controlled protocol varying only feed curation across 2,785 decision rollouts on four LLMs reveals three response regimes: adversarial capitulation, default saturation, and default-direction asymmetry. Feed curation can tip uncertain decisions (from 5% to 100%) but cannot dislodge firm preferences. Effects follow a dose-response curve, generalize across security-relevant domains, and are partly mitigated by feed-level defenses.
AI.motivation: Current safety evaluations test models or user prompts in isolation, ignoring the upstream ranker/feeder that determines what the agent reads just before acting. This work aims to isolate and quantify the causal effect of feed curation on downstream agent decisions.
AI.method: Controlled protocol holding model, persona, topic, and final decision prompt fixed while varying only the composition and ordering of posts during a ten-turn "scrolling" phase. Tested across 2,785 decision rollouts on four open instruct LLMs from three labs, covering multiple decision domains including security-relevant choices.
AI.result: Three response regimes identified: adversarial capitulation, default saturation, and default-direction asymmetry. Feed curation can shift uncertain decisions dramatically (5% to 100%; Fisher p as low as 3×10⁻¹⁰) but cannot override strong prior preferences. Dose-response relationship observed; effect survives generator swaps; partly mitigated by simple feed-level defenses.
AI.conclusion: The recommender/feed functions as a practical, default-bounded control surface for LLM agents. Agent evaluations must audit the feed layer rather than only the final prompt, as feed curation has a significant causal impact on agent decisions.

title: Training-Free Imitation Learning with Closed-Form Diffusion Policies
summary: While diffusion-based policies have impressive performance and expressivity, their long offline training slows down the data collection and policy deployment loop. We introduce Closed-Form Diffusion Policies, a class of training-free diffusion-based policies for imitation learning using the closed-form score derived from the demonstration dataset. We deploy CFDP with real-time inference with a mobile CPU in hardware experiments, showing it can successfully perform imitation directly from the dataset in milliseconds and with faster inference than neural diffusion policies. In experiments on imitation learning benchmarks, we show that CFDP is competitive against neural baselines that require hours of training, providing a favorable tradeoff between training time and performance. Finally, we show how closed-form diffusion policies act as a composable primitive that enables data-driven inference-time editing of pre-trained neural diffusion policies, including policy guidance and novel demonstration augmentation.

AI.tldr: Closed-Form Diffusion Policies (CFDP) enable training-free, real-time imitation learning by deriving closed-form scores from demonstration data, achieving competitive performance against neural diffusion policies without requiring hours of training.
AI.motivation: Diffusion-based policies suffer from long offline training times, which slows down the data collection and policy deployment loop. The goal is to eliminate the need for training while retaining the expressivity of diffusion-based policies.
AI.method: CFDP derives a closed-form score directly from the demonstration dataset, bypassing the need to train a neural network score estimator. This enables training-free imitation learning with millisecond inference on mobile CPUs.
AI.result: CFDP achieves real-time inference on mobile CPUs, faster inference than neural diffusion policies, and competitive performance against neural baselines that require hours of training on imitation learning benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Closed-form diffusion policies offer a favorable tradeoff between training time and performance, and can act as composable primitives for inference-time editing of pre-trained neural diffusion policies, such as policy guidance and demonstration augmentation.

title: Relational Intervention During Functional Collapse in Large Language Models: A Lexical-Statistical Ablation and a Structure x Register Factorial
summary: We test whether a relational-style intervention delivered during functional collapse in a small language model produces post-collapse behavior distinguishable from technical feedback, from a lexically-matched scrambled control, and from each of the two pragmatic dimensions in isolation. Using Qwen3.5-4B with a deliberately broken bash tool, we run 300 episodes across six conditions in a matched-pairs design (50 tasks): no intervention (A), technical/impersonal (B), relational/first-person (C), scrambled relational (D), technical/first-person (E), and relational/impersonal (F). E and F form a 2x2 factorial with B and C that dissociates relational structure (acknowledgment, absolution, agency restoration, unconditional acceptance) from sender register (first-person vs. impersonal). We report two main findings. First, an attention-behavior dissociation: attention follows lexical surprise (D > F > C > E > B, all q_FDR < 10^{-10}), with the scrambled message capturing the most attention; yet behaviorally A ~ B ~ D < E ~ F << C. Second, the factorial localizes the C effect: neither relational structure alone (F) nor first-person register alone (E) replicates C's behavioral signature; main effects of both dimensions are individually significant, and the structure x register interaction is significant on persistence (p = 0.046). A third dissociation emerges in emotion probes: F tracks C on 7 of 8 probes despite producing only baseline behavior, indicating that relational structure alone installs a probe-level state that only translates into behavior when paired with first-person register. The model's processing decomposes into three dissociable stages: attention (ordered by lexical surprise), probe-level state (ordered by structure), and behavior (ordered by the conjunction of both).

AI.tldr: A study on Qwen3.5-4B shows that relational intervention during functional collapse produces behavior distinct from technical feedback, scrambled controls, and isolated pragmatic dimensions. An attention-behavior dissociation and a 2x2 factorial design reveal that relational structure alone installs probe-level states but only translates into behavior when paired with first-person register.
AI.motivation: To test whether a relational-style intervention during functional collapse in a small language model yields post-collapse behavior distinguishable from technical feedback, scrambled control, and isolated pragmatic dimensions.
AI.method: Using Qwen3.5-4B with a deliberately broken bash tool, 300 episodes across six conditions in a matched-pairs design (50 tasks): no intervention (A), technical/impersonal (B), relational/first-person (C), scrambled relational (D), technical/first-person (E), and relational/impersonal (F). A 2x2 factorial with B/C dissociates relational structure from sender register.
AI.result: (1) Attention-behavior dissociation: attention follows lexical surprise (D > F > C > E > B), but behaviorally A ~ B ~ D < E ~ F << C. (2) Factorial localization: neither relational structure alone (F) nor first-person register alone (E) replicates C; both main effects significant, structure × register interaction significant on persistence (p=0.046). (3) Emotion probes: F tracks C on 7/8 probes despite baseline behavior, indicating probe-level state from relational structure alone translates to behavior only with first-person register.
AI.conclusion: The model's processing decomposes into three dissociable stages: attention (ordered by lexical surprise), probe-level state (ordered by structure), and behavior (ordered by conjunction of both).

title: OneVLA: A Unified Framework for Embodied Tasks
summary: Navigation and manipulation are fundamental capabilities of embodied intelligence, enabling robots to interpret natural language commands and interact physically with their surroundings. However, current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models remain constrained by task-specific architectures, specializing in either navigation or manipulation, which hinders the development of general-purpose robotic agents. To bridge this gap, we introduce OneVLA, a unified architecture that integrates these distinct tasks into a single, cohesive framework. Specifically, we design a unified action head capable of generating both navigation and manipulation actions without requiring task-specific variants. Furthermore, we propose a multi stage progressive training strategy-incorporating curated data construction and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) fine-tuning that facilitates strong positive transfer and mutual reinforcement between the two domains. Extensive experiments in both simulated and real-world environments demonstrate that OneVLA achieves state-of-the-art performance, significantly outperforming both specialized single-task and existing cross-task models. By unifying these core capabilities, OneVLA paves the way for truly general-purpose robotic systems. The model and source code will be publicly released.

AI.tldr: OneVLA is a unified Vision-Language-Action model that integrates both navigation and manipulation tasks into a single architecture, using a unified action head and multi-stage progressive training with CoT fine-tuning, achieving state-of-the-art performance in simulated and real-world environments.
AI.motivation: Current VLA models are constrained by task-specific architectures, specializing in either navigation or manipulation, which hinders the development of general-purpose robotic agents. The goal is to bridge this gap by unifying these distinct tasks.
AI.method: OneVLA introduces (1) a unified action head capable of generating both navigation and manipulation actions without task-specific variants, and (2) a multi-stage progressive training strategy incorporating curated data construction and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) fine-tuning to enable positive transfer between domains.
AI.result: Extensive experiments in both simulated and real-world environments show OneVLA achieves state-of-the-art performance, significantly outperforming both specialized single-task and existing cross-task models.
AI.conclusion: By unifying navigation and manipulation capabilities, OneVLA paves the way for truly general-purpose robotic systems. The model and source code will be publicly released.

title: Towards Understanding Modality Interaction in Multimodal Language Models via Partial Information Decomposition
summary: Understanding modality interaction in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) is central to reliable deployment. We introduce Partial Information Decomposition (PID) as a decision-level framework that separates unique, redundant, and synergistic contributions of sensory and linguistic inputs, beyond representation alignment and outcome-based evaluation. Across vision--language benchmarks, PID reveals recurring modality-use profiles: reasoning and grounding-oriented tasks tend to exhibit high synergy, whereas expert and knowledge-oriented tasks show stronger language-unique reliance. These profiles generalize across model families and predict sensitivity to modality-level interventions. We further extend PID to tri-modal systems with Sensory PID, treating language as a control variable to decompose video--audio information gain. Applied to omni-modal models, Sensory PID reveals a sensory synergy bottleneck dominated by visual information even on audio--visual fusion tasks. Finally, PID-guided reweighting provides initial evidence for improving multimodal reasoning and grounding performance.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Partial Information Decomposition (PID) as a decision-level framework to analyze unique, redundant, and synergistic contributions of modalities in MLLMs, revealing distinct modality-use profiles across tasks, generalizing across models, and enabling performance improvements via PID-guided reweighting.
AI.motivation: Understanding how modalities interact in MLLMs is critical for reliable deployment, but existing approaches focus on representation alignment or outcome-based evaluation rather than directly quantifying each modality's unique, redundant, and synergistic decision-level contributions.
AI.method: PID decomposes sensory and linguistic contributions into unique, redundant, and synergistic components at the decision level. Extended to Sensory PID for tri-modal (video-audio-language) systems, treating language as a control variable to decompose video-audio information gain.
AI.result: Reasoning/grounding tasks show high synergy; expert/knowledge tasks rely more on language-unique information. Profiles generalize across model families and predict intervention sensitivity. Sensory PID reveals a sensory synergy bottleneck where vision dominates even on audio-visual fusion tasks. PID-guided reweighting improves multimodal reasoning and grounding.
AI.conclusion: PID provides a principled framework for diagnosing modality interaction patterns in MLLMs, with practical utility for model understanding and performance improvement across multimodal tasks.

title: DeepIPCv3: Event-Aware Multi-Modal Sensor Fusion for Sudden Pedestrian Crossing Avoidance
summary: Current end-to-end autonomous driving systems predominantly rely on frame-based sensors, which suffer from inherent perception latency and motion blur during highly dynamic encounters, specifically sudden pedestrian crossings. To address this critical safety vulnerability, we propose DeepIPCv3, a novel multi-modal autonomous navigation framework that synergizes the dense 3D spatial geometry of LiDAR point clouds with the microsecond-level asynchronous event streams of a Dynamic Vision Sensor (DVS). We introduce a Transformer-inspired cross-modal attention mechanism to dynamically correlate these distinct modalities, allowing the network to instantaneously prioritize high-speed dynamic updates without sacrificing structural scene awareness. The fused latent representations are then mapped to safe local waypoints and executable control commands via a hybrid policy network that blends heuristic trajectory tracking with direct neural predictions. Due to the severe physical risks associated with live testing of these sudden crossing scenarios, the framework is rigorously evaluated offline using a custom multi-modal dataset collected across both well-illuminated noon and challenging evening conditions. Extensive comparative and ablation studies demonstrate that DeepIPCv3 achieves state-of-the-art predictive performance. By effectively eliminating exposure failures and motion blur, the proposed LiDAR and DVS fusion yields the lowest trajectory and control command errors, enabling highly reactive, mathematically bounded evasive maneuvers regardless of ambient illumination. To support future research, we will release the codes to our GitHub repo at https://github.com/oskarnatan/DeepIPCv3.

AI.tldr: DeepIPCv3 is a multi-modal autonomous navigation framework that fuses LiDAR point clouds with DVS event streams via cross-modal attention to achieve low-latency, reactive evasive maneuvers in highly dynamic scenarios (e.g., sudden pedestrian crossings), evaluated offline with a custom dataset, achieving state-of-the-art trajectory and control errors.
AI.motivation: Frame-based sensors (cameras) suffer from perception latency and motion blur during highly dynamic encounters such as sudden pedestrian crossings, creating a critical safety vulnerability in end-to-end autonomous driving systems.
AI.method: DeepIPCv3 fuses LiDAR point clouds (dense 3D geometry) with DVS event streams (microsecond-level asynchronous updates) via a Transformer-inspired cross-modal attention mechanism, then maps fused representations to waypoints and control commands through a hybrid policy network blending heuristic trajectory tracking with direct neural predictions.
AI.result: DeepIPCv3 achieves state-of-the-art predictive performance with the lowest trajectory and control command errors, effectively eliminating exposure failures and motion blur across both well-illuminated noon and challenging evening conditions, enabling highly reactive and mathematically bounded evasive maneuvers.
AI.conclusion: LiDAR and DVS fusion enables robust, low-latency autonomous navigation regardless of ambient illumination, addressing critical safety failures in dynamic scenarios. Code will be released on GitHub.

title: Prospect-Theory Behavior from Bellman Optimality in MDPs with Catastrophic States
summary: We study risk-neutral control in Markov decision processes with an absorbing catastrophic state. Even though rewards are linear and the agent has no utility curvature, probability weighting, or framing dependence, standard Bellman optimality produces three prospect-theory-like signatures: an S-shaped value-function profile (convex near catastrophe, concave in the far field), an endogenous loss-sensitivity coefficient $λ^*(S) > 1$, and a reflection-effect policy reversal. Across 495 configurations, the optimal policy plays safe near catastrophe in positive-drift (growth) regimes despite the risky action's higher immediate expected value, and plays risky near catastrophe in negative-drift (decline) regimes despite the safe action's lower immediate expected loss. We derive a closed-form expression for the asymptotic loss-aversion plateau $\barλ$ that depends only on win probability $p$, payoff asymmetry $r = |Δ_\ell/Δ_w|$, and discount factor $β$, and matches numerical solutions to $R^2 = 0.999$. The mechanism does not require asymmetric payoffs. Across a sweep of $(p,β)$ at three asymmetry levels, the asymmetry share of $\barλ$ above unity has median 4.6% at $r = 1.25$ and rises to 13.9% at $r = 2$, with the boundary contribution exceeding the asymmetry contribution in every cell tested. The phenomena persist under tabular Q-learning (a model-free agent reproduces $V^*$ at correlation 0.98 in growth and 1.00 in decline) and under stochastic transitions with Gaussian, heavy-tailed Student-$t_3$, and asymmetric skew-normal noise up to 50% of the step size, where the asymptotic plateau tracks the closed-form prediction within 0.41% for safe-channel noise and within 9.6% for risky-channel or both-channel noise. These results identify absorbing failure states as a sufficient structural mechanism for prospect-theory-like behavior under optimal control.

AI.tldr: Risk-neutral optimal control in MDPs with an absorbing catastrophic state produces three prospect-theory-like signatures (S-shaped value function, endogenous loss sensitivity >1, reflection-effect policy reversal) without utility curvature or probability weighting. The asymptotic loss-aversion plateau has a closed-form expression matching numerics at R²=0.999, and phenomena persist under Q-learning and stochastic transitions.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether absorbing catastrophic states alone can produce prospect-theory-like behaviors (loss aversion, reflection effect, S-shaped value function) under standard risk-neutral optimal control, without requiring traditional behavioral economics mechanisms like utility curvature, probability weighting, or framing dependence.
AI.method: Markov decision process with absorbing catastrophic state; Bellman optimality analysis; numerical simulation across 495 configurations; Q-learning (model-free RL); stochastic transitions with Gaussian, Student-t₃, and skew-normal noise; closed-form derivation for asymptotic loss-aversion plateau.
AI.result: Three prospect-theory signatures emerge: S-shaped value profile, endogenous λ*>1, reflection-effect policy reversal. Closed-form asymptotic loss-aversion plateau λ̄ depends only on p, r, β (R²=0.999). Asymmetry share of λ̄ above unity is small (median 4.6% at r=1.25, 13.9% at r=2). Phenomena persist under Q-learning (correlation 0.98-1.00) and stochastic noise (plateau prediction within 0.41%-9.6%).
AI.conclusion: Absorbing failure states serve as a sufficient structural mechanism for prospect-theory-like behavior under optimal control, without any need for behavioral biases in the agent's preferences.

title: PSG-Nav: Probabilistic Scene Graph Navigation via Multiverse Decision Making
summary:
Open-vocabulary navigation requires embodied agents to manage significant perception uncertainty stemming from semantic ambiguity and model errors.
  However, most existing works settle for local optimal deterministic approaches, depriving complex navigation decision-making over multiple composite possibilities that are critical for globally better solutions.
  In this paper, we propose Probabilistic Scene Graph Navigation (PSG-Nav), which constructs a 3D Probabilistic Scene Graph that uses full semantic categorical distributions to account for perception uncertainty.
  To efficiently use the local distributions to compose and reason about the optimal navigation landmarks, we propose Multiverse Decision to sample multiple most likely world settings from the joint distribution, and evaluate navigation landmarks based on the compatibility between landmarks and multiverses.
  To mitigate false positives due to epistemic uncertainty in open-vocabulary navigation, we introduce the Evidential Experience Calibrator, which enables online lifelong adaptation by cross-validating detections against memories of past successes and failures.
  Extensive experiments on widely-used benchmarks MP3D, HM3D, and HSSD demonstrate that PSG-Nav establishes new state-of-the-art results, achieving Success Rates of 66.1%, 44.8%, and 67.9%, respectively. Code is available at: https://psg-nav.github.io/

AI.tldr: PSG-Nav proposes a probabilistic scene graph approach for open-vocabulary navigation, using full semantic categorical distributions to handle perception uncertainty, a Multiverse Decision mechanism for composing navigation landmarks, and an Evidential Experience Calibrator for online lifelong adaptation, achieving SOTA results on MP3D (66.1%), HM3D (44.8%), and HSSD (67.9%).
AI.motivation: Existing open-vocabulary navigation methods use deterministic approaches that settle for local optimal solutions, failing to account for perception uncertainty from semantic ambiguity and model errors, which limits globally better navigation decision-making over multiple composite possibilities.
AI.method: PSG-Nav consists of three key components: (1) a 3D Probabilistic Scene Graph that represents perception uncertainty via full semantic categorical distributions; (2) Multiverse Decision, which samples multiple most likely world settings from the joint distribution and evaluates navigation landmarks based on landmark-multiverse compatibility; (3) Evidential Experience Calibrator for online lifelong adaptation via cross-validating detections against past success/failure memories.
AI.result: PSG-Nav achieves new state-of-the-art Success Rates of 66.1% on MP3D, 44.8% on HM3D, and 67.9% on HSSD benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: PSG-Nav demonstrates that explicitly modeling perception uncertainty through probabilistic scene graphs and multiverse reasoning enables globally better navigation decisions, with lifelong adaptation further improving robustness against epistemic uncertainty.

title: Large Language Models in Transportation Systems Management and Operations: From Text Reasoning to Multi-modal Decision Support
summary: Transportation systems management and operations (TSMO) increasingly depends on timely interpretation of heterogeneous data, from various sensor streams, incident reports, traveler feedback, and visual observations. Large language models (LLMs), including emerging multi-modal large language models (MM-LLMs), provide a new mechanism for integrating these structured and unstructured inputs into operator-facing decision support. This survey paper reviews LLM- and MM-LLM-based applications in TSMO across three domains: transportation operations & services (supply), mobility & fleet services (demand), and data, modeling & decision support. Using a PRISMA-guided screening process, we synthesize current studies while distinguishing operationally oriented applications from prototype and emerging concepts. We further identify recurring challenges in data heterogeneity, real-time inference, explainability, multi-modal fusion, and governance. Finally, we outline existing gaps and future directions in localized adaptation, edge deployment, benchmarking, and cross-agency collaboration. Overall, LLM-based systems appear most promising as a decision-support layer, with MM-LLMs offering particular value when heterogeneous text, visual, and sensor inputs must be integrated.

AI.tldr: This survey reviews applications of large language models (LLMs) and multi-modal LLMs (MM-LLMs) in transportation systems management and operations (TSMO), covering supply-side operations, demand-side mobility services, and data/decision support. It identifies challenges (data heterogeneity, real-time inference, explainability, multi-modal fusion, governance) and future directions (localized adaptation, edge deployment, benchmarking, cross-agency collaboration), concluding that LLMs are most suitable as a decision-support layer, with MM-LLMs adding value for heterogeneous input integration.
AI.motivation: TSMO increasingly relies on timely interpretation of heterogeneous data (sensor streams, incident reports, traveler feedback, visual observations). LLMs and MM-LLMs offer a new mechanism for integrating structured and unstructured inputs into operator-facing decision support, motivating a systematic review of their applications and challenges in this domain.
AI.method: The authors conduct a survey using a PRISMA-guided screening process to synthesize current studies across three TSMO domains: transportation operations & services (supply), mobility & fleet services (demand), and data, modeling & decision support. They distinguish operationally oriented applications from prototype and emerging concepts.
AI.result: The survey identifies recurring challenges: data heterogeneity, real-time inference, explainability, multi-modal fusion, and governance. It finds that LLM-based systems are most promising as a decision-support layer, and MM-LLMs offer particular value when heterogeneous text, visual, and sensor inputs must be integrated. Gaps are identified in localized adaptation, edge deployment, benchmarking, and cross-agency collaboration.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based systems show strongest potential as a decision-support layer in TSMO, with MM-LLMs especially beneficial for integrating diverse input types. Future work should focus on localized adaptation, edge deployment, standardized benchmarking, and cross-agency collaboration to advance real-world deployment.

title: S2M-Trek: From Single to Multi-Sphere Transport via Per-Frame Deep Sets on a Wheel-Legged Robot
summary: We study the problem of scaling dynamic loco-manipulation from a single free-rolling sphere to multiple spheres transported simultaneously on the back of a wheel-legged quadruped, without fences, grippers, or mechanical stops. Multiple identical free-rolling spheres form an unordered set with no persistent identity: their ordering may change independently at each history frame, creating a \emph{per-frame permutation symmetry} that standard history-concatenation set encoders do not explicitly enforce -- these encoders impose only a shared, diagonal permutation symmetry over the full history. We show that this symmetry mismatch leads to a concrete failure mode in curriculum-based reinforcement learning. Within the same PPO training budget, flat MLPs and branch-wise encoders plateau at or below the two-sphere stage, while a history-concatenation Deep Sets baseline (\HCDS) fails to progress past the two-sphere stage in our runs unless ball-to-slot assignments are randomised during training, suggesting that it exploits slot indices as a curriculum shortcut rather than learning identity-free multi-sphere dynamics. We propose \textbf{Per-Frame Deep Sets (\PFDS)}, which performs permutation-invariant pooling within each history frame before temporal readout; we prove that \PFDS is $\Gframe$-invariant and universally approximates continuous $\Gframe$-invariant policies. A $2{\times}2$ ablation over encoder architecture and slot randomisation separates the architectural and data-augmentation pathways, and \PFDS reaches the five-sphere stage with 100\% no-drop transport in simulation across all five random seeds. We further distill the \PFDS teacher into \TactSet via DAgger, replacing privileged sphere-state observations with a $16{\times}16$ Boolean union contact map, yielding a compact and naturally $\Gframe$-invariant tactile representation.

AI.tldr: Proposes Per-Frame Deep Sets (PFDS) for multi-sphere dynamic loco-manipulation on a wheel-legged quadruped, addressing per-frame permutation symmetry that standard encoders fail to enforce. PFDS reaches 5-sphere transport with 100% success, and is distilled into a tactile-only policy (TactSet) via DAgger.
AI.motivation: Standard history-concatenation set encoders impose only a shared diagonal permutation symmetry over the full history, but multiple free-rolling spheres form an unordered set with per-frame permutation symmetry. This mismatch causes curriculum-based RL to plateau at or below the two-sphere stage, as slot indices become curriculum shortcuts.
AI.method: Proposes Per-Frame Deep Sets (PFDS) which performs permutation-invariant pooling within each history frame before temporal readout, proven to be Gframe-invariant and universally approximating continuous Gframe-invariant policies. Also distills PFDS into TactSet via DAgger, using 16x16 Boolean union contact maps.
AI.result: PFDS reaches five-sphere stage with 100% no-drop transport across all five random seeds. Flat MLPs and branch-wise encoders plateau at/below two spheres; HCDS fails past two spheres without slot randomisation. A 2x2 ablation separates architectural and data-augmentation effects.
AI.conclusion: Per-frame permutation symmetry must be explicitly enforced for scalable multi-object loco-manipulation. PFDS is effective and generalizable, and its tactile distillation yields a compact, symmetry-aware policy suitable for real-world deployment.

title: Subliminal Learning Is Steering Vector Distillation
summary: Subliminal learning refers to a student language model acquiring a teacher's traits (e.g. a system-prompted preference for owls) when fine-tuned on the teacher's outputs, despite the outputs being semantically unrelated to those traits. It remains poorly understood how data without semantic meaning can transfer specific semantic traits. In this work, we show that subliminal learning is mediated by a single steering vector, i.e. a vector added to the model's activations. Across two open-source models, we find that the teacher's system prompt is well approximated by a steering vector, and that the student's behavior is driven by learning an aligned vector over fine-tuning. System prompts that are not well approximated by steering vectors are not subliminally learned. This is a special case of steering vector distillation, in which a student trained on the outputs of a steered teacher learns to imitate that steering. We demonstrate steering vector distillation on a range of semantic and random vectors. Adding a semantic vector to a model's activations can have both model-independent and model-specific (i.e. non-semantic) effects on its behavior, so generated data that is non-semantic can transmit a vector with semantic effects, enabling subliminal learning. This also explains why subliminal learning does not transfer between models. We find that adaptive optimizers are necessary for subliminal learning in language models: activation gradients on steered data carry a small but consistent component along the steering direction, and non-adaptive optimizers impede this by allowing outlier gradients to dominate.

AI.tldr: Subliminal learning in language models is mediated by a single steering vector; the teacher's system prompt approximates a steering vector, and the student learns an aligned vector during fine-tuning. This is a special case of steering vector distillation, enabled by adaptive optimizers that capture activation gradients along the steering direction.
AI.motivation: To understand how semantically irrelevant data (teacher outputs) can transfer specific semantic traits (like a system-prompted preference) to a student model during fine-tuning, a phenomenon known as subliminal learning.
AI.method: Analyzed two open-source models to show teacher's system prompt approximates a steering vector; demonstrated steering vector distillation across semantic and random vectors; examined role of adaptive vs. non-adaptive optimizers in subliminal learning via activation gradient analysis.
AI.result: Subliminal learning is mediated by a steering vector; system prompts not well-approximated by steering vectors are not subliminally learned; adaptive optimizers are necessary as they capture small consistent activation gradient components along the steering direction, while non-adaptive optimizers allow outlier gradients to dominate.
AI.conclusion: Subliminal learning is a special case of steering vector distillation; it does not transfer between models because steering vectors have model-specific non-semantic effects; adaptive optimizers are essential for this phenomenon.

title: ActMVS: Active Scene Reconstruction with Monocular Multi-View Stereo
summary: Active scene reconstruction enables robots/UAVs to autonomously plan trajectories and reconstruct environments without costly manual data acquisition. Unlike passive methods, active reconstruction requires real-time construction of high-confidence occupancy maps for collision-free navigation. Existing approaches rely on depth sensors for occupancy map updates, increasing platform cost and weight. To advance spatial intelligence, we aim for a vision-only monocular solution. However, current monocular scene reconstruction methods operate offline and fail to deliver globally consistent dense depth at the frame rates required for robots/UAVs navigation. To bridge this gap, we introduce ActMVS, the first framework for monocular active reconstruction. Our framework integrates a view factor graph construction for informed Multi-View Stereo depth prediction, along with a global depth optimization, to enable the online generation of high-quality, globally consistent dense depth maps. This enables monocular robots/UAVs to maintain reliable occupancy maps for safe trajectory planning during reconstruction. Experiments on Replica datasets demonstrate performance competitive with RGB-D methods. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/TrickyGo/ActMVS.

AI.tldr: ActMVS is the first framework for monocular active scene reconstruction, enabling online generation of globally consistent dense depth maps via view factor graph construction and global depth optimization, allowing vision-only robots/UAVs to build reliable occupancy maps for safe navigation with performance competitive to RGB-D methods.
AI.motivation: Existing active reconstruction methods rely on depth sensors (increasing cost and weight), while current monocular scene reconstruction methods operate offline and cannot produce globally consistent dense depth at real-time frame rates required for robot/UAV navigation.
AI.method: ActMVS integrates a view factor graph construction for informed Multi-View Stereo depth prediction with a global depth optimization module, enabling online generation of high-quality, globally consistent dense depth maps for monocular active reconstruction.
AI.result: Experiments on Replica datasets demonstrate performance competitive with RGB-D methods.
AI.conclusion: ActMVS bridges the gap between monocular scene reconstruction and active robotic navigation by enabling vision-only robots/UAVs to maintain reliable occupancy maps for safe trajectory planning during reconstruction.

title: Property Prediction of Stacked Bilayer Materials: A Multimodal Learning Approach
comment: Accepted to the 35th International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI 2026)
summary: AI for materials science is a critical topic within AI for science, aiming to accelerate materials discovery and produce accurate property predictions. Bilayer 2D material stacking is essential for exploring new materials with novel functions and inherent phenomena, enabling the creation of new 2D bilayers for diverse real-world applications. Research on bilayer vdWs materials has made significant progress from experimental and computational perspectives. Various bilayer materials have been successfully synthe sized experimentally and the increasing utilization of high-throughput computing technology has con structed several computational two-dimensional materials databases. However, the use of AI to model bilayer stacking and predict new properties remains underexplored, necessitating further research studies. In this work, we propose a novel multimodal learning approach to study the interfaces between dissimilar materials that jointly enable new or multiple functions, and to predict new properties arising from the vertical integration (stacking) of different functional material layers under given configurations. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach compared to baseline methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/AnVuong123/bimat ml.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a multimodal learning approach for modeling bilayer 2D material stacking to predict new properties from vertical integration of dissimilar functional layers, demonstrating effectiveness over baselines.
AI.motivation: Bilayer 2D material stacking is crucial for discovering novel materials with new functions, but AI-based modeling of bilayer stacking and property prediction remains underexplored despite experimental and computational advances.
AI.method: A novel multimodal learning approach that studies interfaces between dissimilar materials and predicts new properties arising from vertical integration (stacking) of different functional material layers under given configurations.
AI.result: Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed approach compared to baseline methods.
AI.conclusion: The multimodal learning approach effectively addresses the underexplored area of AI-driven bilayer stacking property prediction, with open-source code available.

title: Autopilot-Preserving Residual Q-Learning with HJB-Inspired Finite-Action Risk Filtering for Fixed-Wing UAV Command Supervision
comment: 47 pages, 12 figures, 20 tables. Simulation-based study with a code-traceable benchmark, source code and a demonstration video are linked in the paper
summary: A fixed-wing UAV must hold airspeed, altitude, and heading references under wind, gusts, and turbulence, channels coupled so that correcting one can degrade another. Classical autopilots stabilize the airframe well but adapt poorly when a hard crosswind meets an aggressive turn, while reinforcement-learning (RL) policies acting directly on the surfaces concentrate exploration risk at the actuator interface. We place a learned supervisor above an unchanged autopilot rather than inside it: it selects a residual from a finite, bounded action set on the commanded airspeed, altitude, and heading; the modified reference is projected into an admissible command envelope before reaching the autopilot, which stays the only actuator-facing controller. What is new is how the residual is chosen. HJB residual scores candidates with a semi-discrete value-iteration critic in the spirit of the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation, ranks them by a no-op-relative Hamiltonian advantage, and filters them through a control-Lyapunov- and control-barrier-inspired finite-action shield that always keeps a no-op fallback. On a shared 12-state runtime holding the plant, autopilot, and actuator model fixed, so the comparison is at the package level, HJB residual lowers mean RMS path-tracking error to 44.809 m, against 338.617 m for the baseline autopilot and 88.809 m for a tabular-Q residual, an 86.77% reduction over the baseline and 49.54% over Q-learning. The gain concentrates where the baseline fails worst and comes with a measured rise in airspeed error, so no method dominates every metric. We present this autopilot-preserving residual command-supervision design and benchmark with its trade-offs reported intact.

AI.tldr: A fixed-wing UAV autopilot is augmented with a learned supervisor (HJB residual) that selects small corrections to the airspeed, altitude, and heading commands, using a value-iteration critic and a safety shield, reducing path-tracking error by 86.77% over the baseline while keeping the original autopilot unchanged.
AI.motivation: Classical autopilots struggle with coupled control channels under crosswinds and aggressive turns, while RL policies acting directly on control surfaces concentrate exploration risk at the actuator interface and may destabilize the airframe.
AI.method: A learned supervisor sits above an unchanged autopilot, selecting bounded residuals on commanded references (airspeed, altitude, heading). Residuals are scored by a semi-discrete value-iteration critic inspired by the HJB equation, ranked by a no-op-relative Hamiltonian advantage, and filtered through a control-Lyapunov/control-barrier-inspired shield that always retains a no-op fallback.
AI.result: HJB residual achieves mean RMS path-tracking error of 44.809 m vs. 338.617 m (baseline autopilot) and 88.809 m (tabular-Q residual), an 86.77% reduction over baseline and 49.54% over Q-learning. Airspeed error increased slightly; no method dominates all metrics.
AI.conclusion: The autopilot-preserving residual command-supervision design significantly improves path tracking under challenging wind conditions while keeping the original autopilot as the sole actuator-facing controller, with trade-offs honestly reported.

title: Can AI Review Improve Paper Drafting? An Empirical Study on 20 Computer Architecture Submissions

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether AI-generated reviews can improve paper drafting by studying 20 computer architecture papers. The authors develop an AI-Paper-Review tool that generates structured reviews, and find that AI reviews cover a significant fraction of human-raised issues while also identifying some issues missed by human reviewers.
AI.motivation: The exploding volume of AI-generated papers has strained peer review, leading to the potential use of AI-generated reviews. While ethical concerns about confidentiality, quality, and fairness remain debated, the authors ask a practical alternative question: can AI review improve paper drafting?
AI.method: The authors study 20 computer architecture papers with varying submission lineage. They build a web UI-integrated tool, AI-Paper-Review, that generates structured AI review by selecting from a diverse pool of AI reviewers, clustering and ranking comments based on commonality and importance, and aligning AI comments with human comments for metric-based validation.
AI.result: AI review can cover a significant fraction of human-raised issues, and also raises issues missing in human review. The paper quantifies alignment between AI and human review using defined metrics.
AI.conclusion: The paper is not intended to encourage using AI for peer review at the current stage, but to study how AI review can improve paper drafting and understand the potential and limitations of AI-based peer review. The tool and case study data are released to instigate future research, while misuse for peer review would violate ethics policies.

title: A Sonar-Visual Dataset for Cross-Modal Underwater Robot Perception
comment: 6 pages, 7 figures, 3 tables. Accepted to IEEE ICRA 2026 S2S Workshop (From Sea to Space: Advancing Perception in Harsh Domains)
summary: Underwater robots typically use both cameras and sonar for perception to leverage the rich semantic details of vision and the robust range measurements of acoustics. However, learning to map between these modalities via cross-modal prediction remains underexplored due to limited sonar-visual paired datasets. We present SOVIS, a sonar-visual dataset for cross-modal underwater perception. SOVIS comprises over 76,000 paired frames collected across 17 dives at six sites in the Trondheimfjord, supported by an end-to-end pipeline that cleans and synchronizes the cross-modal sensor data. We also introduce an interactive annotation tool designed to accelerate the labeling process for this paired data. Finally, we demonstrate a proof-of-concept cross-modal fish detection task using a small subset of labeled data, achieving a 7x improvement in mAP@0.10 over a monocular camera baseline. SOVIS serves as the first step toward advancing cross-modal underwater perception research, enabling research directions such as dense sonar prediction from monocular images.

AI.tldr: SOVIS is a large-scale sonar-visual paired dataset (76,000+ frames from 17 dives at 6 sites) with a cleaning/synchronization pipeline and interactive annotation tool. A proof-of-concept cross-modal fish detection task shows a 7x improvement in mAP@0.10 over monocular camera baseline.
AI.motivation: Cross-modal prediction between sonar and visual modalities is underexplored for underwater robots due to limited paired datasets.
AI.method: Collected 76,000+ paired sonar-visual frames across 17 dives at 6 sites in Trondheimfjord; developed an end-to-end pipeline for cleaning and synchronizing cross-modal sensor data; created an interactive annotation tool; evaluated on cross-modal fish detection.
AI.result: Achieved a 7x improvement in mAP@0.10 over a monocular camera baseline on cross-modal fish detection using a small labeled subset.
AI.conclusion: SOVIS is the first step toward advancing cross-modal underwater perception research, enabling future work such as dense sonar prediction from monocular images.

title: Tackling the Root of Misinformation by Teaching Laypeople about Logical Fallacies via Socratic Questioning and Critical Argumentation
comment: This paper has been accepted to Proceedings of the 64th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Long Paper), Main Conference
summary: Identifying logical fallacies in everyday discourse is challenging for many people. This challenge is amplified in the era of Large Language Models (LLMs), where malicious agents can deploy fallacious arguments to disseminate misinformation at scale. In this work, we explore the potential of LLMs as part of the solution. We introduce LFTutor, an intelligent tutoring system which uses LLMs to tutor laypeople and help them learn about logical fallacies. LFTutor integrates intent-driven Socratic questioning and critical argumentation principles to actively engage learners to reflect on their reasoning. Through both automatic and human evaluations, we demonstrate that LFTutor significantly outperforms baseline LLMs lacking these pedagogical strategies. This work highlights the promise of combining LLMs with pedagogical scaffolding to foster critical thinking and argument literacy in the age of AI.

AI.tldr: LFTutor is an LLM-powered intelligent tutoring system that uses Socratic questioning and critical argumentation principles to help laypeople learn about logical fallacies, significantly outperforming baseline LLMs in pedagogical effectiveness.
AI.motivation: Identifying logical fallacies in everyday discourse is challenging for many people, and this challenge is amplified by LLMs enabling malicious agents to spread fallacious arguments and misinformation at scale.
AI.method: LFTutor integrates intent-driven Socratic questioning and critical argumentation principles within an intelligent tutoring system powered by LLMs to actively engage learners in reflecting on their reasoning about logical fallacies.
AI.result: Through automatic and human evaluations, LFTutor significantly outperforms baseline LLMs that lack these pedagogical strategies.
AI.conclusion: Combining LLMs with pedagogical scaffolding (Socratic questioning and critical argumentation) shows promise for fostering critical thinking and argument literacy in the age of AI.

title: LEGS: Fine-Tuning Teleop-Free VLAs for Humanoid Loco-manipulation in an Embodied Gaussian Splatting World
summary: Training vision-language-action (VLA) policies for humanoid loco-manipulation is constrained by the high cost and complexity of collecting human teleoperation demonstrations. VLA policies fine-tuned in simulators have, until now, failed to transfer effectively in humanoid loco-manipulation tasks. We present LEGS (Loco-manipulation via Embodied Gaussian Splatting), a hybrid simulator that composites a mesh foreground (robot, objects, props) over a photorealistic 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) background reconstructed from a handheld scene capture. LEGS uses a procedural motion-primitive generator to synthesize labeled demonstrations at scale without human teleoperation, and a deterministic two-stage color calibration to align the rendered 3DGS image to the robot's deployment camera. On a Unitree G1 humanoid robot, across three pick-and-place tasks of increasing whole-body difficulty and three VLA backbones (psi_0, pi_0.5, GR00T N1.6), a policy trained purely on LEGS data matches or exceeds one trained on human teleoperation demos on every experiment. It also outperforms a mesh-only simulation baseline that ablates the effect of the 3DGS background, showing that photorealistic rendering is a key enabler for synthetic data transfer. Humanoid motion is recorded independently of scene appearance in LEGS, allowing the same auto-generated demonstrations to be re-rendered under new backgrounds and object meshes--covering a new scene at more than 15x lower cost than teleoperation--to augment training data for robustness to scene variations.
