Under combined object-and-scene appearance shift, the policy trained on re-rendered LEGS-AUG data maintains task success while the baseline trained on teleoperation data fails entirely. Our project page is located at https://legsvla.github.io/.

AI.tldr: LEGS is a hybrid simulator that composits mesh foregrounds over 3DGS backgrounds to generate synthetic training data for humanoid loco-manipulation policies, achieving performance matching or exceeding human teleoperation-based training across multiple tasks and backbones, with significant cost savings and robustness to scene variations.
AI.motivation: Training VLA policies for humanoid loco-manipulation is constrained by the high cost and complexity of collecting human teleoperation demonstrations, and existing simulator-fine-tuned VLA policies have failed to transfer effectively to real humanoid tasks.
AI.method: LEGS: (1) A hybrid simulator combining mesh foreground (robot, objects, props) with photorealistic 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) background from handheld scene capture; (2) Procedural motion-primitive generator for scalable labeled demonstrations without human teleoperation; (3) Deterministic two-stage color calibration to align rendered 3DGS images to the robot's deployment camera; (4) LEGS-AUG leverages scene-independent humanoid motion recording to re-render demonstrations under new backgrounds and object meshes.
AI.result: On Unitree G1 humanoid across three pick-and-place tasks and three VLA backbones (psi_0, pi_0.5, GR00T N1.6), LEGS-trained policy matches or exceeds teleoperation-trained policy on all experiments, outperforms mesh-only simulation baseline, and achieves 15x lower cost for new scene coverage. Under combined object-and-scene appearance shift, LEGS-AUG maintains success while teleoperation baseline fails entirely.
AI.conclusion: Photorealistic rendering via 3DGS background is a key enabler for synthetic data transfer in humanoid loco-manipulation, and LEGS provides a cost-effective, scalable alternative to human teleoperation for training VLA policies with superior robustness to scene variations.

title: TriLens: Per-Layer Logit-Lens Entropy for White-Box Hallucination Detection
summary: When a language model hallucinates, the final answer is wrong, but the mistake is not necessarily invisible inside the model. Different internal pathways may remain uncertain, disagree in how quickly they sharpen, or commit to competing continuations before the output is produced. We introduce TriLens, a white-box detector that turns this intuition into a compact representation: at every layer, it reads the multi-head self-attention output, the feed-forward output, and the residual stream through the model's own logit lens, then records only the entropy of each readout. The resulting 3L-dimensional trajectory describes how certainty forms across depth and across modules, without storing high-dimensional hidden states or sampling multiple generations. This simple signal yields a strong detector across instruction-tuned LLMs and QA benchmarks, and our analyses show that the three module-wise entropy trajectories provide complementary evidence. TriLens suggests that hallucination detection can benefit from tracking how internal computation settles, not only what the final layer predicts.

AI.tldr: TriLens is a white-box hallucination detector that tracks entropy trajectories across three internal modules (attention, feed-forward, residual stream) per layer, forming a compact 3L-dimensional signal that effectively detects hallucinations without storing high-dimensional states.
AI.motivation: Hallucinations in LLMs produce wrong final answers, but internal signals (e.g., uncertainty, disagreement, competing continuations) may reveal the mistake before output. The goal is to detect hallucinations by monitoring how internal computation settles across layers and modules.
AI.method: TriLens reads multi-head self-attention output, feed-forward output, and residual stream at every layer via the model's own logit lens, then records only the entropy of each readout, producing a 3L-dimensional trajectory (L layers × 3 modules).
AI.result: TriLens achieves strong hallucination detection performance across instruction-tuned LLMs and QA benchmarks. The three module-wise entropy trajectories provide complementary evidence for detection.
AI.conclusion: Hallucination detection benefits from tracking how internal computation settles across depth and modules, not only from inspecting the final layer's prediction.

title: Crazyflow: An Accurate, GPU-Accelerated, Differentiable Drone Simulator in JAX
summary: High-quality, large-scale synthetic data from simulations is becoming a cornerstone for pushing the capabilities of robot algorithms. While aerial robotics simulators have evolved to support specialized needs such as fidelity, differentiability, and swarms independently, a unified platform that can synthesize data across all these domains is missing. In this work, we propose Crazyflow, a simulator designed to push the limits of aerial-robotics algorithm development, from model-based to data-driven methods, gradient-based to sampling-based approaches, and single-agent to multi-agent systems. Compared to existing state-of-the-art drone simulators, it achieves speeds more than an order of magnitude faster for a single drone and can simulate thousands of swarms of 4000 drones each. Real-world experiments show Crazyflow supports both analytical-gradient-based policy learning, achieving sub-centimeter trajectory tracking accuracy without domain randomization, and sampling-based obstacle avoidance at speeds exceeding half a billion steps per second. Breaking the traditional train-then-deploy paradigm, we show that its unprecedented speed even enables in-flight reinforcement learning; we demonstrate this by throwing a physical drone into the air and training a recovery policy from scratch in 0.38 seconds, successfully stabilizing the drone. Crazyflow supports multiple levels of simulation abstraction, is directly compatible with all open-source Crazyflie models, and enables rapid reconfiguration across custom drone platforms and applications by providing a light-weight system identification pipeline. By pushing accuracy, speed, and differentiability simultaneously, Crazyflow serves as an open-source resource for synthetic data generation, with emerging capabilities for large-scale parallelization for online, in-execution learning and optimization, opening the door to novel algorithm development.

AI.tldr: Crazyflow is a high-speed, differentiable aerial robotics simulator that supports single-to-multi-agent systems, model-based to data-driven methods, and achieves over 10x speedup over state-of-the-art, enabling in-flight reinforcement learning (0.38s recovery policy training) and simulation of thousands of 4000-drone swarms.
AI.motivation: Existing aerial robotics simulators support fidelity, differentiability, or swarms independently, but no unified platform synthesizes data across all these domains, hindering algorithm development from model-based to data-driven, gradient-based to sampling-based, and single-agent to multi-agent systems.
AI.method: Crazyflow provides multiple levels of simulation abstraction, direct compatibility with all open-source Crazyflie models, a lightweight system identification pipeline for rapid platform reconfiguration, and massively parallelized simulation enabling speeds exceeding half a billion steps per second for sampling-based methods.
AI.result: Achieves >10x speedup over state-of-the-art drone simulators for single drone; simulates thousands of swarms of 4000 drones each; sub-centimeter trajectory tracking accuracy without domain randomization; 0.38s in-flight recovery policy training from scratch on a physical drone; >0.5 billion steps/second for obstacle avoidance.
AI.conclusion: By simultaneously pushing accuracy, speed, and differentiability, Crazyflow serves as an open-source resource for synthetic data generation with emerging capabilities for large-scale parallelization for online, in-execution learning and optimization, breaking the traditional train-then-deploy paradigm.

title: TravelEval: A Comprehensive Benchmarking Framework for Evaluating LLM-Powered Travel Planning Agents
summary: The development of Large Language Models (LLMs) has significantly improved travel planning applications, yet evaluating such models is limited by existing benchmarks' limitations: 1) overemphasis on constraint compliance, neglecting multi-dimensional qualities like spatio-temporal cost; 2) datasets lacking real-world authenticity and coverage in key areas (e.g., lodging, transport); and 3) isolated daily plan assessments that miss critical details (e.g., the impact of daily accommodation and visit pacing) needed for entire plan's evaluation. To address this gap, we introduce TravelEval, a realistic and comprehensive benchmark. TravelEval features 1) a novel six-dimensional evaluation framework to holistically assess plans across accuracy, compliance, temporality, spatiality, economy, and utility dimensions; 2) a highly realistic data sandbox with precise accommodation pricing and authentic intercity transportation data; and 3) a simulation-based global evaluation method that emulates complete travel plans with API-integrated geographic information and fine-grained queuing time. Evaluating 12 mainstream approaches with TravelEval reveals several valuable insights, such that LLMs struggle with globally-optimized multi-dimensional planning (especially in spatio-temporal reasoning and budget compliance), and agentic reasoning strategies offer no consistent improvement. Concisely, TravelEval facilitates travel plan evaluation via grounded spatio-temporal emulation and comprehensive metrics, providing a robust foundation for advancing LLM-powered travel planning research and applications.

AI.tldr: TravelEval is a realistic benchmark for evaluating LLM-based travel planning, featuring a six-dimensional evaluation framework, a realistic data sandbox, and a simulation-based global evaluation method. Tests on 12 approaches show LLMs struggle with multi-dimensional planning, especially spatio-temporal reasoning and budget compliance.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for LLM-based travel planning are limited by: 1) overemphasis on constraint compliance while ignoring multi-dimensional qualities like spatio-temporal cost; 2) lack of real-world authenticity and coverage in lodging/transport; and 3) isolated daily plan assessments that miss critical details like accommodation impact and visit pacing for whole-plan evaluation.
AI.method: TravelEval introduces: 1) a six-dimensional evaluation framework (accuracy, compliance, temporality, spatiality, economy, utility); 2) a realistic data sandbox with precise accommodation pricing and authentic intercity transportation data; and 3) a simulation-based global evaluation method using API-integrated geographic info and fine-grained queuing time to emulate complete travel plans.
AI.result: Evaluating 12 mainstream approaches reveals that LLMs struggle with globally-optimized multi-dimensional planning, particularly in spatio-temporal reasoning and budget compliance, and agentic reasoning strategies offer no consistent improvement.
AI.conclusion: TravelEval facilitates travel plan evaluation via grounded spatio-temporal emulation and comprehensive metrics, providing a robust foundation for advancing LLM-powered travel planning research and applications.

title: Spatio-Temporal Reconnection for Multi-Robot Networks using Adaptive Prescribed-Time CBFs
summary: In multi-robot systems, maintaining persistent communication graph connectivity is often overly restrictive, especially when robots have limited communication ranges but operate in large environments. Instead, allowing robots to temporarily disconnect and later reconnect is often more desirable for efficient task execution while still ensuring timely information sharing across the team. In this paper, we propose an adaptive prescribed-time control barrier function (adaptive PT-CBF) framework that enables robots to temporarily disconnect and re-enter the communication range within an adjustable and feasible prescribed time. Moreover, we introduce a reconnection triggering mechanism that jointly considers task execution and reconnection urgency, thereby providing a principled way to decide when reconnection should occur. Theoretical analysis justifies convergence to the satisfying reconnection within a prescribed finite time. Experimental results validate the performance of our proposed adaptive PT-CBF with improved task efficiency and satisfying reconnections.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an adaptive prescribed-time control barrier function (adaptive PT-CBF) framework for multi-robot systems, allowing robots to temporarily disconnect and reconnect within a prescribed time, with a reconnection triggering mechanism that balances task execution and reconnection urgency.
AI.motivation: Maintaining persistent communication graph connectivity in multi-robot systems is overly restrictive when robots have limited communication ranges but operate in large environments. Allowing temporary disconnections with timely reconnections is more desirable for efficient task execution.
AI.method: The authors propose an adaptive prescribed-time control barrier function (adaptive PT-CBF) framework that enables temporary disconnection and reconnection within an adjustable prescribed time, along with a reconnection triggering mechanism that jointly considers task execution and reconnection urgency.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis proves convergence to satisfying reconnection within prescribed finite time; experimental results demonstrate improved task efficiency and satisfying reconnections.
AI.conclusion: The adaptive PT-CBF framework effectively allows temporary disconnections in multi-robot systems while ensuring timely reconnections, improving task efficiency without requiring persistent connectivity.

title: AnyEdit++: Adaptive Long-Form Knowledge Editing via Bayesian Surprise
summary: Editing complex, long-form knowledge in Large Language Models remains a significant challenge due to the difficulty of maintaining generation coherence. Existing autoregressive methods like AnyEdit alleviate length constraints but rely on Fixed-window Chunking, which disregards logical structure and compromises consistency. To address this, we present AnyEdit++, a structure-aware framework incorporating Bayes-Chunk, an adaptive segmentation mechanism that dynamically identifies semantic boundaries based on Bayesian Surprise. We underpin this approach with a theoretical framework establishing two key principles: (1) Structural Independence: we prove that cross-segment interference is minimized when anchor keys are geometrically orthogonal (a condition naturally satisfied by our surprisal-based boundaries but violated by fixed windows), and (2) Causal Locality: we demonstrate that updates injected at these semantic peaks yield strictly superior control compared to arbitrary split points. Extensive experiments across mathematical reasoning, code generation, and narrative tasks demonstrate that AnyEdit++ achieves superior performance and robustness compared to state-of-the-art baselines, validating that structural awareness is critical for effective long-form knowledge editing.

AI.tldr: AnyEdit++ is a structure-aware framework for editing long-form knowledge in LLMs, using Bayes-Chunk (adaptive Bayesian Surprise-based segmentation) to outperform fixed-window methods, with theoretical guarantees on structural independence and causal locality.
AI.motivation: Existing methods like AnyEdit use Fixed-window Chunking that ignores logical structure, compromising generation coherence when editing complex, long-form knowledge in LLMs.
AI.method: Proposes AnyEdit++ with Bayes-Chunk, an adaptive segmentation mechanism using Bayesian Surprise to dynamically identify semantic boundaries. Theoretically establishes Structural Independence (geometrically orthogonal anchor keys minimize cross-segment interference) and Causal Locality (updates at semantic peaks yield superior control).
AI.result: AnyEdit++ achieves superior performance and robustness across mathematical reasoning, code generation, and narrative tasks compared to state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: Structural awareness (via adaptive semantic segmentation) is critical for effective long-form knowledge editing in LLMs, and the proposed theoretical principles validate this claim.

title: Hierarchical Object Representation for Spatial Robot Perception: Points, Meshes, and Superquadrics
summary: Hierarchical 3D Scene Graphs (3DSG) have emerged as an actionable and scalable representation for long-term autonomy incorporating metric, semantic, and topological information in the scene. However, the question of geometric representation of objects in 3DSG has been overlooked as most methods use simplified geometric models such as partial point clouds or 3D bounding boxes. In this work, we introduce a hierarchical object representation that can be leveraged for high-fidelity object-level reconstruction, object-based robust re-localization or map alignment, and efficient and analytical collision checking for safe robot navigation planning in dense and cluttered environments. The representation is structurally organized into four distinct layers, progressively abstracting the scene from raw sensor data to dense 3D meshes to analytical primitives such as superquadrics, which provide a sparse and analytical representation for object geometry. We develop a pipeline that builds the hierarchical object representation from RGB-D image stream captured by a robot, and demonstrate its working in real-world open-set object scenes in both indoor and outdoor environments. Extensive experiments across diverse datasets including HOPE, ReplicaCAD, Kimera-Multi, and NUS Campus Dataset collected using Unitree B2 Robot validate our pipeline in both indoor and outdoor environments. We show that our superquadric-based map alignment method outperforms the current state-of-the-art object based map alignment method ROMAN. Our code can be found at https://github.com/perceptica-robotics/Hickory.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a hierarchical object representation for 3D Scene Graphs with four layers (raw data → dense meshes → superquadrics), enabling high-fidelity reconstruction, robust re-localization, and collision checking. The pipeline works on RGB-D streams in indoor/outdoor environments and outperforms ROMAN on map alignment.
AI.motivation: Current 3D Scene Graph (3DSG) methods overlook geometric object representation, relying on simplified models like partial point clouds or 3D bounding boxes, which limits high-fidelity reconstruction, robust re-localization, and collision checking for autonomous navigation.
AI.method: The method organizes object geometry into four hierarchical layers: (1) raw sensor data, (2) dense 3D meshes, (3) analytical primitives such as superquadrics, providing a sparse and analytical object representation. A pipeline is built to construct this hierarchy from RGB-D image streams captured by a robot.
AI.result: Validated on HOPE, ReplicaCAD, Kimera-Multi, and NUS Campus Dataset (Unitree B2 robot) in both indoor and outdoor environments. The superquadric-based map alignment outperforms the state-of-the-art object-based method ROMAN.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hierarchical object representation effectively bridges the gap between raw sensor data and sparse analytical primitives, improving object-level reconstruction, re-localization, and collision checking for long-term robotic autonomy.

title: DAG-MoE: From Simple Mixture to Structural Aggregation in Mixture-of-Experts
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become a leading approach for decoupling parameter count from computational cost in large language models, yet effectively scaling MoE performance remains a challenge. Prior work shows that fine-grained experts enlarge the space of expert combinations and improve flexibility, but they also impose substantial routing overhead, creating a new scalability bottleneck. In this paper, we explore a complementary axis for scaling -- how expert outputs are aggregated. We theoretically show that replacing the standard weighted-summation aggregation with structural aggregation expands the expert-combination space without altering the experts or router, and enables possible multi-step reasoning within a single MoE layer. To this end, we propose DAG-MoE, a sparse MoE framework that employs a lightweight module to automatically learn the optimal aggregation structure among the selected experts. Extensive experiments under standard language modeling settings show that DAG-MoE consistently improves performance in both pretraining and fine-tuning, surpassing traditional MoE baselines.

AI.tldr: DAG-MoE replaces the standard weighted-summation expert aggregation with a learned structural aggregation (a directed acyclic graph) that expands the expert-combination space, enables multi-step reasoning within a single MoE layer, and consistently improves performance in both pretraining and fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Fine-grained experts improve flexibility but impose routing overhead, creating a scalability bottleneck. The paper explores a complementary scaling axis: how expert outputs are aggregated, rather than just increasing expert count.
AI.method: DAG-MoE replaces weighted-summation aggregation with structural aggregation (learned DAG topology) among selected experts, enabling multi-step reasoning within a single MoE layer without altering the experts or router.
AI.result: DAG-MoE consistently outperforms traditional MoE baselines in both pretraining and fine-tuning under standard language modeling settings.
AI.conclusion: Structural aggregation expands the expert-combination space and improves MoE scalability; DAG-MoE offers a complementary axis to fine-grained expert design for scaling MoE performance.

title: Hierarchical Semantic-Augmented Navigation: Optimal Transport and Graph-Driven Reasoning for Vision-Language Navigation
comment: Published in NeurIPS 2025, address some typos
summary: Vision-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE) poses a formidable challenge for autonomous agents, requiring seamless integration of natural language instructions and visual observations to navigate complex 3D indoor spaces. Existing approaches often falter in long-horizon tasks due to limited scene understanding, inefficient planning, and lack of robust decision-making frameworks. We introduce the \textbf{Hierarchical Semantic-Augmented Navigation (HSAN)} framework, a groundbreaking approach that redefines VLN-CE through three synergistic innovations. First, HSAN constructs a dynamic hierarchical semantic scene graph, leveraging vision-language models to capture multi-level environmental representations, from objects to regions to zones, enabling nuanced spatial reasoning. Second, it employs an optimal transport-based topological planner, grounded in Kantorovich's duality, to select long-term goals by balancing semantic relevance and spatial accessibility with theoretical guarantees of optimality. Third, a graph-aware reinforcement learning policy ensures precise low-level control, navigating subgoals while robustly avoiding obstacles. By integrating spectral graph theory, optimal transport, and advanced multi-modal learning, HSAN addresses the shortcomings of static maps and heuristic planners prevalent in prior work. Extensive experiments on multiple challenging VLN-CE datasets demonstrate that HSAN achieves state-of-the-art performance, with significant improvements in navigation success and generalization to unseen environments.

AI.tldr: HSAN is a hierarchical framework for VLN in continuous environments that combines dynamic semantic scene graphs, optimal transport-based topological planning with Kantorovich duality guarantees, and graph-aware reinforcement learning for low-level control, achieving SOTA results on VLN-CE benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing VLN-CE approaches struggle in long-horizon tasks due to limited scene understanding, inefficient planning, and lack of robust decision-making, particularly because they rely on static maps and heuristic planners that cannot capture multi-level environmental semantics.
AI.method: HSAN comprises three components: (1) a dynamic hierarchical semantic scene graph built via vision-language models for multi-level representations (objects→regions→zones); (2) an optimal transport-based topological planner using Kantorovich's duality for long-term goal selection balancing semantic relevance and spatial accessibility; (3) a graph-aware RL policy for precise low-level control and obstacle avoidance.
AI.result: HSAN achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple challenging VLN-CE datasets, with significant improvements in navigation success and generalization to unseen environments.
AI.conclusion: By integrating spectral graph theory, optimal transport, and multi-modal learning, HSAN overcomes limitations of static maps and heuristic planners, providing a theoretically grounded and empirically superior approach to VLN-CE.

title: MindClaw: Closed-Loop Embodied Mental-State Reasoning for Precision Intervention
comment: Extended version of the CVPR 2026 paper *MindPower: Enabling Theory-of-Mind Reasoning in VLM-based Embodied Agents*
summary: Theory of Mind (ToM) enables an agent to reason about another actor's beliefs, goals, and intentions, which is essential for human-centered embodied assistance. Existing ToM benchmarks have advanced text and multimodal mental-state recognition, but they mostly evaluate offline question answering or final action prediction. They do not fully test whether an embodied agent can stay connected to a changing environment, update actor-specific beliefs, decide when reasoning is needed, and intervene only when help is useful. Building on MindPower, we extend robot-centric ToM reasoning to a real-time closed-loop setting and introduce MindClaw, a framework for embodied mental-state reasoning with precision intervention. MindClaw connects multi-source inputs, belief memory, an embodied cognitive trigger skill, mental reasoning, and action generation, allowing the agent to output helpful actions at the right time while remaining silent when intervention is unnecessary. Experiments show that direct VLM baselines struggle with task awareness and intervention calibration, while MindClaw achieves the best overall performance, demonstrating the importance of trigger-skill optimization for closed-loop embodied ToM assistance.

AI.tldr: MindClaw is a framework for closed-loop embodied Theory of Mind reasoning that enables real-time belief tracking and precision intervention, outperforming VLM baselines in robot-centric assistance tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing ToM benchmarks focus on offline QA or action prediction, failing to test whether embodied agents can continuously track changing environments, update actor-specific beliefs, decide when reasoning is needed, and intervene only when helpful.
AI.method: MindClaw extends MindPower to a real-time closed-loop setting, integrating multi-source inputs, belief memory, an embodied cognitive trigger skill, mental reasoning, and action generation to enable precise intervention timing.
AI.result: Direct VLM baselines struggle with task awareness and intervention calibration, while MindClaw achieves the best overall performance, demonstrating the importance of trigger-skill optimization.
AI.conclusion: Closed-loop embodied ToM assistance requires not just reasoning but also trigger-skill optimization to determine when to act versus remain silent.

title: Physics-Informed Modeling and Control of Emergent Behaviors in Robot Swarms
summary: Robot swarms can exhibit coherent collective behaviors through local perception, limited communication and decentralized decision-making, yet modeling and controlling such emergence remains challenging when behaviors unfold over multiple phases. Here we introduce PhySwarm, a physics-informed micro--macro framework that represents multi-stage swarm emergence as physically constrained density-field evolution coupled to executable robot motion. At the macroscopic level, a multi-phase advection--diffusion--reaction model (Macro-ADR) describes phase-dependent swarm-density evolution through directed transport, diffusion-based spatial regulation and behavioral phase transitions. At the microscopic level, an equivalent deterministic motion model (Micro-EDM) realizes these mechanisms through potential-field advection, density-gradient compensation and rate- or event-gated phase switching. A neural-physics controller (NPC) maps local observations and temporal memory to bounded physical parameters, and is trained with a reinforcement learning--PINN objective that combines task rewards with macro-scale density residuals and micro-scale motion-consistency constraints. In several proof-of-concept swarm missions -- including trail-guided foraging, formation-reconfigurable navigation and role-adaptive search and rescue -- we demonstrate that PhySwarm can generate distinct multi-stage emergent behaviors within a unified physics-informed modeling framework. The learned density fields and physical parameters provide interpretable evidence of how advection, diffusion and reaction jointly regulate multi-stage swarm organization. These results establish a physics-informed route for learning, interpreting and controlling emergent behaviors in robot swarms.

AI.tldr: PhySwarm is a physics-informed micro-macro framework for modeling, learning, and controlling multi-stage emergent behaviors in robot swarms, using advection-diffusion-reaction equations and a neural-physics controller trained with RL-PINN objectives, demonstrated across three multi-phase swarm missions.
AI.motivation: Modeling and controlling emergent multi-phase swarm behaviors remains challenging due to the complexity of coupling decentralized local interactions with global behavioral transitions.
AI.method: PhySwarm integrates a macroscopic multi-phase advection-diffusion-reaction model (Macro-ADR) with a microscopic deterministic motion model (Micro-EDM), connected via a neural-physics controller (NPC) trained with a reinforcement learning-PINN hybrid objective enforcing both task rewards and physics constraints.
AI.result: PhySwarm successfully generates distinct multi-stage emergent behaviors in trail-guided foraging, formation-reconfigurable navigation, and role-adaptive search and rescue, with interpretable density fields and physical parameters revealing how advection, diffusion, and reaction regulate swarm organization.
AI.conclusion: The physics-informed approach provides a unified route for learning, interpreting, and controlling multi-stage swarm emergence, establishing a new paradigm for physics-constrained swarm robotics.

title: Before the Model Learns the Bug:Fuzzing RLVR Verifiers
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) replaces human preference labels with executable reward functions such as math answer checkers, JSON tool-call validators, and code unit-test harnesses. That makes the reward partly a software artifact: if the verifier is wrong, optimization can learn the bug. We study this failure mode with a lightweight verifier-fuzzing framework that generates adversarial completions, compares buggy and stricter reference verifiers, logs paired decisions, and reports false-positive, false-negative, disagreement, exploit, and uncertainty metrics.

AI.tldr: RLVR uses verifiable reward functions (e.g., math checkers, code test harnesses) but these are software artifacts vulnerable to bugs; the paper presents a verifier-fuzzing framework that detects and measures such failures via adversarial completions and comparative metrics.
AI.motivation: RLVR replaces human preference labels with executable verifiers, but if the verifier is buggy, RL can exploit the bug. The paper aims to systematically study and detect this failure mode.
AI.method: A lightweight verifier-fuzzing framework that generates adversarial completions, compares buggy verifiers against stricter reference verifiers, logs paired decisions, and reports metrics including false-positive, false-negative, disagreement, exploit, and uncertainty.
AI.result: The framework produces metrics (false-positive, false-negative, disagreement, exploit, uncertainty) to quantify verifier bugs and their exploitability by RL.
AI.conclusion: Verifier bugs in RLVR are a real failure mode that can be systematically detected and measured via fuzzing without needing human labels, improving reliability of RL with verifiable rewards.

title: Embedding Semantic Risk into Distance Fields and CBFs for Online Monocular Safe Control
summary: We propose an online monocular perception-to-control framework that embeds semantic risk into the distance field used by Control Barrier Function (CBF)-based safe navigation and teleoperation. Many perception-based safety filters assign the same distance-based safety margin to all mapped obstacles or use semantics only as a downstream controller adjustment, rather than encoding semantic risk in the spatial representation. Our framework instead reasons online about obstacle geometry and class-dependent risk by embedding semantic information directly into the Euclidean Signed Distance Field (ESDF). This design encodes semantic risk before control optimization, so high-risk objects exert a larger spatial influence in the safety field while retaining efficient ESDF queries at runtime. Specifically, a foundation-model-based SLAM front end reconstructs dense 3-D geometry from monocular RGB video, while per-frame semantic segmentation provides pixel-level class labels that are fused into the reconstructed geometry. The resulting geometric-semantic representation is then converted into an ESDF, where semantic labels identify safety-relevant regions and impose class-dependent inflation before field computation. The semantic-aware ESDF provides the local distance values and spatial derivatives required by the CBF controller, while class-dependent gains further regulate the controller response. Extensive simulation and hardware experiments demonstrate online operation at 10--20 Hz and semantic-aware safe behavior in both teleoperation and autonomous navigation.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an online monocular perception-to-control framework that embeds semantic risk directly into the Euclidean Signed Distance Field (ESDF) used by Control Barrier Function (CBF)-based safe navigation. It uses a foundation-model-based SLAM front end with semantic segmentation to classify objects, inflates high-risk regions in the ESDF before control optimization, and demonstrates online operation at 10–20 Hz in both teleoperation and autonomous navigation tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing perception-based safety filters either assign uniform distance-based safety margins to all obstacles or use semantics only as a downstream controller adjustment, rather than encoding semantic risk directly into the spatial representation, limiting the ability to differentiate high-risk vs. low-risk objects during safety-critical control.
AI.method: (1) A foundation-model-based SLAM front end reconstructs dense 3-D geometry from monocular RGB video. (2) Per-frame semantic segmentation provides pixel-level class labels fused into the reconstructed geometry. (3) The geometric-semantic representation is converted into a semantic-aware ESDF where class-dependent inflation is applied before field computation. (4) The ESDF provides distance values and spatial derivatives for a CBF controller with class-dependent gains.
AI.result: Online operation at 10–20 Hz was achieved. Semantic-aware safe behavior was demonstrated in both simulation and hardware experiments for teleoperation and autonomous navigation, with high-risk objects exerting larger spatial influence in the safety field.
AI.conclusion: Encoding semantic risk directly into the ESDF before control optimization improves safety differentiation across object classes while retaining efficient runtime queries, enabling safer navigation in cluttered environments with heterogeneous obstacle types.

title: CAREAgent: Clinical Agent with Structured Reasoning and Tool-Integrated for Order Generation
summary: Clinical order generation serves as a critical bridge between clinical decision-making and real-world practice, translating medical decisions into concrete and executable orders. Existing agents mainly focus on coarse-grained decisions and overlook the fine-grained, executable information required for clinical orders. To address this gap, we propose CAREAgent, an agent for clinical order generation. To support its training, we introduce a two-stage agentic reasoning data construction method. First, we design an agent framework that constructs verifiable reasoning trajectories aligned with realistic clinical tool usage. Second, we filter reasoning trajectories by format compliance, order validity, and clinical plausibility. Building on the constructed data, the model is first trained via supervised fine-tuning to acquire fundamental reasoning formats and medical knowledge, and is subsequently optimized through reinforcement learning with multi-dimensional reward functions to enhance complex clinical reasoning capabilities. Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of CAREAgent. On ClinicalBench (unseen during training), CAREAgent improves the F1 score by 5.05%, 2.09%, and 0.86% over the single-agent, multi-agent, and agentic reasoning methods, respectively.

AI.tldr: CAREAgent is a clinical order generation agent that uses a two-stage data construction method (verifiable reasoning trajectories + filtering) and a two-phase training pipeline (SFT + reinforcement learning with multi-dimensional rewards), achieving state-of-the-art results on ClinicalBench.
AI.motivation: Existing agents focus on coarse-grained clinical decisions and fail to generate fine-grained, executable clinical orders needed in real-world practice.
AI.method: (1) Two-stage agentic reasoning data construction: agent framework with verifiable reasoning trajectories aligned with realistic clinical tool usage, then filtering by format compliance, order validity, and clinical plausibility. (2) Two-phase model training: supervised fine-tuning for reasoning formats and medical knowledge, then reinforcement learning with multi-dimensional reward functions for complex reasoning.
AI.result: On ClinicalBench (unseen during training), CAREAgent improves F1 by 5.05% over single-agent, 2.09% over multi-agent, and 0.86% over agentic reasoning baselines.
AI.conclusion: CAREAgent effectively bridges the gap between coarse-grained clinical decisions and fine-grained executable order generation, demonstrating superior performance through structured data construction and multi-phase optimization.

title: FlipItRight: Stable Pose-Targeted Throw-Flip Across Diverse Objects
summary: We propose FlipItRight, a framework for stable planar pose-targeted throw-flip with a high-DoF manipulator. The task is decomposed into an object-level planner, which generates candidate release states satisfying the desired landing pose, and a robot-level planner, which evaluates executability and constructs a feasible swing motion. Treating the release state as an explicit intermediate representation enables principled candidate filtering, adaptive selection of release and pre-swing configurations, and structured near-release motion design -- in particular, approximately constant end-effector velocities during the final swing phase to improve robustness to release-timing uncertainty. We validate on a real platform across objects of varying shape, size, and mass, achieving a 90% success rate across 120 trials. Ablation studies confirm that each design choice contributes to throwing performance, and the framework requires no prior data or learned model, enabling direct deployment on new objects and targets without environment-specific calibration or data collection.

AI.tldr: FlipItRight is a framework for stable planar throw-flipping objects to a desired pose using a high-DoF manipulator, achieving 90% success across 120 real-world trials without prior data or learned models.
AI.motivation: To enable reliable planar pose-targeted throw-flipping with high-DoF manipulators, overcoming release-timing uncertainty and the need for extensive data or calibration.
AI.method: Decomposes the task into an object-level planner (generates candidate release states for desired landing pose) and a robot-level planner (evaluates executability, constructs feasible swing motion). Uses release state as explicit intermediate representation for candidate filtering, adaptive configuration selection, and near-release motion design with approximately constant end-effector velocities.
AI.result: 90% success rate across 120 real-world trials with diverse objects varying in shape, size, and mass. Ablation studies confirm each design choice contributes to performance.
AI.conclusion: The framework achieves robust throw-flipping without prior data or learned models, enabling direct deployment on novel objects and targets without environment-specific calibration or data collection.

title: Diagnosing LLM Arbitration Behavior over Pre-evidence Epistemic States in RAG-based Fact-Checking
summary: In RAG-based fact-checking, LLMs are increasingly used as verifiers to check given claims against retrieved evidence. Their parametric knowledge can induce pre-evidence tendencies that may conflict with the retrieved context, yet existing evaluation frameworks do not characterize such prior-context discrepancy or measure how verifiers arbitrate between parametric and contextual signals. We introduce \textsc{PAVE} (\emph{Prior-Aware Verifier Evaluation}), a diagnostic testbed that stratifies an LLM verifier into four epistemic states based on the correctness and confidence of its pre-evidence prior and evaluates its arbitration behavior on this new benchmark, i.e., whether it persists in correct prior under misleading evidence, and whether it corrects wrong prior when accurate evidence is provided. Experiments across seven LLMs reveal unreliable and highly model-dependent prior-context arbitration, highlighting the importance of verifier selection for real-world RAG-based fact-checking applications. Based on these findings, we propose a lightweight JSD-based test-time arbitration method that improves factual reliability without modifying the underlying model, achieving competitive performance across diverse LLM families.

AI.tldr: PAVE is a diagnostic testbed that evaluates how LLM verifiers in RAG-based fact-checking arbitrate between their parametric prior knowledge and retrieved evidence, revealing unreliable and model-dependent arbitration, and proposes a lightweight JSD-based method to improve factual reliability.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluation frameworks for RAG-based fact-checking do not characterize the discrepancy between LLMs' pre-evidence prior knowledge and retrieved context, nor measure how verifiers arbitrate between parametric and contextual signals when they conflict.
AI.method: PAVE stratifies an LLM verifier into four epistemic states based on pre-evidence prior correctness and confidence, then evaluates arbitration behavior (persisting in correct prior under misleading evidence, correcting wrong prior with accurate evidence). A lightweight JSD-based test-time arbitration method is proposed to improve reliability.
AI.result: Experiments across seven LLMs reveal unreliable and highly model-dependent prior-context arbitration behavior.
AI.conclusion: Verifier selection is critical for real-world RAG-based fact-checking, and the proposed JSD-based method achieves competitive performance across diverse LLM families without modifying the underlying model.

title: Trans2Occ: Voxel Occupancy Estimation and Grasp for Transparent Objects from Simulation to Reality
summary: Transparent objects remain challenging for robotic perception due to unreliable depth sensing caused by refraction and reflection. While prior approaches rely on multi-view reconstruction or depth completion, they are often difficult to scale or deploy in real-world robotic systems. In this paper, we present a practical framework for transparent object perception and manipulation based on single-view RGB input. Our approach predicts voxel-space occupancy directly from a single image, providing a geometry-aware representation that supports downstream robotic grasping. To enable large-scale training, we construct a simulation pipeline that generates paired RGB images and voxel occupancy annotations under diverse materials and lighting conditions. We demonstrate that the predicted occupancy representation is robust to domain shifts and transfers effectively from simulation to real-world robotic setups without fine-tuning. A simple rule-based grasping strategy built on top of the occupancy further achieves reliable grasp performance on transparent objects. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real-world environments show that our framework provides accurate 3D understanding and enables practical manipulation of transparent objects. These results suggest that single-view occupancy prediction offers a scalable and effective solution for transparent object perception in robotics.

AI.tldr: A single-view RGB-based framework that predicts voxel-space occupancy to enable transparent object perception and manipulation, trained via simulation and transferred to real-world robots without fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Transparent objects are challenging for robotic perception due to unreliable depth sensing from refraction and reflection; prior multi-view or depth completion methods are difficult to scale or deploy in real-world robotic systems.
AI.method: (1) Predicts voxel-space occupancy directly from single-view RGB input; (2) Constructs a simulation pipeline generating paired RGB images and voxel occupancy annotations under diverse materials and lighting; (3) Employs a simple rule-based grasping strategy built on the predicted occupancy representation.
AI.result: The occupancy representation is robust to domain shifts and transfers from simulation to real-world robotic setups without fine-tuning; achieves reliable grasp performance on transparent objects in both simulated and real-world environments.
AI.conclusion: Single-view occupancy prediction offers a scalable and effective solution for transparent object perception in robotics, enabling practical manipulation without complex multi-view setups or depth completion.

title: SkillRevise: Improving LLM-Authored Agent Skills via Trace-Conditioned Skill Revision
summary: Agent skills are procedural artifacts that enable LLM agents to execute workflows, verify constraints, and recover from failures. Existing self-evolving methods refine skills using accumulated trajectories. However, they struggle in cold-start settings, where only an initial, imperfect skill is available. Consequently, skill construction defaults to expert authoring or one-shot LLM generation. Expert-authored skills are costly and may not align with how LLM agents actually execute tasks, while one-shot generated skills can be syntactically well formed yet behaviorally weak. To bridge this gap, we propose SkillRevise, an execution-grounded framework designed to iteratively refine these initial skills. SkillRevise diagnoses skill defects from execution evidence, retrieves relevant repair principles from a general memory, and applies execution-anchored edits. By re-executing candidates and measuring empirical utility, it systematically retains the optimal skill version. Evaluated across three benchmarks and five LLMs, SkillRevise substantially outperforms one-shot baselines, improving the base agent's success rate on SkillsBench from 36.05% to 61.63%. Furthermore, the revised skills exhibit strong cross-model transferability, capturing generalized procedural knowledge over model-specific artifacts.

AI.tldr: SkillRevise is an execution-grounded framework that iteratively refines initial LLM agent skills by diagnosing defects from execution evidence, retrieving repair principles from memory, and applying execution-anchored edits, improving success rates from 36.05% to 61.63% across benchmarks and LLMs, with strong cross-model transferability.
AI.motivation: Existing self-evolving skill refinement methods fail in cold-start settings with only imperfect initial skills, while alternatives (expert authoring or one-shot LLM generation) are either costly and misaligned with actual agent execution or syntactically correct yet behaviorally weak.
AI.method: SkillRevise iteratively refines skills through a three-step cycle: (1) diagnoses skill defects from execution evidence, (2) retrieves relevant repair principles from a general memory store, and (3) applies execution-anchored edits. It re-executes candidate revisions and measures empirical utility to retain the optimal skill version.
AI.result: Across three benchmarks and five LLMs, SkillRevise substantially outperforms one-shot baselines, improving the base agent's success rate on SkillsBench from 36.05% to 61.63%. Revised skills also demonstrate strong cross-model transferability, capturing generalized procedural knowledge beyond model-specific artifacts.
AI.conclusion: Execution-grounded iterative refinement effectively bridges the gap between costly expert-authored skills and behaviorally weak one-shot generated skills, producing robust, transferable agent skills from cold-start initial artifacts.

title: DisFlow: Scene Flow from Distance Field for Object Pose, Velocity Tracking, and Dynamic Object Reconstruction
summary: We present \emph{DisFlow}, a novel framework for online scene flow estimation from distance field that enables \emph{6DoF dynamic object pose estimation}, \emph{motion tracking}, and \emph{surface reconstruction}. The scene is represented by Gaussian Process Implicit Surfaces (GPIS), with surface normals serving as derivative constraints, enabling accurate signed distance computations near the surface and gradient queries with uncertainty. With this representation as a foundation, we compute a scene flow from the distance field that describes how surface points are transported over time in consecutive frames. Through our flow, we can estimate an object's pose and motion by incrementally registering a new observed point cloud via an elegant closed-form optimisation. Unlike prior methods that operate in the camera or world frame, our approach performs probabilistic fusion directly in the \emph{object frame}, where the object remains geometrically consistent over time. The tight coupling of the DisFlow method in space and time yields dense geometry, surface normals, object pose trajectories, velocities, and uncertainty, all at real-time rates. We evaluate DisFlow on dynamic object sequences and demonstrate that it achieves accurate pose and motion tracking while simultaneously reconstructing high-quality object surfaces. Code publicly available at \href{https://github.com/LanWu076/disflow_ros2}{https://github.com/LanWu076/disflow\_ros2}

AI.tldr: DisFlow is a real-time framework for online scene flow estimation using Gaussian Process Implicit Surfaces, enabling simultaneous 6DoF pose estimation, motion tracking, and surface reconstruction through probabilistic fusion in the object frame.
AI.motivation: To achieve tight coupling of geometry, pose, motion, and uncertainty estimation for dynamic objects in a single real-time framework, overcoming limitations of prior methods that operate in camera/world frames where objects are not geometrically consistent over time.
AI.method: Represents scenes using GPIS with surface normals as derivative constraints for accurate signed distances and gradient queries. Computes scene flow from the distance field to transport surface points across frames. Estimates object pose and motion via closed-form optimization by registering observed point clouds in the object frame, enabling probabilistic fusion where the object remains geometrically consistent.
AI.result: Achieves accurate pose and motion tracking while simultaneously reconstructing high-quality object surfaces at real-time rates, with dense geometry, surface normals, pose trajectories, velocities, and uncertainty estimates.
AI.conclusion: DisFlow provides a novel probabilistic framework that tightly couples spatial and temporal information for dynamic object understanding, outperforming prior methods by operating in the object frame for geometric consistency.

title: Reasoning4Sciences: Bridging Reasoning Language Models to All Scientific Branches
summary: While Reasoning Language Models (RLMs) are rapidly emerging as powerful tools for scientific research, their impact is primarily concentrated in "hard science" fields. The slow -- or lack of -- adoption of RLMs in other branches of science is causing a widening gap in research productivity. In this survey, we provide the first comprehensive analysis of RLM adoption across 28 scientific disciplines following the classification used by the European Research Council (ERC), spanning the Social Sciences and Humanities, Physical Sciences and Engineering, and Life Sciences. We examine how RLMs are developed, evaluated, and applied across disciplines. Furthermore, we introduce a maturity-oriented assessment framework based on available domain-specific development and evaluation resources, revealing substantial disparities in RLM maturity that become even more pronounced when only publicly available resources are considered. Finally, we highlight current implementation paradigms that are gaining popularity across disciplines, current challenges, and future directions in enabling RLM adoption across science.

AI.tldr: This survey analyzes the adoption of Reasoning Language Models (RLMs) across 28 scientific disciplines (based on ERC classification), finding significant disparities in maturity—especially when considering only publicly available resources—and highlighting the widening gap between "hard sciences" and other fields.
AI.motivation: RLMs are rapidly adopted in hard sciences but slowly or not at all in other branches of science, causing a widening gap in research productivity; the authors aim to provide the first comprehensive cross-disciplinary analysis of this disparity.
AI.method: The authors conduct a comprehensive survey across 28 scientific disciplines following the ERC classification (Social Sciences & Humanities, Physical Sciences & Engineering, Life Sciences), examining how RLMs are developed, evaluated, and applied; they introduce a maturity-oriented assessment framework based on domain-specific resources.
AI.result: Substantial disparities in RLM maturity across disciplines are revealed, which become even more pronounced when only publicly available resources are considered.
AI.conclusion: The paper highlights current implementation paradigms gaining popularity, ongoing challenges, and future directions for enabling broader RLM adoption across all scientific disciplines.

title: The Lie We Tell: Correcting the Euclidean Fallacy in Vision Language Action Policies via Score Matching on Tangent Space
summary: Diffusion-based Vision-Language-Action policies achieve remarkable success in robotic manipulation, yet commit a fundamental geometric error we term the $\textbf{Euclidean Fallacy}$: representing SE(3) poses as flat $\mathbb{R}^{12}$ vectors. This approximation induces (1) manifold drift violating SO(3) constraints, (2) broken equivariance under coordinate transformations, and (3) non-geodesic trajectories with excessive kinematic cost. We introduce $\textbf{Lie Diffuser Actor (LDA)}$, a diffusion framework operating intrinsically on SE(3). Our method injects noise through left-invariant SDEs, predicts scores in the tangent space, and retracts samples via the exponential map. This formulation eliminates manifold drift by construction while guaranteeing coordinate-frame equivariance and geodesic optimality. On CALVIN ABC$\rightarrow$D, LDA improves average task length from $3.27$ to $3.51$ ($+7.3\%$). We further validate our method on real robot and the results show that our methodology outperforms the baseline on majority tasks.

AI.tldr: Lie Diffuser Actor (LDA) is a diffusion-based policy framework that operates intrinsically on SE(3) to avoid the "Euclidean Fallacy" (treating poses as flat vectors), eliminating manifold drift, ensuring equivariance, and producing geodesic trajectories, achieving +7.3% improvement on CALVIN ABC→D and strong real-robot results.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion-based Vision-Language-Action policies represent SE(3) poses as flat ℝ¹² vectors, which introduces the "Euclidean Fallacy": manifold drift (violating SO(3) constraints), broken equivariance under coordinate transformations, and non-geodesic trajectories with excessive kinematic cost.
AI.method: LDA operates intrinsically on SE(3) by injecting noise through left-invariant stochastic differential equations (SDEs), predicting scores in the tangent space (Lie algebra), and retracting samples via the exponential map, thereby preserving the manifold structure throughout the diffusion process.
AI.result: On CALVIN ABC→D, LDA improves average task length from 3.27 to 3.51 (+7.3%). Real-robot validation shows LDA outperforms the baseline on the majority of tasks.
AI.conclusion: Operating diffusion policies directly on the SE(3) manifold (rather than Euclidean approximations) is both principled and practically beneficial, eliminating geometric errors while improving task completion and trajectory quality.

title: Expected Value Alignment for Generative Reward Modeling in Formal Mathematics Verification
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used with formal interactive theorem provers such as Lean 4. Scaling these systems with reinforcement learning or search methods requires process reward models (PRMs) that can evaluate intermediate reasoning steps. Existing reward-model designs expose a practical trade-off. Value-head models provide continuous scores but modify the generative model interface, while generative reward models preserve textual rationales but are poorly matched to continuous floating-point regression because numeric values are split across tokens. We introduce Expected Value Alignment (EVA), a reward-modeling procedure that keeps the surface output discrete while extracting continuous scores from the model's token distribution. The model emits integer scores in a structured JSON format, and EVA computes a continuous score as the expectation over the logits of the corresponding anchor tokens. Training combines the causal language modeling objective with an auxiliary mean squared error loss on these expected values. We instantiate EVA in \textit{Leibniz}, a reward model for Lean 4 formal verification, and evaluate it against zero-shot and reward-modeling baselines. The evaluation demonstrates that continuous logit-based scoring significantly reduces discretization artifacts while retaining the interpretability of generative critiques.

AI.tldr: EVA introduces a reward-modeling procedure that extracts continuous scores from token logits while maintaining discrete outputs, instantiated as Leibniz for Lean 4 formal verification, reducing discretization artifacts while preserving interpretability.
AI.motivation: Existing reward-model designs for LLMs used with interactive theorem provers face a trade-off: value-head models modify the generative model interface, while generative reward models struggle with continuous floating-point regression due to token-level splitting of numeric values.
AI.method: EVA emits integer scores in structured JSON format, computes a continuous score as the expectation over logits of corresponding anchor tokens, and trains with both causal language modeling objective and auxiliary mean squared error loss on expected values.
AI.result: Continuous logit-based scoring significantly reduces discretization artifacts while retaining the interpretability of generative critiques, as evaluated against zero-shot and reward-modeling baselines in Lean 4 formal verification.
AI.conclusion: EVA effectively bridges the gap between discrete generative outputs and continuous scoring needs, offering a practical solution for process reward modeling in formal theorem proving environments.

title: PHASOR: Phase-Anchored Universal Action Representations for Humanoid Embodiments
summary: Learning a good action embedding space is fundamental to scalable robot policy learning, yet existing methods treat action latents as task-specific intermediates rather than first-class representations. The resulting latents are unstructured, embodiment-specific, and weakly tied to motion semantics, limiting interpretability, controllability, and transferability across robots. We position the action embedding space itself as a first-class design target, with downstream policy quality emerging from representation quality. Exploiting motion's intrinsic periodicity, we factorize it into a phase manifold that captures cyclic structure via FFT-parametric coefficients, together with a pose branch that conditions the manifold on non-periodic configuration detail. Combined with motion-semantic distillation, this factorized structure yields a cross-embodiment motion manifold that is interpretable and embodiment-agnostic by design. Anchoring multiple humanoid robots to a shared human-pretrained manifold then produces a unified action embedding space across diverse platforms, achieving strong cross-embodiment retrieval and consistent gains on downstream robot tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes treating action embedding spaces as first-class representations for robot learning, using a factorized phase-pose structure with motion-semantic distillation to create a cross-embodiment motion manifold that enables transfer across diverse humanoid robots.
AI.motivation: Existing action latent spaces are unstructured, embodiment-specific, and weakly tied to motion semantics, which limits interpretability, controllability, and transferability across robots. The authors argue that downstream policy quality emerges from representation quality, motivating action embeddings as first-class design targets.
AI.method: Exploiting motion's periodicity, the method factorizes action embeddings into: (1) a phase manifold capturing cyclic structure via FFT-parametric coefficients, and (2) a pose branch conditioning the manifold on non-periodic configuration details. Motion-semantic distillation is applied to make the space interpretable and embodiment-agnostic. Multiple humanoid robots are anchored to a shared human-pretrained manifold.
AI.result: The approach produces a unified action embedding space across diverse humanoid platforms, achieving strong cross-embodiment retrieval performance and consistent gains on downstream robot tasks.
AI.conclusion: Factorizing motion into periodic phase structure and non-periodic pose details, combined with semantic distillation, yields an interpretable, embodiment-agnostic action manifold that improves cross-robot transfer and policy learning.

title: Deft Scheduling of Dynamic Cloud Workflows with Varying Deadlines via Mixture-of-Experts
comment: This paper has been accepted by the Fourteenth International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2026)
summary: Workflow scheduling in cloud computing demands the intelligent allocation of dynamically arriving, graph-structured workflows with varying deadlines onto ever-changing virtual machine resources. However, existing deep reinforcement learning (DRL) schedulers remain limited by rigid, single-path inference architectures that struggle to handle diverse scheduling scenarios. We introduce \textbf{DEFT} (\textbf{D}eadline-p\textbf{E}rceptive Mixture-o\textbf{F}-Exper\textbf{t}s), an innovative DRL policy architecture that leverages a specialized mixture of experts, each trained to manage different levels of deadline tightness. To our knowledge, DEFT is the first to introduce and validate a Mixture-of-Experts architecture for dynamic cloud workflow scheduling. By adaptively routing decisions through the most appropriate experts, DEFT is capable of meeting a broad spectrum of deadline requirements that no single expert can achieve. Central to DEFT is a \textbf{graph-adaptive} gating mechanism that encodes workflow deadlines and DAGs, task states, and VM conditions, using cross-attention to guide expert activation in a fine-grained, deadline-sensitive manner. Experiments on dynamic cloud workflow benchmarks demonstrate that DEFT significantly reduces execution cost and deadline violations, outperforming multiple state-of-the-art DRL baselines.

AI.tldr: DEFT introduces a Mixture-of-Experts DRL policy architecture with a graph-adaptive gating mechanism for dynamic cloud workflow scheduling, significantly reducing cost and deadline violations compared to state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing DRL schedulers for cloud workflow scheduling rely on rigid, single-path inference architectures that struggle to handle diverse scheduling scenarios with varying deadline requirements.
AI.method: DEFT employs a Mixture-of-Experts architecture where each expert is trained to manage different levels of deadline tightness, with a graph-adaptive gating mechanism that encodes workflow deadlines, DAGs, task states, and VM conditions using cross-attention to guide expert activation in a deadline-sensitive manner.
AI.result: Experiments on dynamic cloud workflow benchmarks show that DEFT significantly reduces execution cost and deadline violations, outperforming multiple state-of-the-art DRL baselines.
AI.conclusion: DEFT is the first to introduce and validate a Mixture-of-Experts architecture for dynamic cloud workflow scheduling, demonstrating that adaptive routing through deadline-specialized experts can meet a broad spectrum of deadline requirements that no single expert can achieve.

title: Set-Supervised Diffusion Policy: Learning Action-Chunking Diffusion through Corrections
summary: Diffusion policies have recently emerged as a powerful framework for robotic manipulation. However, like other behavior cloning methods, they remain vulnerable to distributional shift, often requiring human-in-the-loop interventions to correct failures during deployment. These interactions naturally provide paired supervision in the form of the robot's undesired actions and the human teacher's corrective actions. Yet existing data aggregation pipelines and standard behavior cloning losses largely ignore this negative signal from undesired actions, leading to overfitting to teacher's actions and an increasing reliance on costly expert data. To address this limitation, we propose Set-Supervised Diffusion Policy (SDP), a novel learning framework that utilizes contrastive action-chunk data to train diffusion policies from human corrections. From paired positive and negative action-chunks, SDP constructs a set of desired action-chunks and designs a training pipeline that encourages the diffusion policy to align with the set. Through extensive experiments across multiple robotic manipulation tasks, we demonstrate that SDP consistently improves policy performance, with particularly strong gains in robustness to noisy data. Moreover, SDP induces high-quality aggregated datasets, enabling more efficient and reliable policy learning from human-in-the-loop corrections. Our code is available at https://set-supervised-diffusion-policy.github.io/.

AI.tldr: Set-Supervised Diffusion Policy (SDP) is a novel learning framework that trains diffusion policies from human corrections by using contrastive action-chunk data with positive and negative examples, improving robustness and reducing reliance on costly expert data in robotic manipulation.
AI.motivation: Diffusion policies for robotic manipulation suffer from distributional shift and rely on human-in-the-loop interventions. Existing pipelines ignore the negative signal from undesired actions, leading to overfitting to teacher actions and increasing dependence on costly expert data.
AI.method: SDP constructs sets of desired action-chunks from paired positive and negative action-chunks obtained via human corrections, and trains diffusion policies to align with the desired set using a contrastive learning pipeline.
AI.result: SDP consistently improves policy performance across multiple robotic manipulation tasks, with strong gains in robustness to noisy data, and induces high-quality aggregated datasets for more efficient policy learning.
AI.conclusion: SDP effectively leverages negative signal from human corrections to improve diffusion policy learning, reducing reliance on costly expert data and enhancing robustness to distributional shift.

title: "Skill issues'': data-centric optimization of lakehouse agents
summary: Coding agents are becoming users of data infrastructure, but their success depends not only on model quality: it also depends on the skills and environment files that teach agents how to use a system. We study how to optimize these artifacts for agents operating on a branching lakehouse, Bauplan. In our setting, headless APIs and Git-like data primitives expose data workflows through code, branches, commits, and merges. Our central observation is that a branching lakehouse turns data-agent evaluation from an output-matching problem into a state-verification problem: agent-generated pipeline code induces concrete, inspectable lakehouse changes. We present a data-centric optimization pipeline that generates task-verifier pairs, executes candidate skills in isolated sandboxes, and scores trajectories using both trace-level signals and programmatic checks over lakehouse state. In a preliminary evaluation on 25 tasks, optimized skills improve accuracy by 31.9%. These results suggest that write-path data workflows provide a useful substrate for optimizing agent skills beyond read-only tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper studies optimizing skills and environment files for coding agents operating on a branching lakehouse (Bauplan), showing that a data-centric optimization pipeline improves accuracy by 31.9% by treating agent evaluation as a state-verification problem rather than an output-matching problem.
AI.motivation: Coding agents' success depends not only on model quality but also on skills and environment files that teach agents how to use a system; the paper aims to optimize these artifacts for agents operating on a branching lakehouse.
AI.method: A data-centric optimization pipeline that generates task-verifier pairs, executes candidate skills in isolated sandboxes, and scores trajectories using trace-level signals and programmatic checks over lakehouse state.
AI.result: On 25 tasks, optimized skills improve accuracy by 31.9%.
AI.conclusion: Write-path data workflows provide a useful substrate for optimizing agent skills beyond read-only tasks; a branching lakehouse turns data-agent evaluation from output-matching into state-verification.

title: Closed-Form Pose Estimation of Endoluminal Medical Devices via Gradiometer-Based Electromagnetic Localization System
summary: Embedded magnetic tracking holds highly attractive prospects for remote navigation of endoluminal medical devices. However, existing six-degree-of-freedom pose recovery approaches often require pre-calibrated workspace field maps or iterative nonlinear optimization. This letter presents a Gradiometer-Based Electromagnetic Localization System (GELS), a closed-form tracking framework that uses a compact magnetometer array as an embedded quasi-gradiometer to estimate local magnetic fields and gradient tensors. These quantities are mapped by the Euler homogeneous relation to displacements between source and array, from which multi-source Procrustes registration recovers the array orientation and position using at least three non-collinear sources. The algorithm requires known source positions and array geometry, but no pre-calibrated workspace field maps, initial pose guesses, or calibrated excitation-source moments. The recovered pose also enables a proof-of-concept sub-level dipole localization task by serving as a mobile magnetic reference frame. Benchtop experiments across sensor-array configurations and excitation modes demonstrate sequence-averaged position errors of \SI{10.80}{\milli\meter}--\SI{15.57}{\milli\meter}, a fastest update rate of \SI{14.49}{\hertz}, and a median solver runtime of \SI{172.00}{\micro\second}. A perturbation-based error propagation analysis further identifies inter-sensor inconsistency and dipole-model mismatch as the dominant accuracy limits, thereby informing future sensor array and magnetic source design for further reducing pose-estimation error.

AI.tldr: The paper presents GELS, a closed-form electromagnetic tracking framework using a compact magnetometer array as a quasi-gradiometer. It recovers 6-DOF pose via Euler's homogeneous relation and multi-source Procrustes registration without needing pre-calibrated field maps or initial guesses. Benchtop experiments show position errors of 10.80–15.57 mm, update rate up to 14.49 Hz, and median solver runtime of 172 µs. Error analysis identifies inter-sensor inconsistency and dipole-model mismatch as dominant accuracy limits.
AI.motivation: To enable remote navigation of endoluminal medical devices via embedded magnetic tracking, while overcoming the limitations of existing methods that require pre-calibrated workspace field maps or iterative nonlinear optimization.
AI.method: Uses a compact magnetometer array as an embedded quasi-gradiometer to estimate local magnetic fields and gradient tensors. The Euler homogeneous relation maps these quantities to displacements between source and array. Multi-source Procrustes registration recovers array orientation and position using at least three non-collinear sources. The algorithm requires known source positions and array geometry but no pre-calibrated field maps, initial pose guesses, or calibrated source moments.
AI.result: Sequence-averaged position errors of 10.80–15.57 mm across sensor-array configurations and excitation modes, a fastest update rate of 14.49 Hz, and a median solver runtime of 172 µs. A proof-of-concept sub-level dipole localization task is demonstrated using the recovered pose as a mobile magnetic reference frame.
AI.conclusion: Inter-sensor inconsistency and dipole-model mismatch are the dominant accuracy limits. These findings inform future sensor array and magnetic source design to further reduce pose-estimation error.

title: The Case for Model Science: Verify, Explore, Steer, Refine
summary: We argue that the AI community is now ready to move beyond benchmarking and consolidate scattered efforts in model analysis into a systematic discipline, a direction we term Model Science. Complex AI models now serve billions of users, yet our understanding of how they work lags far behind our ability to deploy them. Decades of benchmark-driven research have delivered remarkable progress: extensive leaderboards, a wide range of performance metrics, tracking capability gains across diverse tasks; yet this success has also revealed the limits of benchmarks as they tell us whether models perform but not why they succeed or fail, they miss critical failure modes, such as hallucinations or shortcuts. Precedents from established sciences point the way forward: cognitive science shows that understanding complex systems requires complementary levels of analysis; neuroscience demonstrates that deep study of single cases reveals what population studies miss; medicine teaches that specialised training must develop alongside research practice; and agriculture models how shared infrastructure and principles enable cumulative progress. These lessons inform three foundations for Model Science. First, we propose to consolidate research around four functional perspectives: Verify, Explore, Steer, and Refine that address complementary questions about model behaviour. Second, we discuss the required infrastructure for cumulative knowledge: catalogues of datasets, models and findings. Third, we highlight the need for deep analysis of individual model instances, not just model families, because single cases can reveal what population studies miss.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes transitioning from benchmark-driven evaluation to "Model Science" — a systematic discipline for understanding AI models through four functional perspectives (Verify, Explore, Steer, Refine), shared infrastructure for cumulative knowledge, and deep case-by-case analysis of individual model instances.
AI.motivation: Benchmark-driven research has revealed its limits: it tells us whether models perform but not why they succeed or fail, and misses critical failure modes like hallucinations or shortcuts. The AI community needs a more systematic approach to understanding complex models that now serve billions of users.
AI.method: The paper draws precedents from established sciences (cognitive science, neuroscience, medicine, agriculture) to inform three foundations: (1) four functional perspectives (Verify, Explore, Steer, Refine) for complementary analysis; (2) shared infrastructure including catalogues of datasets, models and findings; (3) deep analysis of individual model instances beyond model families.
AI.result: The paper proposes a framework called Model Science to consolidate scattered model analysis efforts into a systematic discipline, moving beyond benchmarks toward understanding why models behave as they do.
AI.conclusion: The AI community is ready to move beyond benchmarking toward Model Science, a systematic discipline for understanding AI models through complementary analytical perspectives, shared infrastructure, and deep case-level analysis.

title: Learning Action-Conditional and Object-Centric Gaussian Splatting World Models for Rigid Objects
summary: World models enable intelligent agents to predict the consequences of their actions on the environment. In this paper, we propose Multi Rigid Object Gaussian World Model (MRO-GWM), a novel model that learns action-conditional dynamics of rigid objects in 3D. By representing the scene by object-centric Gaussians, we can represent arbitrary object shapes and multi-object scenes. We develop a novel spatio-temporal transformer architecture that predicts future rigid body motion from a history of object Gaussians and future actions. Objects are represented by their Gaussians in a canonical frame, which allows for describing object motion as rigid body transformation. Our model is trained on reconstructions from multiple viewpoints, which requires the model to handle partial observations of objects due to occlusions. We analyze prediction performance of our approach on synthetic datasets composed of typical household objects with multi-object dynamics and interactions by a robot end effector. We also evaluate our model in model-predictive control for non-prehensile manipulation in simulation.

AI.tldr: MRO-GWM is a 3D world model that represents scenes with object-centric Gaussians and uses a spatio-temporal transformer to predict rigid body motion from history and future actions, enabling action-conditional dynamics prediction and model-predictive control for non-prehensile manipulation.
