AI.tldr: This paper introduces the "last-mile forecasting" problem—the underexplored stage of revising statistical forecasts using weakly structured business context—and presents an LLM-agent framework that sits atop a forecasting backbone to produce decision-ready forecasts through tool-based evidence retrieval, reasoning-to-action conversion, structural safety constraints, long-horizon decomposition, and reflective memory.
AI.motivation: Statistical forecasts alone are rarely business-ready; they require revision using weakly structured contextual information (e.g., holidays, campaigns, events, expert feedback). This practical stage is largely overlooked in forecasting literature, motivating a systematic framework to bridge statistical prediction and decision-ready forecasting.
AI.method: An LLM-agent framework built on top of any forecasting backbone. It maintains a unified forecast workspace, invokes tools to retrieve contextual evidence, converts reasoning trajectories into explicit forecast revision actions under structural safety constraints, supports long-horizon forecasting via map-reduce-style decomposition, and enables post-hoc reflection through a memory bank.
AI.result: Through real-world case studies, the system demonstrates that LLM agents can effectively bridge the gap between statistical prediction and business-ready forecasting, producing controllable and auditable forecast revisions.
AI.conclusion: The last-mile forecasting problem is a critical yet underexplored stage; the proposed LLM-agent framework offers a controllable, auditable solution for converting statistical forecasts into decision-ready outputs using business context, with demonstrated effectiveness in real-world settings.

title: SafeSteer: Localized On-Policy Distillation for Efficient Safety Alignment
comment: 19 pages, 8 figures, 14 tables. Submitted to EMNLP 2026
summary:
Aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) with human values often degrades their general capabilities, termed the alignment tax. Existing methods mitigate this by balancing dual objectives, which heavily rely on massive general-purpose data or auxiliary reward models.
  In this paper, we argue that, because safety features are inherently sparse within the output distribution, alignment requires localized modifications rather than global trade-offs. To this end, we propose SafeSteer, which performs on-policy distillation confined to safety tokens. First, we construct a safety teacher via activation steering. Based on this teacher, we develop a safety token selection algorithm. Consequently, SafeSteer restricts the reverse KL penalty to these tokens during training to preserve general capabilities.
  Experimental results across diverse models show that our SafeSteer achieves a superior trade-off between safety and general capability compared with existing methods, attaining strong safety performance on seven safety benchmarks with only minimal degradation on five general capability benchmarks. Notably, SafeSteer requires only 100 harmful samples without using any general-purpose data, less than 1% of what previous baselines used, considerably reducing alignment cost. More details are on our project page at https://anjingkun.github.io/SafeSteer.

AI.tldr: SafeSteer proposes a method to align LLMs with human values by localizing modifications to safety tokens only, using on-policy distillation from a safety teacher built via activation steering. It achieves strong safety with minimal capability degradation using only 100 harmful samples (less than 1% of prior methods' data).
AI.motivation: The alignment tax (degradation of general capabilities during safety alignment) is costly to mitigate because existing methods require massive general-purpose data or auxiliary reward models. The authors argue that since safety features are sparse in the output distribution, only localized modifications are needed.
AI.method: SafeSteer first constructs a safety teacher via activation steering, then develops a safety token selection algorithm to identify safety-relevant tokens. During training, it applies on-policy distillation with reverse KL penalty restricted to these identified safety tokens, preserving general capabilities elsewhere.
AI.result: SafeSteer achieves superior safety-performance trade-off across seven safety benchmarks with minimal degradation on five general capability benchmarks. It requires only 100 harmful samples (less than 1% of data needed by prior baselines), significantly reducing alignment cost.
AI.conclusion: Safety alignment can be efficiently achieved through localized, token-level modifications rather than global trade-offs, substantially reducing data requirements and capability degradation.

title: Tracking the Behavioral Trajectories of Adapting Agents
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure. To appear at the Second Workshop on Agents in the Wild: Safety, Security, and Beyond (AIWILD) at ICML 2026
summary: Text files such as skill files, memory files, and behavioral configuration files play a central role in defining how modern agents act. Through edits by humans or the agents themselves, these files may evolve over time, directly steering the agent's behavior in future interactions. We present a methodology and framework for measuring agent $traits$ by defining traits as directions in the embedding space of a text embedding model. We train a linear model on labeled "before" versus "after" skill file diffs to learn a trait vector, then score arbitrary skill edits by projecting their embedding diffs onto this vector. Evaluated on 68 labeled skill diff pairs for the trait of propensity to seek sensitive data, our method achieves 91.2% sign classification accuracy and a Spearman rank correlation of $ρ= 0.82$ under leave-one-out cross-validation. We build this trait evaluation into a broader agent-to-agent protocol that enables one agent to evaluate another's skill file updates through a trusted intermediary.

AI.tldr: A method to measure agent traits by representing them as directions in embedding space, applied to skill file edits. Achieves 91.2% accuracy in classifying propensity to seek sensitive data, and integrates the evaluation into an agent-to-agent protocol.
AI.motivation: Text files (skill, memory, behavioral config) evolve via edits by humans or agents themselves, directly steering future agent behavior. Measuring how these edits change agent traits (e.g., propensity to seek sensitive data) is important but lacks a principled methodology.
AI.method: Define traits as directions in a text embedding model's space. Train a linear model on labeled "before" vs "after" skill file diffs to learn a trait vector. Score new skill edits by projecting their embedding diffs onto this vector. Validate with 68 labeled skill diff pairs using leave-one-out cross-validation.
AI.result: 91.2% sign classification accuracy and Spearman rank correlation ρ=0.82 for the trait of propensity to seek sensitive data, under leave-one-out cross-validation.
AI.conclusion: The trait vector approach effectively measures behavioral changes from skill edits. The framework is built into an agent-to-agent protocol where one agent can evaluate another's skill file updates via a trusted intermediary.

title: ClinEnv: An Interactive Multi-Stage Long Horizon EHR Environment for Agents
summary: Clinical practice is not the selection of an answer from enumerated options: a physician gathers heterogeneous information incrementally and commits to sequential, irreversible decisions under uncertainty. Static benchmarks cannot probe and existing interactive medical benchmarks each compromise on at least one of them. We present ClinEnv, an interactive benchmark that evaluates LLMs as attending physicians over real inpatient admissions under a paradigm we term Longitudinal Inpatient Simulation. Each case is automatically constructed into an ordered sequence of decision stages; at every stage the model must actively query four specialized agents before committing to medications, procedures, and diagnoses. ClinEnv scores both what the model decides, through deterministic ontology-grounded matching, and how it gathers information. Across seven models, the strongest reaches only 0.31 decision F1, and outcome quality is sharply decoupled from process quality. Difficulty concentrates in management decisions and later stages, where models recover discharge diagnoses far more reliably than management actions (0.51 vs. 0.17 F1) and continue to issue redundant queries as cases progress. ClinEnv makes this information-acquisition gap, invisible to outcome-only evaluation, directly measurable.

AI.tldr: ClinEnv is an interactive benchmark that evaluates LLMs as attending physicians using Longitudinal Inpatient Simulation, where models must query specialized agents and make sequential decisions across real inpatient cases. The best model achieves only 0.31 decision F1, with a large gap between outcome quality and process quality, especially in management decisions (0.17 F1) vs. diagnosis recovery (0.51 F1).
AI.motivation: Existing medical benchmarks fail to capture the incremental, irreversible, and uncertainty-laden nature of real clinical decision-making; static benchmarks cannot probe this, and prior interactive benchmarks each compromise on key aspects.
AI.method: ClinEnv constructs real inpatient admissions into ordered decision stages; at each stage, the LLM must query four specialized agents before committing to medications, procedures, and diagnoses. Scoring covers both ontology-grounded decision correctness (decision F1) and information acquisition quality (process quality).
AI.result: Best model achieves 0.31 decision F1; diagnosis recovery (0.51 F1) far exceeds management action recovery (0.17 F1); models issue redundant queries as cases progress; outcome quality is sharply decoupled from process quality.
AI.conclusion: ClinEnv reveals an information-acquisition gap invisible to outcome-only evaluation, highlighting that LLMs' clinical process quality (especially in management decisions) critically lags behind outcome-based metrics.
